div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS,
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS,

THE person who is always talking to himself ia linre to have an interested listener. SPEAR; what you think, be what you are, and pay your debts of all kit-la.—Emerson. "Bat why do you weep? The acting is certainly not so touching." " Excuse me, lam bewailing the money I paid to come WE believe it was a well-meaning citizen who alleged as a reason for not wishing to live on a hill that the climb-it did not suit him. ON the piazza—" Are you going to drive this lovely afternoon, Mrs. Goldhug " "Faith, and 01 Sin? With me son's new tantram I " SOME one, referring to a very fat minister said, "If he leaves the congregation it will be a great loss, and if he dies it will he a dead loss." FRIENDSHIP —Mr. H.—" I think Miss Robin has one of the best voices I have ever heard." Miss Z. —"She certainly has, or it would have been worn out years ago." SAID Juliana to Augustus—" Do you really think that a miss is as good as a mile?" "Yes, Miss Juliana, and a great deal better, for one Cln kiss a miss, but whoever heard of anyone kissing a mile 7 " "MY son, av&d this road to vice, lest some day you might love it; be wise and take your pa's advice. I've seen the folly of it." "Pop! right you are, but boys like we are smarter than were you. Bes,ides, dear pop, I want to see the folly of it too." BOB—" I say, Sam, why did von jilt her?" Sam —" Oh, hang it she lisped 1"" Well, that is a charming detect in a pretty girl." "If you heard her say thweet Tham, instead of sweet Sam, you would'nt wonder." "Why, I never had any diffi- culty that way. She used to call me darling Bob." Miss LIGHTED—"I was very much admired at the wedding reception last night: I noticed one gentleman who never took his eyes off me the whole evening." Miss Sharpe—" Did the gentleman have a black meustache, waxed on the ends 2" "Yes; • do you know him 7" "I know of him. He is a detective, lie was there to watch the presents.' OLD. LOVER—"I know lam old enough to be Tour grandfather, but, my darling, I have an im- mense fortune to bestow upon you." Young heart—" I hesitate to answer." Old lover—" Do not keep me in suspense. I have heart disease, and under excitement I am likely to die at any moment." Young heart—" Then I will be yours." LORD NEWTON, one of the Scotch judges, was seen by a friend staggering homewards so early as nine o'clock on a fine summer evening in Edinburgh. "How now ?" Tie :led the individual. "You're early up from your dinner the day." "True enough," . Muttered the Judge; "but, than, ye maun ken that we sat down yestreen.'• BOBBY has been playing on the porch while his mother was calling within. She suddenly appears at door with hostess, ready to take her leave, when Bobby burst into tears and cries—" Mamma, ain't you going to stay to lunch?" "No, dear," " Boo— hoo—hoo—well, you said you would—boo—boo— hoo." (Painful silence followed by rapid leave- taking). A LATE judge, whose personal appearance was as unprepossessing as his legal knowledge was profound and his intellect keen, interrupted a female witness —" Hunsbugged you, my good woman. What do you mean by that ?" he said, sternly. "I don't know bow to explain it exactly; nut if a girl called your Lordship a handsome man she would be humbug- ging you." GAR RICK was once accosted on the street in Lon- don by a man in rags with "Hallo., Garrick, don't you know me?" "I do not," replied the actor. "Strange," said the tattered man, "we acted to- gether at the Drury Lane Theatre.' "Impossible," replied Garrick; "in what play 7 " "In 'Hamlet.' I took the part of the cock, and crowed three times behind the curtain." STRoNG ENouGH.—A horticultural journal ad- vises: "Plant an onion beside a rosebush and in- crease its odour." But who wants the odour of the onion increased? That esculent is fragrant enough for culinary purposes. AN AGLICULTVRAL CONUNDRUM. A farm journal asks: "Why do the young rush to the -towns and cities?" The answer is easy enough. It is because they are anxious to get there. And the fact that there are no farms in the city may have something to do with it. WHAT IT LACKED.—" Yes, my brother Tom has a pretty fine iwuse," said the Western man, on a visit East; "but he had some queer ideas about furnishing his parlour. It is full of pictures, bric-a- brac. expensive carpe's, fine rugs, and all that sort of thing, but there is not a spittoon to be seen. I had to raise a window and throw a quid of tobacco into the streets. IT :MIGHT HAVE FLA,PPENED.—ACCOrdhIg tO a news item, "A man in 6hanereville declares that his wife is a witch, and that be can see her flying around the room astride of a broom." When a man comes home in a demoralized condition, as this Shanersville man evidently does, his wife generally flies around with a broom—but not astride of it. GOING TO COURT.—" A country juryman, aged 70 years, walked twenty-five miles to court," read Dahlman, in the daily paper. "What a lively and susceptible old chap he must have been," he com- mented. "I wouldn't walk twenty-five miles to court if the girl's father was a millionaire, and I've not yet reached thirty years." AN ExcurerloN TO HIS OWN RULE.—Jones : AlWays be honest and truthful, and you are bound to prosper. Brown: I suppo,e you are right. You always lived up to this pie uciple, I believe? Jones: I have endeavoured to. Brown: And you are not worth a hundred pounds? Jones: My dear sir, you must be aware that there are exceptions to ail

rules. A LARGE CIVIL LlST.—Mistress : Bridget, I told you the other day that I did't object to you giving your cousin a meal when he comes, but I find you feeding the policeman, the butcher's boy, the grocer's boy, the milkman, three hustlers from the next street, and the ashman. Bridget: Shure 0211111, they're all my cousins 1 LOST SARCASll.—Sarcastlo Father—" Julia, that young man Bmiley has been here three nights in succession, and it has been nearly midnight when he left. Hadn't you better invite him to bring has trunk and make his home with us?" Innocent Daughter—" Oh, papa! may I? It is just what he wanted, but was too bashful to ask you. Nell be delighted when I tell him this evening. WHY HE KEPT LATE HOURS.—"Say, grandpa," said his fourteen•year-old grandson, "you are eighty years old, and still as lively as a cricket. I s'pose when you were a young man you took good care of your health—went to bed with the chickens and got.up with the lark. 'Early to bed and early to rise' was your motto?" "No, my boy," said grandpa. "I didn't follow that maxim. I went to bed at 4 a.m., and didn't get up until noon." " Gracious! you must have been a wild one, grandpa 1" "No. I was night editor on a morning paper." THE famous Dr. John Brown, the commentator, experienced a full share of the world's vicissitudes. At Duns, on one occasion, when his funds were low, he entered a shop to invest in the luxury of a halfpennyworth of cheese! The shopman declared his inability to accommodate him with so small a portion. "Then what's the least you can sell? in- quired the dootor. "A. pennyworth," replied the dealer, and instantly set about weighing that quantity, which he speedily placed on the counter in anticipation of payment. "Now," said the doctor, taking up the knife, "I will instruct you how to sell a halfpennyworth of cheese in future S" upon which he cat the modicum in two, and, ap- propriating the half, paid down his copper and departed. SPEAKING of the pioneers in electrical applica- tion who have reaped golden harvests, Progreesive Age (an American paper) says Professor A. G. Bell was at one time walking about Washington anxious to sell telephone stock for ten cents. on the dollar. Before thgt he was teaching a deaf and dumb school in Boston. The telephone brought him fame and riches, and he has now an income of hundreds of dollars a day and a fortune of 6,000,000 dollars. O. F. Brush is said to have been working at 15 dollars a week before he struck the electric light which made him a millionaire. • OLD MAID (sin,ing)—" I would I were a bird!" Bad boy—" I know one bird you can't be!" Old maid—" What is that, you wicked thing?" Bad boy—" A chicken. I heard dad say you were no chicken, yesterday."

Dr. Maclagan, the Bishop of Lichfield, who has been offered the vacant Archbishopric of York, is a thin, wiry-looking man, rather below the medium size. Although in his sixty-fifth year the erect bearing of the Bishop is evidence of a former mili- tary training, Dr. Maclagan, before he entered the ministry, having served in the East India Com- pany's army, where he attained the rank of captain.

Mr. Howorth finds encouragement from the results of the last three elections, which have shown that the rural voters do not rise to the Tory bait of free education, to return to the charge of inconsistency against his colleagues. It seems that the Tories have put the parsons in a pitiful position. They are secretly in revolt, as Mr. Howarth is con- vinced from the budget of letters he receives, but they cannot openly oppose the scheme.

Mr. Leon is proving to be a popular candidate in North Bucks. The Tories are importing a host of M.P.'s to support Mr. Hubbard, whose "personal and family claims "'are considered by his supporters to be an important point in his favour. Mr. Leon does not rely on personal or family claims, but on his programme. The allotment question will have an important bearing on the contest, and Mr. Leon's sturdy advocacy of a system of allotments which would bring new life to the village and bring back the people to the land will secure -him the votes of the labourers.

Latest about the Allotments Act. One hundred 1 and six labourers at Wells (Norfolk) applied to the Earl of Leicester for thirty-three acres of his land for allotments. After negotiation through the sanitary authority the land was offered at a rent of £2 Ss. 6d. per acre. This is just double the average agricultural rent in the neighbourhood. The County Council was invoked on behalf of the applicants, and a sub-committee endeavoured to get the rent reduced, but in vain. Such is the demand for allot- ments that some of the men are now taking small plots at the rent demanded. Truly the Tory Allot- ments Act is a grand measure—for the landlords.

Mr. Gladstone's illness has interrupted the paint- ing of the right hon, gentleman's portrait by Mr. J. C. Forbes, a clever Toronto artist, who has re- ceived a commission for the work from a committee of the leading Liberals of Canada. When completed it is to be presented to the National Liberal Club, and a replica is ordered for the hall of the Domin- ion Parliament at Ottawa. A portrait of the late Earl Granville is also being painted for the Nation- al Liberal Club by another artist. Mr. Forbes has painted successful portraits of Lord Dufferin, Sir John Macdonald, the Canadian Premier, and the Hon. E. Blake, the former Liberal leader.

Another Congress this week is the Labour Elec- toral Congress, meeting in Westminster Hall. The , object of the Labour Electoral Association is to pro- mote the return of labour representatives to Par- liament and to local bodies. It has been the means of electing a number of labour candidates on School Boards and County Councils, and eight labour can- didates now seeking Parliamentary honours have its support. The Congress on Monday passed re- solutions advocating:payment of members by the State, and of the returning officer's charges out ot the rates—two reforms which must be obtained be- fore labour can have many direct representatives in I Parliament.

A German contemporary says the golden time with hairdressers in Germany is iio more. Fashion with ladies headdresses renders unnecessary the artistic skill of the barber, as in the new Grecian " frisur " but little false hair is needed. The so- called "golden time" lay in the manipulation of the long, pendant " zopfe," or " olats," a pair of which often cost a lady as much as £2O. Some Berlin hairdressers, it is asserted, in the short space of eight years have acquired fortunes. But the ! business now barely covers expenses. Fashion is at present satisfied with the natural hair gathered up into the Grecian knot, or the high comb of the I Japanese ladies' headdress.

The abdication of King Charles of Portugal may, I bear, be expected at any moment. Although not yet thirty, he has grown so unwieldy as to be almost unable to move; and he wholly lacks both the energy and peculiar tact which made Dom Luis, his father, so popular with his subjects. King .Charles deeply offended the Portuguese by what they describe as his " unseemly levity" during the pompous funeral ceremonies of his father, and they entertain a rooted belief that their present Sovereign (who is, like the King of the Belgians, one of the lucky Dukes of Saxony) is entirely under the influence and sway of his near relative Queen Victoria.

The reason of the attendance of Mr. Matthews at Sheen House is to be found in the fact that the newly-born princess is in the direct line of succes- sion. At the time of the marriage of the Princess Louise with the Duke of Fife there was some talk about her renouncing her claims to the succession, but such an act would have been contrary to all precedent, and tantamount to a declaration that she had contracted a quasi-morganatic marriage. As matters stand the child who. made her appear- ance on Sunday morning stands fifth in the order of succession, the Prince of Wales, the Duke of , Clarence, Prince George of Wales, and her own mother coming before her. • It will be long before 1 p,.ople will realise that the ever-youthful Princess of Wales is indeed a grandmother.

Sir William Fraser tells some amusing stories of I Airs. Disraeli in his new book. That lady was cer- tainly the most comical spouse that a great man ever had. Mrs. Malaprop was commonplace com- pared with her. Disraeli took a genial pleasure in playing on his wife's foibles, and he would relate her sayings with the greatest relish. The most famous story, which Sir William Fraser does not tell, is about the visit of the Disraelis to Strathfield- saye in the time of the old Duke of Wellington. Going up to the bedroom Disraeli found his wife and her maid moving the bed from one side of room to the other. When he inquired the reason his wife said," Well, my dear, the duke sleeps on the other side of the wall, and if I lie against it I can boast , that I have slept between the two greatest men in England."

The following story of Barnum is told by "Pro lessor" Hutchings, the " lightning calculator." Barnum used to go at one time to a certain New York barber, by name Higginson. One day the showman entered the shop in a hurry and found , his particular chair being filled by a bucolic Iritih- man. "I'll pay for you if you will give me first chance," said Barnum, addressing the son of Erin. It was a bargain. But next day when Barnum en- , tered the shop he was presented with a bill for just ' seven dollars fifty cents. The Irishman had seized the opportunity for a bath, a hair cut, an elaborate shampoo, whiskers trimmed and curled, boots blacked, &c. Barnum paid the bill. He also sought out the Irishman, and gave him a season ticket to his museum. The old showman dearly loved a joke even at his own expense.

Deep and widespread must be the regret evoked ny the news of Lord Edward Cavendish's death. He had always suffered from some weakness of the lungs and bronchial tubes, and in 1887 was at deaths door with a pulmonary illness. When be was attacked by influenza it was felt by his family that if the disease touched the respiratory organs the outlook would be grave, and on Tuesday morn- ing we learned that the worst anticipations were realised.

Lord Edward Cavendish closely resembled his lamented brother Lord Frederick alike in his appear ance. manner, and character. Both were singularly modest and unassuming men, "hating the solemn vice of grerness, pride." and concealing real and marked ability under a diffident and embarrassed addtess. Both were thorough Englishmen in all their tastes and sympathies and ways of think- ing; both the soul of honour, high principle, and consistent steadfastness in well-doing. Lord Edward Cavendish was born in 1838, and served in the Rifle Brigade. He Wi a keen soldier, and a considerable expert in scientific gunnery. He first entered Par- liament in 1865, and was a steady Liberal till the split in 1886, when he followed his father and elder brother. He married his first cousin, the Hon. Emma Lascelles, formerly one of the Queen's Mnid of Honour. It had long seemed probable that Lord

At ft re cent performance of Mr. Harry Furniss's most humorous" Humors of Parliament," one of the most attentive and evidently delighted of his auditors was Mr. Tenniel, the famous cartoonist, whose handsome face was simply beaming with pleasure and amusement. Edward was destined eventually to succeed to the dukedom of Devonshire. He leaves three sons, the eldest just twenty-three years old. The deepest sympathy is due to his widow, his brother, and sister, and to the venerable duke, now eighty-three years old, and in failing health.
THE NORTH_ BUCKS ELECTION.

The contest in North Bucks was conducted with much activity on both sides on Wednesday. On behalf of the Conservatives Sir George Baden-Powell, M.P., spoke at Stantonbury,and other meetings in the Unionist interest were held. For the Liberal candidate Mr. Lawrence Gane, Q. C. , M.P., and Mr. James Rowlands, M.P., spoke. ,The Conservatives held dinner-time meetings at Wolver- ton, as did also the Liberals.
ACCOUCIIEMENT OF THE DUCHESS OF FIFE

H.R.H. the Duchess of Fifa was safely confined of a daughter early on Sunday mulling at Sheen Lodge. Dr. Williams issued the following bulletin on Monday' morning : "Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Fife and her child have passed a good night, and are progressing favourably." Telegrams of inquiry and congratulation were received on Monday morning by the Duke of Fife from the Queen, the Emperor and Empress of Russia, the German Emperor and other Monarchs.
THE PAPAL ENCYQLICAL ON SOCIAL

I • QUESTIONS, The Press Association has been favoured by CardinaP Manning with an abstract of the forthcoming encyclical on the social question. Theencyclical &gins by rejecting the Socialist solution which would abolish private pro- perty. It then speaks of the solution to be drawn from the Catholic teaching, putting, the Church first of all, and exhorts masters and workmen to live in harmony, and even brotherly union. The encyclical lays down harmony, of all in a general way that the State must do its part in benefiting the working-classes, and ought to intervene' whenever it has to fulfil its duty of protecting the rights of parties, private property, public tranquility, and the advantage of the workmen themselves, whether of mind or body. The encyclical deals with holiday strikers, working holidays, strikes, wages, and hours of labour. In connection with the nature of work, the document approves of the sustaining of corporations, while leav- ing due freedom to all, aid calls upon individuals to ful- fil their personal responsibilities.

div.head: PULPIT IN THE MIDDLE
div.p: THE PULPIT IN THE MIDDLE
AGES. BY JAMES PARTON.

stll(ients of history have been examining of late the ancient manuscripts of Europe to see what kind of sermons were preached six or seven hundred years ago, when the Church was an institution which overshadowed and controlled all others. From the specimens gives and the com- ments of investigators, we may conclude that the famous preachers of old followed about the same methods as the famous preachers of to-day. It is not certain that the art of preaching has been greatly improved in modern times. There were preachers of all the types now known to us: out-of-door preachers, revivalists, preachers skilled in addressing learned audiences, and some who were noted for preaching to children. There was a prodigious amount of preaching done in the Middle Ages. Besides the two Sunday sermons and those on holy days, sermons were delivered at almost every kind of solemnity and feetival. Councils and synods were, of course, opened with a sermon. A sermon was preached at the coronation of kings, upon the admission of knights, at the opening of tournaments, parlia- ments, negotiations, fairs and markets. When the pilgrims set out on their long journey to distant shrines, a sermon was preached to them, and on their journey home they were welcomed with another sermon. The arrival and departure of ea embassy were sigualised in the same manner, Betrothals, weddings, and wedding feasts, all had their special sermons, and every kind of anniversary was accompanied by a sermon. Begging sermons were in great vogue during this period. Vast importance was attached to the giving of alms, particularly to the religious orders wile had chsrge of the poor. People were urged' hi many of these sermons not to put off giving alms until they were dead. Here is a passage from a begging sermon delivered in France before Columbus was born: "When a man comes to dinner in the evening at the house of one of his neighbours or friends' his host Benda a servant for him with a lantern, to keep him from stumbling and falling in the mud. But if the servant carries that lantern behind the guest's back, surely it would not hinder him from stuneb- liug or falling. So it is, also, with the alms which you put away to be distributed after your death. You prepare a lantern which will be carried be- hind your back. Give during your lifetime, and carry the lantern before you, or cause it to be ac carried. "I am told that this very night a poor man has died of cold and hunger. I say to those who ret him die, that their alms will not hinder them from stumbling and falling into the abyss of hell." Nothwithstanding the solemnity of pulpit themes preachers were noted then, as they are now, for their inclination to merriment. The people, too, were aware of the preat difference often existing between preaching and practice. Satirical anecdotes of the popular preachers were part of the staple of conversation. The effect of preaching upon the appetite of the speaker was early recognised, and a bountiful re- past was always provided when a famous preacher was expected to hold forth. A story was current of an arch-deacon, who was se impatient for the usual feast that he strode through the church, where several noble ladies were waiting for the sermon, and hurried to the vestry behiud the altar, and began to eat his dinner without ceremony. One of the ladies came in search of the preacher. " Why, Lord Arch-Deacon," said she, "from- the beginning of the day we have been waiting for

you.,, "Oh 1" said he, in reply, preaching." "Very well," said the lady; "he who confided to you the care of our souls evidently did not take much interest in them." Another clergyman—the Bishop of Cambria— who had hurried through his sermon to get at the feast which was to follow it, scolded the servants violently because the dinner was not ready. "What I" cried one of his hearers. " You who have preached patience to us, can you not show little patience ?" "My dear friend," he replied, "I owe you an example of patience, but I am in no hurry to pay my debt, and you must grant me credit." But the preachers had their turn in satirising the auditors. It was quite as common, six hund.- red years ago, for people to fall asleep under a sermon as it now is. A story is related of an abbot who was preaching to the monks of his monastery, and observed that a large number of them were asleep in their seats. He paused a moment, then suddenly began again in a louder voice: "Once upon a time there was a king who was named Arthur." At these words all eyes were opened and every head was erect. The preacher then re- sumed : " When I spoke of God you slept, and to hear fables you awake." Many other expedients are recorded in the old manuscripts. One preacher, who was declaiming against the malice of women, noticed that many of the ladies present were offended. He changed the subject thus: "Do you wish now," said he, "that I should speak to you of the geed woman? lam going to talk to you of that old woman yonder whom I perceive fast asleep. For God's sake, if any one has a pin, let him wake her. Those who sleep during the sermon are sure to be wide awake at the table.' It is evident, also, that a good many men were In the habit of going out before the sermon began. We know this because many of the sermons which have come down to us contain passages in which this custom is reproved. It is very evideet that women were then as now, more under the influence of the priests than men. At the same time the preachers were remarkably free in their comments upon the follies of the sex. They were as severe in descanting upon excesses in dress and decorations as the Puritans of a later day. One of the old sermonisers explained why women are not permitted to preach: "In the first place," said he, "because they have not sufficient Intelligence; secondly, because an inferior part has been assigned them; and finally, In memory of the folly of the first woman, who, according to St. Bernard, by opening her mouth once, overturned the world." One of the most ancient customs of the church was the separation of men and women during service. As there were no pews in the old churches, ladies et rank sat during the sermon upon stools, or cush- ions, brought by their servants. The rest of the oongregation sat upon benches provided, and kept in the church. It was formerly supposed that the whole oongregation remained standing during the sermon, and this was certainly the case during the first centuries. It is now, however, known that as early as the twelfth century seats were generally provided for the congregation. Even St. Augustine alludes to his auditors as being seated. It is certain that congregations were far front being as quiet and orderly as at the present time. In many ancient sermons we find such interruptions te this : Fur God's sate, brethren, be silent and keep still, for you know that when the hearers are quiet the preacher endeavours to speak better, and the people get more from what be says.' It wan doubtless the uneasiness of the audience, must of whom sat on hard benches without backs, Was compelled the ancient preachers to tell stories aud fables to stimulate the attention of the people. All the fables of 2Esop were used again and again In illustration of moral truths, and certain anec- dotes occur repeatedly in sermons, showing they were part of the common stook of the pulpit.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE CONGRESS.
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE CONGRESS.

The business of the Co-operative Congress was begun at Lincoln on Monday ; Mr. A. Acland, M P., in the chair. lifor. E. Vansittart Neale delivered a farewell ad- dress on resigning the position of secretary of the Co- operative Union, and 'was presented with various tokens of the esteem in which he is held by co-operators. On the re-assembling of the Congress on Tuesday, the report of the Central Board was presented, showing that during the past year 1,554. co-operative societies had made returns to the Board, their sales for the year show- ing a net profit of £4,170,038, an increase of £394,574 compared with last year. There was an. increase of 30 in the number of societies registered, owing partly to the fact that Ireland, for the first time, made a considerable Increase. Rochdale was selected as the place for next year's congress. A resolution Was passed in favour of establishing a National Co-operative Orphange. The Union concluded its Congress on Wednesday, when, after prolonged di set Ission on Mr. Arnold's paper on the best means of bringing co-operation and trade unions into closer relatioaship, it was resolved that cop-, ies`of the paper be sent to the various co-operative socie- ties and to the trades councils in the United Kingdom, accompanied with a strong recommendation that joint conferences of trade unionists and co-operators should be held wherever possible.

div.head: COLD SPRING, AND WHAT TO DO.
div.p: A COLD SPRING, AND WHAT TO DO.

There is not very much comfort for the aged this chilly and variable spring in Dr. Richardson's law of the variations of temperature in relation to , human health. Up to the age of thirty, these atmospheric changes are found to exert no marked influence ; but after that age a fall of temperature, sufficient to cause an increased nunaber of deaths, acts in a regxtlar manner, as it may be said, in waves or lines of intensity, according to the ages of the people. "If we make these lines," says this authority, "nine years long, we discover that they double in effect at each successive point. Thus, if the fall in the temperature be sufficient to increage the mortality at the rate of one person of the age of thirty, the increase will run as follows: One death at 30 years of age will become two deaths at 39 years of age, four at 48 years, eight at 57 years, 16 at 66 years, 32 at 75 years, and 64 at 84 years." When thermometers in mid-May drop, as they have done this week, to freezing point, and bluster- ing wet winds drive holiday-makers indoors, it is not unseasonable to be reminded of Dr. Richard- son's simple rules for meeting a "wave of cold," and thus avoiding influenza and pneumonia. Cloth- ing is the first thing, particularly to envelop the body in some non-conducting substance. The next is an equable temperature in bedrooms. A bedroom fire on occasion sustains external warmth and en- courages ventilation. Chilly mortals are also for- bidden to remember that though, contrary to com- mon belief, there is no hartn in going to meet thel cold air when thoroughly warm, it is important, when 'we return, to accompany the warming pro- cess gradually. • Come when it will, low tempera- ture requires, we are reminded, good nutritious warm food,and particularly heat-forming foods,such as bread, sugar, butter, oatmeal porridge, and pota- toes. Excessive exercise and overwork at such ' times are particularly to be avoided. As to that favourite remedy for a chill, a glass of hot brandy and water, Dr. Richardson's doctrine is that when it warms a cold man the.credit belongs to the hot water, while any discredit that may follow may safely be attributed to the brandy. ,

THE LANCASHIRE YEOMANRY • HUSSARS AT SOUTHPORT. The review took place on the sands on Friday, but owing to the great change in the weather which resulted from the considerable fall in the temper- ature, turning a bright, genial spring almost back • into winter again, there was as might be expected, only a very poor attendance of spectators. Amongst those present were :—Colonel Macfie, Colonel Crosbie, dajorJ. Formby, Major and Adjutant Hobart, the Countess of Sephton, Captain Price, Major Reif, Commander Bragg, IL., Major Murdoch, the lion. Miss Molyneux, Captain and Mrs. Worthington, Major Molyneux, late Duke of Lancaster's Own Yeomanry ; Mr. F. J. Knowles, Mr. and Mrs. Worth- ington, Dr. Beaman, Captain Beaman, and several officers of the 12th Lancers, Seaforth Barracks At the conclusion of the inspection, the regiment was formed in three-line squadrons, so as to con- stitute three sides of a square, and from the centre of the !wive the inspecting officer then addressed the troops.—Colonel Duncoinbe said the parade movements, were all of them very good and dressing well kept. As a result of the horse inspection prizes were awarded as hallows :—A Troop : 1, Corporal Miller, owner and rider ; 2, Quartermaster Glover, owner Mr. Reeves ; 3, Corporal Hill, owner Mr. Painter. B Troop : 1, Pri- vate Pendlebury, owner the Hon. Robert Gerrard ; 2, Private Westard, owner Colonel Gamble ; 3, Sergeant- Major Cook, owner Mr. Stock. C Troop : 1, Corporal Nailor,rider and owner ; 2,Private Bond,owners Messrs. Evans and Co., of Havdock ; 3, Private linsworth,owner Miss Wiswell. D Troop : 1, Quartermaster Blundell, owner Mr. J. Woosey ; 2, Private Stead, owner Mrs. Parr. There was also a special prize for 1) Troop, the prizes being awarded to :-1, Sergeant-Major Potter, owner and rider ; 2, Corporal Cave, owner Mr. R. Tay- lor ; 3. Private Thomas Coxhead, owner and rider. A regimental inspectimi, was also made in West-st., the winner of the first prize being Private Pendlebury (13 Troop). A second, or reserve, prize was also given, this being awarded to Corporal Miller, of A Troop. In addition to the above prizes, a series of consolation , prizes were awarded to men who had never won a prize of any description. This is an innovation by Sergt.- Major Strange, which has proved vary welcome. The following were the awards : Sword exercise: 1, Private G. Clarke ; 2, Private Chick; 3, Private Smith. Farmers' prize: 1, Sergeant Abbott; 2, Corporal • Long,ton : 3, Corporal Hilton. Cleanest turnout : 1, Private W. Bond ; 2, Sergeant Abbott ; 3, Corporal Squire. There was much difficulty in awarding the prizes in these cases, as all the men were particularly smart and clean. All the above belong to "C" Troop, Newton.

div.head: PERO IVAL_ GORDON;
div.p: PERO IVAL_ GORDON;
OR, THE CHILD OF TIIE REGIMENT.
BY SYLVANITS COBB.
CHAPTER XII.

TnottLaz ALL AROUND. Lord Elmdale had noticed the warn flush upon his daughter's cheeks, and the unwonted bright< ness.and joyousness of her azure eyes. He noticed this more quickly, and the more particularly, because of late she had been rather inclined to soberness; smiling but seldom,—she. Who was wont to be at - home .in smiles,—bearing herself much of the time as though not happy. But she was happy now. He had never seen her when she appeared more so; nor was it a mere flitting Whim of emotion but something ~deep and soul- reaching, and her look of solemn content and holy eace plainly signified. • Was it possible that the general's conversation had done all this ?—or .could it have been this brave-looking, handsome young stranger? The itnorning air and the early run in the garden had done something; but not so much as this. These thoughts had flashed through his mind as the party from the garden, with Caroline in the lead, advanced from the entrance. He exchanged greetings with his host, as we have seen; for it will be remembered that this was Wenham Castle, and that Harry Maxwell was now its lord and master,— and then, following Lord Wenham's mo- tion he turned to the youthful stranger. "'My dear Lord Elmdale,permit me to present to you rn3. very dear friend; and chief of my pet sonal staff,—Captain Percival Gordon." With a gracious bow, and with a warm, pleasant smile, the earl extended his hand. The name had been distinctly spoken; but, as applied to a staff officer of high rank, it did not strike him as at all significant or even familiar. "Captain Gordon," he said, holding the young man's hand while he spoke, "it affords me pleasure to know you. A' friend of Lord Wenham should be a friend of mine." He released the captain's hand, and stepped back; then pointed to Caroline as he added, with a genial, pleasant smile : "My daughter, sir, I think, has already been naade known to you." Percival was sorely perplexed. He saw plainly that the :man had not thought ol him in connection with the boy-hussar of the brigands' cavern; he had no wish to reirsaisi unknown; and yet he knew not how to speak as he ought. But he was not to be left long in suspense: Caroline came quickly to the rescue lkavely and loyally. . ' "Papa! papa !" she asied, taking him by the arm, "don't you know him? Is it possible you have forgotten? 0 !. I knew him the moment he spoke. It is Percival Our own Percival I—our hero of the robbers' cave !" The Earl of Elmdale started back like one stricken a heavy blow. He looked first into his daughter's face, in a dazed sort of a way, and then he tursied his gaze upon the youth. He saw it now. Amid the rush d thought, that well nigh unmanned him, one thought was clear and promi- nent: The hope and the care of years he saw ren- dered of no avail in this unfortunate hour ! The one persen in all the world whom he had hoped and prayed his child might never see again had come and had come too, in a shape most dangerous to his peace of mind. But Richard Archer was not a coward; nor was he without heart. With one of the most desperate efforts he had ever been called to make he put back his surging regret Irons the surface, and put on an friendly an expression as he could command. "Percival Gordon !" he said, putting forth his band a second time, "allow me to greet you in your true character. I certainly did not recognise you. I have not forgotten,—l can never forget— how much I owe you. lam well eatisfied that you have worthily won the honourable' position you now occupy, and I congratulate you." "1 thank you, my lord, for your expression of good-will; and I can but rejoice that we are per- mitted to, meet, in health and peace, beneath the roof of him who has proved himself friend to us both. And with him I know we both sympathise in the sad bereavement that has called us to- gether." The youth had spoken, hardly knowing what he was saying, for he had keenly observed his lord- ship's manner when his identity had been first made known to him, and it had cut him deeply. However, he had spoken feelingly, and eloquently, and Archer bowed with graceful assent, while Max- well thanked him with all his heart. At that moment the first breakfast bell sounded, and our friends separated to dress for the meal. After breakfast came preparations for the funeral, and until late in the day but little opportunity was had for social intercourse. Towards the middle of the 'forenoon, an hour be- fore the time set for the services to commence, Sir Edmund and Lady Cooper, together with Matthew Egerton, arrived, and were received by an usher in waiting, and presented to the .earl. The baronet and Lady Rachel, Harry Maxwell remembered very pleasantly, they were very nearly of the same age, thegeneral being only three years older than Sir Edmund. But the young man he bad never seen before, or, at least, he did not remember him. He saw him now, however, and read him as he would have re-di a descriptive role presented with the per- son of the culprit described. Yet his reception was urbane, and he intended that his utter disgust should not manifest itself upon the surface. "Sir Edmund, and my lady," at the same time bowing to the son, by way of including him in the address, "this is Captain Gordon, of my staff." Our hero bowed, and the others bowed in return, and PiLSSea On. With something very much like an oath, when they had got beyond the hearing of other parties, Matthew wondered why Lord Weuham had stared at bins so outrageously. His soother whispered to him that he must be

misi,tken. " Not a bit of it," he retorted. "Those sharp ' eyes of his tell their own story. Blast him, what's he got against roe?" " Vellum ;1 It is all your fancy, Matt. If he ; 10el:ea at you wonderingly, it was simply because yon bed grown so. You were but a small boy when he last saw you." " A nil say," pursued the irrepressible, " who is that stuck-up youngster that heseemsto be so proud of ? Capt,in who did he say ?" " Captain Gordon," his mother informed him, soothingly. "Gordon? Gordon? Why that's the name of . the young chap that Carrie was so sweet on—the fellow that Wellington put into the Gazette." An- other utterance that sounded more oath-like than had the former—and he added: "He'd better keep out of my way. If he thinks to make him- self agreeable to Lady Caroline here, he'll hear from Inc !" And with this direful threat he clenched his hands mightily and shut his teeth like h vice. Lady Rachel grasped her husband's arm with sudden fervour. "Edmund, we must keep our eyes open? I verily believe Matt. is right. If so, we must look to it that the young fellow has no opportunity to make trouble for us; for be sure he could do it if he tried." The baronet was feeling particularly uncomfort- able. When we first met him he was thirty-eight, and his step-son was twelve. Now he was fifty- two and the other was six-and-twenty. Then he was master in his own house; now he was not master. The young man, whose brow was very soon to bear a coronet, asserted his claim to rank and sought to make his authority felt. Only in I the immediate presence of the dying earl was he even respectful ; to all others be was dictatorial and overbearing. His mother alone put up with his "oddities," as she called them, and we will do him the credit to confess that towards his mother he was often loving and kind, for he respected her, knowing, as he did, that through her came his sue- ' cession to pomp and power. Sir Edmund podded assent to all that his wife said, and then put the matter aside. He had come to feel—the step-son had himself made him feel— that he eared not a straw whether the youth ever became Earl of Oxton or not. Awl, moreover, he felt, very often, that he could willingly set the Lady Caroline free from the bonds of betrothment. Beautiful girl I—so pure, so gentle, and so good 1— he felt that it would be cruel to force her to wed with such a man. But he dared not breathe such thoughts aloud ; nor did he always feel in that mood. There were times when he looked upon the princely domain of Oxton and thought of the wealth and power of its lord, that he should insist upon the uuiou of Oxtoa and Eitndele. Later, however, be promised his wife that he would help her in the work of keeping the interloper at a dis- tance; though for the life of him he did not see how he was going to do it. The funeral ceremonies were impressive, but not long. A vast concourse was present, and the capa- city of the old castle was taxed to its utmost in the entertainment of the people ; and in this respect the new earl was nut a niggard. His father had been beloved and respected by his whole *tuantry,

and Harry knew that the hard-handed yeomen and the denizens of the village—traders, artisans, and all—mourned sincerely. If he had feared that the refreshments—the many butts of ale, the casks of wine, the saddles arid sides of beef, and so on,— would not suce, he IV4S to be happily reassured; for, when all had eaten and drank their fill, he could have fed a regiment of his hussars upon the

leavings. A few of the guests, particular friends of the host, were to remain over night, and of those were Lord Elnalaie and his daughter. Towards the close of the day, while Sir Edmund's groom and driver was in quest of his coach, Matthew Egerton sought an opportunity to speak with Lady Caroline. He met her in the main hall, arid without ceremony, caught her by the arm, and drew her aside. "Say, Carrie, is that Captain Gordon that pins to his lordship's skirts, the young fellow that—" " Sir 1 Take your hand from my arm. How dare

you 1" "0, come now, don't do that. It won't go down with me. I want to know." She broke from his grasp, and faced him, her eyes blazing, and her whole frame quivering with a passion of indignation beyond control. "0 ! coward coward and brute as well as coward. Leave me, sir, or I will call for help. I will, as sure as I live." At that moment Lord Wenham appreached. Caroline saw him, and had almost started to dart towards him, when she thought better of it, wish- ing to prevent a scene. " See," she whispered, to the cur, "General Maxwell is coming. Let him not find you here." Something told Matthew that it would be well for him not to meet the earl, while such tell-tale marks were upon the lady's face, so, with a fierce oath, swearing all sorts of revenge upon anybody who should dare to cross his path, he turned and Left her. " Dear lady, what is it ?" his lordship tenderly asked, coming up and taking her hand. "What was that man saying to you? Did he dare—" "0, no, no; it was nothing." But finally she told him the whole story, whereupon the earl shook his head in sober thought. "We must look to this," he said, after a brief pause. "It often happens that arrant cowards are the most dangerous enemies. I can see that this fellow will nurse a bitter hatred of our hero, and I must put him on his guard, 0, pooh 1 pooh 1" as the frightened girl cried out in her terror of alarm. "There is nothing to fear, I assure you. Forewarned, to the true soldier, is forearmed. Be sure Percival is amply able to take care of him- self; only he must know where the danger lurks. I am glad that this is known to me." The good man spoke a few cheering words, and with a closing benediction he bade her good night. Late that evening, after most of the household had retired, Harry Maxwell—General Maxwell— Earl of Wenham—sat in the grand old library alone, given up for the time entirely to his own thoughts. It was late enough for honest people to be abed, yet early for the followers of Fashion to retire from waking festivity; but Wenhairt Castle was regarded as a house of mourning, where- fore the household and the guests hushed their confab at a comparatively early hour. It was a strange situation in which the earl found himself, and not yet had he fully made up his mind upon his exact course. Had he not promised his father that, when he should come to the title, he would devote himself exclusively to the care of the broad estate and a supervision of the affairs of a numerous tenantry, he would have found a worthy representative to take his place at home, leaving him free to return to his beloved profession of arms. Should he remain in the army, he knew that a pleasant and honourable position would be given him, for he possessed the warm friendship of the king and his ministers, as well as of the nabobs of the Department of War. But he could not do it. He could not break faith with his sainted father. And, moreover, he had seen enough since his return home to con- vince him that his care and attention and his guiding hand were much needed on the estate. During the sickness of the late earl the estate had suffered for the want of an intelligent, intdrested head, and it must be brought back. Furthermore, he felt it to be his duty to take his place in the House of Lords, where there was pressing need of good and true men; not that he thought him- self better than his fellows but he believed that his extended intercourse with the world, and his intimate relations with the affairs of other nations, peculiarly fitted him for a leading place among those, many of whom knew of political matters only what they had read in books and periodicals. Thus he sat when he was aroused by a rap upon the door communicating with the hall. It was not the call of a servant. "Come in 1" was the quick response. The door was opened, and Lord Elmdale entered. " Ah, Dick ! is it you 1" the general cried, forget- ting for the moment the changes of later years. " Yes, Harry," the other replied, falling into the same strain. "May I have a few moments of your time'?" "As many as you want, my dear man. Sit down, and pray excuse my not rising." Richard Archer sat down, and having offered a few remarks touching upon the events of the day, he spoke of the wondrous change of outward circum- stances that had befallen them both since the days when they were at Oxford together. A little while in this strain •, then lie sank into silence, and pulled in pieces a bit of paper. he had picked up from the table. "Elmdale 1" called the host, speaking soberly now, "what is it? What has called you hither at this hour? You know you may command me or confide in me." "Dear Maxwell," the visitor replied, with an effort, "it is a delicate matter ; but I will be perfectly frank with you, and state the case plainly. You are, of course, aware that the scn of our old- time friend—she that' was Rachel Trevelyan—is the heir of Oxton. The young man, Matthew Egerton, was present at the funeral to-day." "Yes," nodded Wenham. "I saw him." "V's ell, when it had been discoverd that, through his mother, this young man would succeed to the title upon the death of Walter Buckley, his step-father, Sir Edmund Cooper, came to me, and expressed the wish that the boy and my daughter should be affianced. Matthew was then twelve years of ago." "And your daughter little more than six." "sYou are right, General. Caroline was not quite` seven years old at that time, though lacking only a month of it. However, I considered the pr • position. If my child lived to grow to woman- hood, she must marry somebody; and where would we find a better match? The two estates of Oxton and Elmdale lie side by side, or at least they touch at one point. You will not wonder that the prospect was pleasing." "I am willing to acknowledge," said Maxwell, "that, in the hands of a good, loyal, true man, with intellect and heart, so vast an estate might be made the source of beneficent power; but I should fear to put it into the hands of one unworthy of the trust. With such a man—a man hard of heart, and selfish, the greater the power, the greater the evil." The lord of Elmdale winced, and moved uneasily in his seat. "I will not dispute you," he said, with a new effort. "But, to come back. I considered the proposition of Sir Edmund in all its bearings, and finally consented to the arrangement. The articles of betrothment were drawn up, and duly signed and sealed in presence of old Murray and two other witnesses. And there the matter rested. My daughter was solemnly affianced to Matthew Egerton, the marriage to be solemnized as soon after his accession to the title and estate of Oxton as might be deemed most fitting by those concerned. "And there, my dear Maxwell, the matter has rested from that time; and—" • "One word—allow me," interrupted Lord Wenham. "Has your daughter ever given her consent to this arrangement ?" Elmdale caught his breath, and hesitated pain- fully ere he answered. " No ; she was never asked to consent." "And you never spoke with her tssn the subject ?" The unhappy father trembled from head to foot. " Why—yes—l spoke of it in her presence, of course." "And asked her, perhaps, how she would like to have Matthew Egerton for a husband ?" " Yes —I believe I did ask her like that." "And her answer?" Richard Archer did not respond, but sat uneasily, and tore up the last bit of paper he had left. At this point Harry Maxwell turned a steady, searching gaze upon his companion. His brilliant eyes were aflame, and his handsome face—still surpassingly handsome, notwithstanding his three- and-fifty years—was full of righteous indignation. "Lord Elmdale," lie said, sternly, "you need not beat about the cover more. I know all you would say, and can answer without your expla- nation. Your beautiful, gentle, ,true-hearted, ten- derly-loving daughter doubtless told yo_u that. she

èjisedMidtheW Egerton. now could she help it? She had loathed and despised him since first she knew him; and you, yourself, have ion.'' since ceased to respect him. Ah ! I know your heart, Dick. I know you can be proud and opinionated, but it is not your nature to be unjust. Your pride of family and station is great; but you could not do a mean thing, knowingly, to uphold it. "Dick, this young staff officer of mine has be- come your 'black beast.' Years ago he saved your life and mine, together with the life of your sweet child; and your little cherub fell in love with him and called him her hero. You suffered their intimacy then because you believed when once they had parted they would never meet again. It seems that, infants though they were in that long- gone time, they pledged a mutual love as deep and enduring as ever warmed and gladdened a human heart; and you know that through all the years your slaughter has held the image of her hero in answering and unfailing affection. "And now, sir, the loving twain have met again, and they find each other true and loyal. I saw them together in my garden' and I said to myself, it would be cruel to part them. I tell you, my lord—and I speak the solemn truth—l am older than you, I am wealthier, and my family is far more ancient than is yours; yet, had I a daughter —were the Lady Coroline my child instead of yours—l would give her to Percival Gordon with all my heart, feeling that I had done a blessed, righteous thing. "There, sir; you have all the answer I can give you. Only, I will add thi9 ; I have known Per- cival from his infancy up, every event of his life having transpired under my own observation, and ; I assure you, upon my honour, that I never knew him to do an evil thing, nor an ungentlemanly act. He is the very soul of honour, a prince among men —one of nature's noblemen." - -

Lord Elmdale arose from his chair with a sigh, and brushed his hand across his eye. "Harry, you do not understand. My honour is pledged." "Then sticinto your honour, and let Caroline adhere to her love, and we ,'hall see who will win. Go to your bed, Dick, and sleep upon it. Don't talk with your daughter until you see Inc again." With another sigh, and with simply a whispered good-night, the lord of Elmdale turned from the presence of his host and sought his own apart- ment
(To be continued ).

div.head: NEW ARCHBISHOP OF YORK.
div.p: THE NEW ARCHBISHOP OF YORK.

The announcement of Tuesday receives confirmation. by the official intimation that the Queen has been pleased to approve the nomination of the Bishop of Lichfield to the Archbishopric of York. Dr. Maclagan was born in 1826, in Edinburgh, where his father, who had served as medical officer in the Peninsular campaign, held the post of physician to the forces. On the completion of his education, which he received in his native city, young Maclagan entered the Army, and served in India, retiring, with the rank of lieutenant, in 1852. He then went through the ordinary university course at St. Peter's College, Cambridge, taking the B.A. degree in 1856. He was ordained deacon in 1856, and priest in 1857. He has been married twice. His first wife died in 1862. His second wife, the Hon. Augusta Barrington, sister of Viscount Barrington, whom he married in 1878, is still living. He has two sons living by the first mar- riage, one of whom is the Rev. Walter Douglas Dal- rymple, curate of St. Paul's, Alnwick, and a son and daughter by a second marriage. Dr. Maclagan, though not a great pulpit orator, is distinguished by great ad- ministrative talent, and his management of the great diocese of Lichfield has been very successful. His Grace's removal from the Sec at Lichfield will be regarded with great regret, as he has acquired a large amount of popularity amongst all classes and creeds of the diocese. A most valuable work has alzo been car- ried out by Dr. Maclagan in the establishment of a mis- sion to bargenaen and boatmen upon the canAls which intersect Staffordshire in the diocese.

div.head: WIIO SCOFFS Al WARMING PANS?
div.p: WIIO SCOFFS Al WARMING PANS?

In the trial of the breach of promise case so funnily described in the "Pickwick Papers," Sergeant Buzfuz, for the plaintiff, reads a note from Mr. Pickwick to Mrs. Bardell, in which that lady is told not to trouble herself about the warming pan. "Now, your lordship," cried the Sergeant to the Judge, "whoever does trouble him- self about a warming pan ?"
The Sergeant's question was careless and shallow. A warming pan is a valuable thing in its way, and

_ should be used oftener than we fear it is. If it were universally employed, Mr. Patrick Cain, of 8, Birkland- st., Bulwell, near Nottingham, would never have written the followin4 statement :—" In 1802 I was takan ill through sleeping in a damp bed. Up to that time I had been a strong, healthy, man. I was then serving with

the South Staffordshire Militia at the annual training at Whittington Common, Lichfield. We had been at Lich- field only a week, when I was seized with inflammation and stoppage of the bowels, and confined to the Bar- racks Hospital during the remainder of our training time.

Getting a little better, I returned to Bulwell, where I soon had another attack of a difforent nature. My appetite left me, and when I did eat, the food gave me great rain,filling me full of wind. I had severe pains in the back and aide, my stomach swelled, and every now and again I had dreadful attacks of cramp; the pain nearly made me scream. During those spells a doctor attended me, and I was poulticed bask and front, and rubbed with liniments until my wife became exhausted with the labour.

"Off and on I went on like this for seven years, the attacks growing more frequent and violent. I atn sure I was off my work twenty times for a few days at a time, and this was a great loss to me, and kept me down. In the March of this year (1890) I had a worse attack than usual, and became so weak and low I never thought I should get over it. I said to my wife, I'm afraid lam gainy to leave you, for I think it is my last time round."

"About this time I heard from a fellow-workman, named William Napp, about Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and I got a bottle from Mr. Bloor, chemist, Austin Street, and after taking four or five doses I felt relief, and by the time I had used three bottles I was cured, and have never lost a day's work through illness since. I suffer no more pain, can eat anything that is ; put before me, and never ail anything. "My wife had suffered from dizziness and indigestion, and seeing what Seigel's Syrup had done for me, she took some of it and was greatly benefited. "In the first week of November my little boy, three years old, was taken with convulsions,and we thought he would not live. Thinking the boy was dying, my wife wanted to fetch the doctor, but I said No, I will give him a dose of Mother Seigel's Syrup.' I did so, and in an hour and a half the twitching ceased,and he fell sound asleep, and has been well ever since. (We advise in such cases that a doctor be called.) You are at liberty .to

• . publish this statement. Now what had the dame which Mr. Cain slept in 8 years ago to do with all he suffered afterwards? The answer is plain and easy. He took what he familiarly called a "cold," which means that the nervous system is in a weak and depressed ,condition. As the stomach and bowels are full of nerves the attack became localised there, and developed finally into chronic indigestion and dyspepsia. The reader must remember that it is not overeating alone that brings on this malady. Any cause which overthrows the balance of the body or mind, al- most invariably" settles" in the stomach, and the re- sult is indigestion and dyspepsia, with all its fearful con- sequences. A damp bed did it for Mr. Cain; something else may do it for you. In any case the demonstrated remedy is the one he at last employed—Mother Seigel"s Curative Syrup.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF CeMMONS.—THITRSDAY. The Speaker took the chair, after the recess, at five minutes past three o'clock. The Furniss Railway Bill was read a second time. Tim PAISLEY VACANCY.—On the motion of Mr. Arnold MonLey, a new writ was ordered to issue for the elec- tion of a new member for Paisley in the room of Mr. Barber deceased. FREE EDUCATION.—Mr, PzaroN asked when the bill to Provide free education would be introduced. (Opposi- tion cheers.) The CHANCEELOR of the EXCHEQUER said be would be better able to make a statement on the sub- iect when the Land Bill was through. Mr. PICTON': Through Committee? The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEWER : I have answered the hon. members' question. THE LAND PURCHASE BILL._ _ .

The House then went into Committee on the Purchase of Land and Congested Districts (Ireland) Bill. Mr. BALFOUR moved a new clause to provide for the allocation of the sum available for the purchase of hold- ings in proportion to the value of the holdings. Lord LYMINGTON Opposed the clause on the ground that the relief would be confined solely to the very poor and im- poverished properties, and that it would serve to increase agitation by excluding the larger farmers from its bene- fits. The discussion was continued by Mr. Rathbone, Mr. Macartney, Mr. Sinclair, Mr. Picton. and Mr. T. Yealy. The clause was eventually carried by a major- ity of 85. Amendments ,to the clause were then con- sidered in Committee. The House adjourned at five minutes past twelve o'clock.
VIE FATAL FIRE ESCAPE ACCIDENT.

Inspector Doherty, who was seriously injured in the accident caused by the breaking of a fire escape in Dub- 'hi on Wednesday, has succumbed to his injuries. This naakes the second death from the accident.

div.head: ALLEGED MURDER BY A WOMAN.
div.p: ALLEGED MURDER BY A WOMAN.

At South Shields, on Thursday, Harriet Flaileigh, a young woman, was charged with the murder of George Dixon, rnoulder, with whom she had been cohabiting, by stabbing him with a knife. The accused was com- mitted for trial.

div.head: AN UMBRELLA FATALITY.
div.p: AN UMBRELLA FATALITY.

In the course of an inquest held in London, on Wednesday on the body of John Hackett Jones, it was stated that a man named John Edwin Jones had thrust an umbrella into one of deceased's eyes injuring the brain. A verdict of " Manslaughter " was returned, and Jones was committed for trial.
ATTEMPTED MURDER AT LEEDS.

A desperate attempt at murder was made on Wednes- day, at Leeds. A man named William Walker, living in York-st., met in Meadow-lane, a young woman. He attacked her, dragged her into the middle of the road.and Was attempting to cut her throat with a pocket knife, When he was seized and given into custody. William Walker was remanded at Leeds on Thursday, •oharged with cutting the throat of his paramour, a girl named Moore. The girl is expected to recover.
THE MANIPUR MASSACRE
CAPTURE OF THE SENAPUTTY.
The following telegram has been received at the India 'Office from the Viceroy:

_ . " Collett telegraphs. 18th :—Prince Angao Leno,known -to the Manipuris as the Setiaputty, was arrested to-day by Major Maxwell's men, and is in custody." _ Telegraphing the Calcutta correspondent of the " Times" says : Angao Lena, otherwise called Doloroi Hanjuba, the third brother of the Manipur Royal Family, has been arrested. Fie is the man who assumed the title of Senaputty after the Regent assumed that of Maharajah last year, but he must not be confounded With Tenkendrajeit, the Senaputty who was the moving 'fiaUse of the massacre.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY AT GLASGOW.
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AT GLASGOW.

Lord Salisbury was presented with the freedom of the eity of Glasgow on Wednesday, and in acknowledging the honour spoke upon foreign affairs. It was, he said, I almost a tradition that wars were caused by the ambi- tions and intrigues of rulers, but the risks of war had become so tremendous, and the power of destruction war let loose so terrible, that there was no ruler who did not shrink from the possibility that his actions might involve war. For years one of the most anxious questions for statesmen had been how to keep the Mahometan corn- unities from crumbling into dust, And to prevent the disturbance that such disappearance must cause. He Was glad to say that that danger was passing away, ,although, perhaps slowly. Morocco still remained the home of the worst abuses. In Turkey things were much better. A more hopeful revival had taken place in Persia, r and in Egypt the improvement had been won- d fel. Then he touched upon the coming development of Africa and the share the three Companies would have in that work, and referred to the negotiations with the Portuguese, saving the Government could not ignore the claims of that people, but desired the high lands in South Africa, where white men could work, while offering Portugal land she could rule without sending settlers in- to it. With regard to the territory leading from the Pemba to the Victoria Nyanza Lake, he said it would take a long time for the Sir William Mackinnon Company to carry out civilisation there, but the great object had been to deal a blow at the slave trade, and a railway from the coast lino to the lake was suggested. If that railway were constructed caravans would soon become a rnatter of antiquity and the slave trade be abolished. Prom a Foreign Office point of view he took a deep inter- est in the project, but whether the Treasury would give The assistance required he did not know, for he always viewed the Treasury with awe. His Lordship was after- wards entertained at a banquet, and spoke upon legisla-. tion and municipal government. Lord Salisbury left Glasgow at ten o'clock on Thurs- day morning for L-ndon. The Premier passed a good night, the neuralgic pains and insomnia having dis- aPpeared.

div.head: OLDHAM MURDER.
div.p: THE OLDHAM MURDER.
EXECUTION AT STRANGEWAYS GAOL

The interior of Strangeways Gaol before eight o'clock ; au Tuesday morning doubtless had a depressing effect upon the few individuals whose melancholy duty it was t° witness the execution of Alfred William Turner, a Young labourer, for tile murder of his sweetheart, Mary Ellen Moran at Oldham, on the 29qi March last. After a good night's rest, during which he only awakened twice for a few minutes on each occasion, the prisoner rose at six o'clock, and, having dressed in his ordinary attire, Partook of breakfast. During the past few days he seemed penitent, but apparently by his demeanour was looking forward to a reprieve. As the chapel bell tolled, and just on the str)ka of eight, a small door which leads to the scaffold was opened and the prisoner stepped for- ward accompanied by a couple of warders and preceded by the Rev. J. Dre,aper, the Protestant chaplain of the gaol. He walked, or rather "shuffled" along unsup- ported, and as the chaplain read the service he uttered the responses in a feeble voice. He gazed for a moment at the member of the press. who stood in front of him, awl as he turned to the hangman Berry slipped the White cap over his face and adjusted the rope. The Poor wretch trembled on the fatal trapdoor, and as he sobbingly uttered the words, " Give my best love to my mother," the executioner drew the lever, the trapdoor+ parted, the prisoner shot down below without a struggle, and the mechanical strangulation was completed. Less of 'consciousness appeared to be immediate, and beyond the usual tightening of the hands, there was nothing to show that there had been the slightest struggle. The criminal, who was 51t. 3iin, in height and weighed 9st. all but a pound, was allowed a drop of 6ft. 9in. The last execution in the gaol took place over two years ago, the criminal on that occasion being William Dukes, the Bury murderer. The inquest on the body was held in the gaol at a quarter-past eleven o'clock by Mr. F. Price' county coroner. The stepfather of the deceased was present. None of the jury had any questions to ask the governor. Mr. John dwards, prison surgeon, said he was present at the execution, and examined the body on hour afterwards. Death WRS caused by strangulaticm, with dislocation of the neck, and was practically instan- taneous, there being no movement of the body after the drop fell. A formal verdict to the effect that death was caused by hanging according to law was returned.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SATURDAY MAY 23 1891 NOTES ON GAMES AND 1 WHITSUNTIDE AT RUNCORN. ATHLETICS. • CRICKET. In the match, Lancashire v. Next Sixteen, played at Old Trafford, on Monday, the Sixteen were captained by Mr. S. M. Crosfield, who scored nine. Mr. R. Smith, of Warrington, who was out lbw. to Watson, made 30. He had already been tried for the county. He com- menced hitting freely, though not too safely, but he had the satisfaction of placing Briggs clean over the screen, and despatching Watson for two 4's succession. He, however, quickly lost the company of his captain, and, while vartner with Mr. Fletcher, had a share in the free hitting which followed. When the century was reached Mr. Smith was joined by Mr. Gossage, and became the chief scorer with another drive to the boundary. Mr. Smith's contribution of 30 iucluded five fours. Mr. T. Jolley, who is a member of the Warrington Cricket Club, was very unsuccessful, being unable to score.

Continuing the match on Tuesday,the Warringtonians were very much in evidence, as in the following depart- ment Messrs. Smith and Jolley each secured two wic- kets, the former's costing 19 runs and the latter's 32 runs. In the second innings, Mr. S. M. Crosfield gave an exhibition of sound hitting, scoring 51 runs (not out), the highest individual score of the match. Mr. R. Smith failed to enhance his reputation, by having the much despised duck egg opposite his name.

The balance sheet of the Halifax C.A. and F. Club shows a total expenditure for the year (cricket and football) of £2,459, but after paying £5OO off the mert- gage on the Thrum Hall estate, spending £420 on the ground, and other extras, there was a balance of income over expenditure amounting to £336. The gate and stand receipts amounted to £1,236, about £l3O more than last year. The Thrum Hall estate is valued at £8,127, and the mortgage upon it has been reduced to £4,000.

TllE MURDER OF A BOY

div.head: AT LIVERPOOL.
div.p: AT LIVERPOOL.
IDENTIFICATION.

Late on Tuesday laxly of the boy whose re- mains were found n a bag floating in the Sandon Dock Basin, Liverpool, was identified as that of Nicholas Mar- tin aged ten years and four months. His father, Nicho- las,Martin, lives in Bridgewater-st., off Park-lane, and is employed at the soap works of Messrs. Keen and Co., Blundell-st. He has a family of ten children,and alllived together. The last seen of the deceased was about nine o'clock on Saturday evening. He had been playing with several of his companions, and then followed his mother towards St.James'sMarket. He was told to return home, and went in the direction of Bridgewater-st., which is a wide thoroughfare leading down to the Queen's Dock. The police are making active inquiries, especially on foreign vessels, and in boarding-houses frequented by foreipn sailors, but though several clues have been fol- lowed up, nothing definite has yet been ascertained. The supposition that an atrocious outrage had been com- mitted on the hapless lad before he was murdered, still obtains general belief, but the proof of this will depend upon the result of the post-mortem examination, which the Coroner has ordered. Drs. Paul and Lowndes made an examination of the remains on Wednesday afternoon, 'end will submit a report to the Coroner: The inquest will be opened on Friday. When questioned, the doctors would not express a definite opinion as to whether the body had been outraged in any way, but they have re- moved certain parts for microscopic examination. They admitted that the throat had been cut and the legs cut off with considerable skill. The knife found in the bag is an ordinary sailor's sheath knife, and not a butcher's knife, as at first supposed.

div.head: FATHER'S STATEMENT.
div.p: THE FATHER'S STATEMENT.

On Wednesday forenoon, Mr. Martin, the father of the boy, attended at the Coroner's Court, and made the fol- lowing statement :—My name is Nicholas Martin, and lam an under-warehouseman, residing at 34, Bridge- water-st. I identified the remains at the deadhouse as those bf my son, Nicholas Martin, ten years of age. He was last seen alive in Bridgewater-st., by his mother about nine o'clock on Saturday night last. He was a few yards from his own house at the time, and wanted to go to the market with his mother, but she told him to go home. He was then alone, playing at ball. I cannot throw any light.on the matter. The boy was not in the habit of going to the docks. He was a very timid boy. I gave him on Saturday evening a penny, and as far as is known, that was all the money he had in his possession. He went to school at St. Vincent's, Norfolk-st. There are soma boarding-houses for. seamen in Bridgewater-st., nearer the docks than where deceased lived.

div.head: AN ARREST.-SUPPOSED CLUE:
div.p: AN ARREST.-SUPPOSED CLUE:

As the result of the most searching inquiries, prose- cuted without intermission, the police obtained informa- tion which implicated a man whose connection with the murder, either as a witness or an associate in the crime, was sufficient to call for his apprehension. A numerous staff of detective officers were in consequence detailed to make a search through the boarding-houses at the south- end, Liverpool ; and in one of these, late en Wednesday night, the individual in question was run to earth. The man arrested is apparently not a sailor, but has the 'ap- pearance rather of a riverside labourer. He was taken to the dectictive office and there detained. IMPORTANT EVIDENCE. ,

The man arrested on Wednesday night in con- nection with the murder, gives the name of Conway, and is also known as Brown. He is a ship's fireman, and has been a delegate at a meeting of the Sea- mores and Firemen's Union. It is alleged that he pur- chased the bag in which the remains were found, and also the blankets. The police say that the prisoner has made an important statement, the nature of which, how- ever, they decline to disclose. Tho police on Thursday entered the office of which the prisoner had charge in connection with the Firemen's Union, not far from Bridgewater-st., and found a large quantity of blood on the floor. The supposed scene of the murder is a top room of the house, the office of the union being on the ground floor. The walls and floor of the room are smeared with blood, and efforts have been made to ,ash it off. On a search being made at the accused's lodgings, the other half of the "Financial News" was found, corresponding with the half found in the bag.

• FURTHER DETAILS. It transpired on Thursday that the person arreste.d.on the previous night by the Liverpool polise on suspicion of murdering the little boy Nicholas Martin, is named John Conway. He is about sixty years of age, and went through the Crimean War, but has since followed the sea as a fireman. He is a paid delegate of the Seamen's and Firemen's Union, and occupied as an office a house rented by the Union, at 19, Stanhope-street, his lodging being at 56, Bridgewater-St. It appears that during their inquiries on Wednesday , the police ascer- tained from a woman who keeps a sailors' outfitting shop at 48, Park-lane, that the bag in whick the body was found had been bought from her on Monday. She described the purchaser as minutely as possible from memory, and when inquiries were made in Bridgewater- st. it was found that the prisoner answered pretty closely to the description. On Thursday the police discovered in an upper room of the house officially occupied by prisoner at 19, Stan- hope-st., convincing indications that the crime had been committed there. Some boys then informed the police that alrut nine on Monday night they saw the prisoner leave the house carrying a sailor's bag, and enter a han- som cab drawn by a grey horse. Further inquiries resulted in the driver of the vehicle being found, and he identified the prisoner as the man with a sailor's bag whom he drove to the George's Landing-stage on Mon- day night. Prisoner, who had a severe attack of illness on Thursday, admits the ownership of the bag, but denies all knowledge of the murder.
