div.head: WARRINGTON BIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: WARRINGTON BIGHWAY BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Surveyor's Offices, Masonic Buildings, Sankey- et., on Wednesday afternoon. This was the first meeting of the Board as newly constituted. There were present Captain Withington, and Messrs. T. Blackburn, H. Bate, J. Stormier, J. Millington, W. Royston, R. T. Lowe, R. Owen, jun., J. Houghton, J. Grounds, E. White (deputy clerk) and J. Thompson (surveyor). THE CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMEN. _ _
Captain Withington was re-elected chairman, Mr. Royston senior vice-chairman, and Mr. Houghton junior vice-chairman, for the ensuing year.
TILE FINANCE COMMITTER was re-appointed with the substitution of Mr. Lowe for Mr. Davies. TIM ATTENDANCE OF THEI MEMBERS.

The list of attendances at the ordinary meetings dur- ing the past year, of which there had been seven, was read, and was as follows :—Houghton 7, Withington 6, P. Bate 6, Kerfoot 6, Royston 5, Grounds 5, H. Bate 4, Bent 4, Davis 3, Millington 3, Gough 2, Wright 2, Owen 2, Arnott 1, Stannier 1.
THR TELEPHONIC AND THE POLICE.

An application; from Messrs. W. A. Shaw and Co., for permission to erect a line of telephone poles from Lane Head to Padgate for the purpose of connecting each police station on the route with the superintendent's office at Legh,was acceded to on condition of payment to the Board of Is. per annum per pole.—The Chairman re- marked that this would save a great deal of police work. —A member obe• ried that the telephone system would supersede the telegraph system some day. THE ASSISTANT SULLYETOR'S EXPENSES. The question of allowance for expenses to the assistant survcyor,which had been remitted to the now Board ,was then considered, and it was resolved that he be allowed a reasonable amount of pocket expenses, not to exceed £5 per year.

div.head: ESTIMATES FOR TICII YFAR .
div.p: ESTIMATES FOR TICII YFAR .

The Deputy-Clerk read the estimates for the Board's work for the year ending March, 1892, which amounted to a total of £4,639 so that, there being a balance of £790 from last year, a sum of £3,848 would have to be raised, for which an Bd. rate was necessary.—The Board authorised the levy of an Bd. rate, and the issue of the necessary precepts. TER MAINTENANCE OF MAIN ROADS. An offer from the County Council for the maintenance and repair of 17 miles, 3 furlongs, 59 yards of main roads for the ensuing year at a sum not exceeding £1,960 was accepted.

WAY WARDENS' LICENSES. On the motion of Mr. ROYSTON seconded by Mr. 1101.1CMTON the Clerk was authorised to obtain the necessary licenses for the way-wardens for the carting of stone for the Board. This was all the business of importance.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The Rev. F. Marshall announces he will not seek re- election as the Yorkshire football president for the ensu- ing year, but will instead sit on the county bench as ex- ptesident. His reverence, however, does not intend to take a less active part in football matters. Professionals pleass note.

The Yorkshire Union is threatened with a serious split over the proposal to divide gates in the Cup ties. If tke idea is carried out, there Is certain, it is said, to be a. secession on the part of several of the strongest organi- sations in the county. And whatever the committee may think, the Yorkshire Union without such clubs as Bradford, Huddersfield, Halifax, &c., would be like Hamlet without the Dane. If a Yorkshire club does not join the Yorkshire Union it ceases to be a member, and the Union ceases to have the slightest control over it. The clubs concerned are alive to this fact. If the Union decides to divide gates, the leading clubs will simply not renew their subscriptions. They will then have a free hand, and can form a League just as they choose.
RUFFIANLY ATTACK ON CONSTABLES.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednesday, William Morris and John Smith, both having the London accent, were charged before Alderman Holmes and Mr. J. Fairclough, With be- ing drunk and disorderly at Arpley that morning, and also with assaulting Police-Sergeant Jones and P.C. Wade. P.S. Jones said he found the two men asleep in a shed near the cricket field, between one and two that morning, and on his rousing them' up and asking their names, they refused to give them. They were both drunk and Morris struck him across the chest, while he was speaking to Smith ; then Smith took off his belt and swearing at witness, said he would give him a bit of the London touch, and struck him with the belt three times. He, assisted by P.C. Wade, took Morris into custody, and they had great difficulty in getting him there, as he resisted them so much. They came back and found Smith in a field, and brought him to the Sta- tion, but he was very violent all the way. The pri- soners had every chance allowed them to go away, as they had money to pay for their lodgings, and would not have been locked up if they tad behaved thenaselves. Alderman Holmes asked how Smith had come by a black eye hich he had.—P.S. Jones said he had got that in being turned out of a lodging-houso in Rose and Crown- st. for fighting. Smith, added the Sergeant, did his best to get the officers down the embankment into the river. —P.C.Wade gave corroborativeevidence.—Smith,whose face was much bruised and scratched, said it was quite clear when he left the lodging-house.—P.C. Wade, in answer to the Bench, said the man's injuries were caused by his struggling on the ground.—The Chief Constable said the marks on Smith's ear looked as though they had been caused by a heavy stick or a staff.—P.S. Jones: I used my stick, but not on the head.—The Chief Con- stable: Why didn't you say so, then ; there is no harm if you did use your stick in self-defence. Mr. Hunt added that he wished the police would be more frank in saying what they did, as well as what prisoners did.—The two men were fined 103. and costs each ; the alternative be- ing 14 days' hard labour in prison.
John Martin, of Bootle, described as a labourer, was remanded by the county magistrates, on Wednesday, on a charge of shooting John Quinn, of Sefton Moss, Ford, with intent to murder him.

div.head: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.
div.p: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.

The children, attending the schools in connection with this church, numbered 300, and beaded by the Rev. Dr. Preston and several of the officials marchee through the town to a field off Canal-st., kindly lent by Mr. Jonathan Horsefield. Having spent some time in enjoyment there an adjournment was made to the school where tea was provided. Subsequently an entertainment was given by the members of the Band of Hope and others, and the young sons of Mr. C. Timmins performed pleasing selec- tions on the violin.

div.head: NURSE MISSIOkiS IV SUNEE.
div.p: NURSE MISSIOkiS IV SUNEE.

Headed by the drain and fife baud an-A the energetid • missionary, Mr. W. Shaw, the scholars of this mission, numbering 245 walked through the main streets. There were also in the procession a number of captains, seamen, and flatmen, which was a testimony to the interest felt by watermen in the work of the organisation. After spending some time in a field, the children were enter- tained to tea and an entertainment followed. ST. JOHN THE EVANGELIST, WESTON.—The scholars at- tending the schools in connection with this church, held their annual demonstration on Whit-Monday. The young people assembled at the school, where they were formed in processional order, and marched along the highway to the Vicarage at Higher Runcorn. They were headed by the Weston Church Brass Band, and then came the issau- tiful school banner, followed by the Rev. A. J. Jameson, the curate-in-charge, who has always taken a deep inte- rest in the Sunday School,to which b 3 has devoted much of his energy with good results. The choir were next in order, and then came about 160 scholars. After spend- ing a short time at the Vicarage, the scholars returned to the school, where they were regaled with an excellent tea, provided by subscription and superintended by Mrs. Aaron. Subsequently they engaged in sports in a field kindly lent by Mr. Thomas Ford, and before departing home, Mr. Jameson gave each child a bun and an orange.

div.head: SHIP CANAL MISSION,
div.p: SHIP CANAL MISSION,

On Whit Monday, about 280 children of this mission were conveyed on the Ship Canal railway to a field on Marsh Farm, Astmoor, kindly lent by Mr. Finch. The youngsters spent a happy time in various games, and weis afterwards supplied with a capital tea.

div.head: LABOUR ELECTORAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: LABOUR ELECTORAL ASSOCIATION.

The fourth annual Congress of the Labour Electoral Association of Great Britain and Ireland was opened on Monday at Westminster. The Chairman (Mr. G. D. Kelley) urged the importance of trade unionists placing their representatives in Parliament. The report of the Council said the Government were open to censure for the manner in which they had slighted the organized trades of the country in the appointment of the Labour Com- mission. A resolution was passed calling for the pay- ment of members of Parlianient by the State. The greater part of Tuesday's sitting was occupied with the discussion of means for securing increased re- presentation in Parliament and on local governing bodies, in regard to which several resolutions were passed. It was decided to hold the next Congress at Leicester. On Wednesday among other things, it was resolved to get the support of Parliamertary candidates to a measure making it illegal for employers to give out piece-work without stating in writing the quantity and price of such .work, to get a direct representative in Parliament Mr railway men, and to obtain the selection of magistrates from the ranks of the working classes in view of the biased ruling too often apparent on the magisterial and judicial benches.

div.head: PROCESSION OF CLUBS AND SUNDAY SCHOOLS.
div.p: PROCESSION OF CLUBS AND SUNDAY SCHOOLS.

Whit-Monday, Runcorn's great annual holiday, was cAlebrated in that town with the usual pomp and circumstance on the present anniversary. For- tunately the weather was suitable for outdoor en- joyment. The air was glorious with golden sun- shine, flags fluttered from a hundred points,and the town presented a scene of gaiety. In the hives of industry the hum of labour was not heard.. The workmen of the chemical industry had ceased work for two days, and the tradesmen had put up their shuttemand before nine o'clock people were throng- ing the streets. Visitors came from the Lancashire side of the river in hundreds and from Northwich, Winsford, and district came large numbers of peo- ple to witness the demonstrations of the day. By ten o'clock when the

div.head: PROCESSION OF CLUBS
div.p: PROCESSION OF CLUBS

was fixed to start the thoroughfares in the centre of the towns were all but impassable,so crowded were they with sight seers. It was thought that eight clubs would be "on parade" but only four put in an appearance at Devonshire Square. They filed out in the following order: Runcorn's Pride, G.U.O. ; the Loyal Ancient Order of Shepherds; Star of Freedom, G.U.O. and Lily ;of the Valley, G.U.O. Each club was headed by a brass band and a large banner, and the chief officials were attired in curious and gay costumes, while the ordinary members wore bright coloured sashes. Conspicuous amongst the shepherds was a lurry, arranged to represent a garden and displaying all the symbols of their craft. Mr. Thos. Nixon and his sister attired in the character of shepherd and shepherdess, occupied a position in the centre. The total number in the procession was about 300. Consider- ing that there are at least 2,000 members of friendly societies in the town this cannot be considered by any means a representative shove. The procession to the music of brass bands paraded the principal streets and then wended their way to Halton, returning about noon. At one o'clock the

DEMONSTRATION OF SUNDAY SCHOOLS took place. Conforming to their annual custom, the Nonconformists and Catholics joined in one procession, the total number in the ranks being over 3,000. The scene as the scholars marched along the crowded thoroughfares was most picturesque. Bands of music were discoursing sweet sounds; from the scholars ascended at intervals strains of vocal harmony • and banners of varied hues reflected the bright sunlight. Each school was led by the minister of the church with which it was connected and the superintend eats occu- pied positions in the front ranks. The position of the schools in the procession was determined by the date of their establishment and the order was as fellows : Brunswick (Wesleyan), 700; St. John (Presbyterian), 250; St. Lukes (Congregational), 150; Bethesda (Con- gregational), 201; St. Edwards Catholic), 250 ; Primi- tive Methodist, 290; Mill Brow (Wesleyan) ; 436 : United Methodist Free Church, 207 •, Camden (Wesley- an), 550; Nelson-street (Wesleyan), 150 ; Gospel Mission, 130. Admirably marshalled the procession wended its way up Halton-road and back through the centre of the town to a field belonging to Picow Farm, in the Hallo- way. Here various games were indulged in for a couple of hours, and then the scholars returned to their respec- tive schools and were provided with tea and an enter- tainment. The following particulars have been cbtained. BRUNSWICK (WEst.nyeN).—The Rev. H. Bursom, the superintendent minister,was unfortunately unable to be present at the demonstration through illness and the procession was headed by Mr. John Simpson and Mr. E. Taylor. Next were the members of St. Pauls choir who sang hymns as they progressed through the streets. The number in the procession was over 700 and was 30 in excess of last year. After leaving the field an excellent tea was supplied at the school, and subsequently an entertainment was given under the presidency of Mr. E. Taylor. An interesting programme was gone through. Miss Johnson and Miss Ellison contributed a duet, Miss A. M. Taylor, and Messrs John Leathwood and T. Clegg. Mr. Arnold Povah performed a violin solo and Mr. Win. Sirnkin a violincello solo. Dialogues, recitations, &c., were given by a number of the scholars who had been tutored by Misses Crosby and Cook. Mr. John Simpson in the sours° of the evening made a few remarks appro- priate to the occasion. Mr. R. B. Musgrove was an efficient accompanist. Sr. JOHN'S (PRESBYTERIAN). —This procession was led by the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, Mr. James Pritchard,Mr. John Pritchard, and Mr. James Kirkham. Sr. LUKE'S (CONGREGATIONAL).-11l front of this school walked Messrs. J. J. Speakman, G. Lacey, John Coats, Walter Lacy, R. Lowe, and S. Booth. Tea was provided at the school, and afterwards, by permission of the Cricket Club, the young people engaged in a variety of games in the field. Sweetmeats and currant bread were distributed. _

BETHESDA (CONGREGATIONAL).—Heading the procession of this school were the Rev. J. S. Simpson, the pastor ; Mr. EL Chadwick, the secretary; and Mr. T. Lydiate (representing the superintendent). The scholars had tea in the schoolroom, and a miscellaneous entertainment followed. - -

ST. EDWARD'S CATHOLIC SCHOOL.—The procession of this school was headed by the League of the Cross Brass Band. Owing to the-illness of the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, the Rev. Father George, one of the Jesuit Order,from Ditton, headed the procession, which was marshalled by the teachers. After leaving the field, the children were re- galed with an excellent tea in the schoolroom at Mill Prow.
MILL BRow (Wesramm).—This procession was headed by the Rev. W. Kendrew, Messrs. J. R. Frith, and S.
THE SHIP CANAL.
SERIOUS ACCIDENT.

On Saturday,a man named Frederick Smith, a labourer on the Ship Canal, while at work was struck by a plank and seriously injured on the back of the neck and head. He at once received medical attention, and is now pro- gressing favourably. A SUDDEN DEATH.

On Friday morning, a man named John King was taker/ to the Ship Canal hospital, where he expired immediately on arrival. On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Blount, deputy- coroner, held an inquest on the body. Ellen Davies, in the course of her evidence, said the deceased had lodged with her for over eight months. During that time he had suffered from a bad cough and a swelling in the legs, and complained of hit} chest. He was a man who drank heavily. On Friday morning last he went as usual to his work at 5.30, and afterwards she heard he had been taken to the hospital.—John Rowlands said he was cross ing Walton Arches and saw the man leaning against the railings. Witness asked him what was the matter with him, and deceased said that something had struck him there, pointing to his chest. He evidently meant some- thing inwardly. Witness asked him if he would go to the hospital, and decased said he would. He was put on an engine, but died on arrival.—Dr. Parker was called, and the jury returned a verdict of death from natural causes.
EXPULSION OF QUEEN NATALIE.

An unsuccessful attempt was made on Monday to forcibly expel Queen Natalie from Belgrade. At one o'clock in the afternoon the Prefect of Belgrade appeared at the Queen's residence with a carriage, which he com- pelled her to enter, and which then drove • off in the direction of the quay of the Save Steamship Company, where the Royal yacht Deligrad was waiting to take her Majesty on board. On the way, however, the carriage was intercepted by university students, who detached the horses and dragged it in triumph back to the Queen's residence, after severe collisions with the gendarmes, who endeavoured to disperse them. Throughout Monday night the town was in a fever of , excitement. The Palace of Queen Natalie was sur- , reunded by seine 500 citizens and students, who had constituted themselves her Majesty's guard, and who resolutely resisted the efforts of the authorities to gain admission. Towards eleven o'clock the gendarmes made a determined attempt to break through the line of civi- lian guard, and there was a prolonged and severe struggle between the two parties, in which heavy blows were exchanged on both sides. In the end the gen- darmes were driven back. During the fighting one man was killed and quite 50 wounded. As soon as the day dawned the gendarmerie resumed their attack, and thus made a break through the ranks of the people and forced their way into the Palace. M. Simonovitch the Queen's Chamberlain, was summoned, and was desired to arouse her Majesty at once. On Queen Natalie presenting herself after a short delay, M. Todovoirtch, Prefect of Belgrade, informed her that she must immediately leave Servia. The Queen snide answer that she would yield to force in order to prevent further bloodshed, and she thereupon requested her Volunteer Guards to offer no further re- sistance. Her Majesty was then led to a private carriage, and conveyed under an escort of gendarmes to the railway station. The Queen was conducted to a train which immediately proceeded to the Hungarian frontier. DEMONSTRATIONS AT HER DEPARTURE.

VIENNA, WEDNESDAY NIGHT. —MS morning at ten Queen Natalie left Semlin by the Lloyd steamer Kagan for Turn•Severin. Yesterday she received many hundreds of visitors who had come to Belgrade to Semlin to see her. To her more intimate friends she spoke of her son, repeating,' with tears in her eyes, that she feared he was in bad hands, and that the Regents would have an evil influence upon his character. As the ship moved slowly away deputations from Belgrade with flowers were still arriving. By order of the Austrian Government the cap- tam steered the ship through a deserted arm of the Danube to avoid passing in view of the quay of Belgrade, where many thousands had assembled to bid farewell to the Queen. On board are a number of Servian police, who are to make sure the Queen is not put ashore any- where in the Servian dominions. TURN &MERIN, WEDNESDAY.—Queen Natalie arrived here this evening, and proceeded inunediately for Galatz, whence she will continue her journey to Jassy by rail.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. ,
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. ,
The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Messrs. E. Aaron, J. Bagu- ley, Parr, Lewis, Baxter, Edwards, J. Ashton, (clerk.)
WATER FOR FRODSHAIf.

• On the recommendation of the Frodsham Parochial Committee, it was resolved that the executors of Messrs. Timmins, engineers, be allowed to make an experi- mental boring for water, if they were able to make suit- able arrangements with the owner of the land for any damage that might be caused thereby.

div.head: PUBLIC SEWER.
div.p: A PUBLIC SEWER.

A letter was read from Mr. C. L. Evans, of Norton Hall, who said he understood that some 18 months or two years ago the Sanitary Authority laid a pipe and made a tank in a field of Major Orred's opposite the cot- tage.; where Messrs. Knowles, i'Velsby, and others live in Halton. He should be glad to know who gave permis- sion to do this as he must have some acknowledgment. He was informed also that the Authority claimed an out- fall for the sewage from certain cottages adjoining Major Orred's property. If he was correctly informed he should be glad to know how it was that such a right was claimed ',as he could trace nothing of the kind amongst any deeds Major Orred had.—The Inspector having read certain minutes passed in 1887 and 1883 and showing that the Authority had paid £l5 13s. ed. for making the sewer effective, and he said the Law Clerk at that time decided that it was a public sewer.—Mr. Aaron moved that the Clerk reply to Mr. Evans and inform him that it was a public sewer and belonged to the Runcorn Rural Sani- tary Authority.—The motion was seconded and carried.
WORKS OF WATER SUPPLY.

The Inspector reported that-the notices with regard to the provision of a water supply to Aston, Dutton, and Preston Brook would not expire until the next ;fleeting, when the Board would have to decide the question. He had received a letter from Mr. Collin, manager for the Ship Canal Company, who said he thought the Company would be able to deal with the question of water supply to Preston Brook without the Authority takiag action under the Public Health Act.
THE NIOHTSOIL DIFFICULTY AT STOCKTON HEATH.

The Inspector read a letter from Mr. J. Shaw Green of Warrington, stating that there was no difficulty in emptying the aslipits of his property at Preston Brook, but the difficulty was in getting anyone to remove the contents after they were emptied. The whole of Stock- ton Heath was in the same condition, for complaints to him from other owners were numerous. He was a member of the Town Council of Warrington and he knew the pains and troubles they took, and he must confess that he thought Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority was sadly negligent. He did not say this complainingly, because he would second any effort they might make,and if they could give him a suggestion he should be happy to act upon it.— the Inspector said the clerk and he had, in accordance with instructions,drawn up a placard ask - ing the ownera and occupiers to co-operate in dealing with this question of nightsoil removal at Stockton Heath.—ln reply to Mr. Aaron he said that according to the bye-laws of Appleton the duty of removing the night- soil devolved upon the occupier, and if the owners and occupiers did not co-operate in dealing with this matter the authority would be under the necessity of taking the mattes in hand,and this they did not wish to do.—Mr. Aaron: Who would you summon if the ashpits were not emptied ?—The Inspector: The tenant.—Mr. Aaron : And how would you do at Weston? —The Inspector : I should summon both owner and occupier.—Mr. Aaron: Then you had better get to work at once, and summons them at d get some ashpits emptied.—The Inspector said the removal of nightsoil had become a difficult matter in many places in the union.
CHEMICAL GASES AT HATTON.

Mr. Parr made a complaint of the noxious fumes in the neighbourhood of Hatton, which he said came from the Widnes Chemical Works. Last Tuesday night the gases were very strong and disagreeable and were a great detriment to vegetation. He must admit that since the company was formed there had not been the same cause for complaint as previously.---Mr. Aaron said the company now employed men whose only duty was to find escapes of gas and to prevent nuisances.—Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., said the United Alkali Company were using every endeavour to mitigate as much as possible the nuisance complained of. He believed that in a short time there would not be the slightest cause for complaint. —The Clerk read a letter which had been received some weeks ago from the Secretary t 3 the company, and which was published at the time bearing out the remarks made.—The matter then dropped.

Ten men belonging to a French labour recruiting schooner have been treacherously murdered by the natives of San Christoval Island, • one of the Solomon group. div.head: WIDNFS LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNFS LOCAL BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Dr. O'Beeffe (in the chair), Messrs. R. Cook, J. Taylor, B. Brown, D. Wright, H. S. Oppenheiin (clerk), S. Hoyle (accountant), J. Carr (gas engineer), and J. S. Sinclair (surveyor).—The prin- cipal business of the meeting was to have a conference with a deputation from the Runcorn Improvement Com- missioners for the discussion of a suggestion made by the Commissioners that the County Councils of Lancashire and Cheshire should be approached with a view to con- sidering the advisability of constructing a vehicular bridge acmes the Mersey to connect the towns of Widnes and Runcorn. The Clerk now stated that in reply to the letter from the Secretary to the Commissioners asking the co-operation of the Board in the matter, he had, as directed, written requesting that a deputation from the , Commissioners would meet the Board that day. The ' Secretary, however, replied that that was not a con- venient day for a deputation to attend, and suggesting the advisability of dealing with the matter in the first instance in committee.—On the motion of Mr. Wright. seconded by Mr. Brown, the matter was referred to the General Purposes Committee.—The minutes of a special meeting of the Gas and Water Committee on the 15% inst. were read. These contained the feilowing :—Coke onhitete Letter, 6th May, from Mr. R. White, COTTI. plaining of the quality of the coke being supplied to him, and the clerk was instructed to reply that the terms of the contract were being complied with.—Tender for Engine and Pumps, Netherley : Recommended that the tender of Hawthorn, Davey, and Co., be accepted.—The minutes weie adopted on the proposition of Mr. Brown, mended by Mr. Wright.—This was all the business.
DEATH OF LORD EDWARD CAVENDISH.

Lord Edward Cavendish, M.P. for West Derbyshire, died at Devonshire House, Piccadilly, London, on Mon- day morning, at twenty m noes past five. The Marquis of Hartington, Lady Edward Cavendish and her two sisters, Mrs. Grenfell and the Hon. Miss Mary Lascelles, and two sons of the deceased, Victor Cavendish and John Cavendish, were present. His lordship's second son. Mr. Richard Cavendish, is ill at Oxford. The cause of death was bronchial catarrh, following an attack of influenza. Lord Edward Cavendish was the youngest , son of the Duke of Devonshire, and was born in 1838. He sat for East Sussex as a Liberal from 1865 to 1868, and for North Derbyshire from 1880 to 1885, since which he had sat for the Western Division of Derbyshire. Deceased was the first Whip of the Liberal Unionist party. He married in 1885 the Hon. Elizabeth Emma, daughter of the late Right Hon. W. S. Lascelles and had issue living :—Victor Christian William, born in 1868 (and who seems likely to succeed to the dukedom even- tually) ; Richard Frederick, born 1871; and John Spencer, born 1875.

The illness was only of ten days' duration. When his lordship came to town to attend his Parliamentary duties after the Easter recess he was in good health, but he fella victim to the influenza epidemic which had afflicted so many members of the House of Commons. This brought on an attack of bronchial catarrh.and dur- ing Saturday and Sunday he suffered from great ex- haustion. His lordship was very popular, an the news of his death has evoked wide-spread expressions and regret._

The death of Lord Edward Cavendish creates another parliamentary vacancv,and will no doubt lead to a severe electoral contest in West Derbyshire. The Devonshire interest is strong in the constituency, and the late mem- ber enjoyed a well-deserved popularity with the electors, to which was, in large measure, due his unopposed re- turn in 1886. In the election of 1885, in which Mr. Ark- wright polled 4,138 against Lord Edward's 5,020, shows that there is a good deal of Conservative feeling in the division, but it may be doubted whether it would be sufficient to ensure the return of a Unionist in 1891.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT

div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

At the Widnes Town Hall, on Tuesday morning, an inquiry was held by Colonel W. M. Ducat, R.E.. Inspector to the Local Government Board, wita respect to the application of the Board for permis- sion to borrow £9,783 for sewerage and street improvement works and for the erection of a shed. There were present Messrs. R. Cook, J. Taylor, and D. Wright (members of the Local Board), also Mr. H. S. Oppeuheim (clerk to the Board), and J. S. Sinclair (surveyor),Mr. J. Carr (gas engineer), and Mr. S. Hoyle(accountant). The Clerk gave particulars as to the proposed expenditure. He explained that the works that it was the Board's intention to proceed with included the straightening, sewering, macadamising, and improving of faugsdale- road, at an estimated cost of £l,OBB, the flagging and sewering of certain public highways, at an estimated cost of £BOO, and the erection of a shed that was estimated to cost £2OO. The private im- provement expenses contemplated were the paving, sewering, &c., of Market, Eleanor, and Chapel Streets, Luton-road, and part of Bath-st. at an estimated cost of £2,932; the paving, sewering, &c., of certain streets and passages in the Ann-street district, at an estimated cost of £3,835, and the paving and sewering of Sutton's-lane at an estimated expenditure of £930. The Board asked that the repayment of the cost of the public improvements might be spread over a term of 30 years, and that with regard to the private improve- ments a period of 10 years be allowed for repayment. They asked this in order that they might make arrange- ment with the property owners concerned for repayment by instalments. It was found that in many cases these expenses pressed hard on property owners; and it was a great boon to them when the Local Board was enabled to arrange for the extension of the period of repayment as he had suggested.—Mr. Sinclair having explained to the Inspector the necessity for the proposed improvements, Mr. Hoyle submitted a statement showing the borrowing powers of the Board. The rateable value of the Board's district, he said, was £139,339; the assessable value, £114,449; and the outstanding debt, £62,885. The population for 1891 was not yet published, but it was over 30,000.—The Inspector suggested that in regard to the private improvement expenses repayment of gum should be spread over one year, and of the remainder over a period of 10 years.—Mr. Hoyle said he thought this would be satisfactory.—The inquiry then came to an end.

Councillor MASSEY, of St. Helens, Stipendiary is a Conservative, but he is so Magistrates. much of a Reformer that he has given notion of a motion for to appointment of a stipendiary magistrate for the borough. We do not suppose that the administration of justice is more defective at St. Belens than it is in other towns; and yet it may well be that there are good grounds for thinking that it would be an advant- age to have a paid magistrate. It is commonly urged in favour of justices's justice that it cannot go far wrong, seeing that the magistrates have the advantage of the guidance of a legal authority in the shape of a clerk. But there are clerks and clerks, and some are far from being proficient as legal authorities. Besides, even when they are in the right, they have no power to enforce their views; and it is notorious in some towns that certain magistrates, who are a law unto them- selves, disregard any opinion but their own. The result is that the Home Secretary is occasior- ally appealed to, to right some glaring wrong. Only the other week, it transpired that Mr. MATTLIMIWS had been under the necessity of com- municating to the Warrington magistrates on the irregular practice of inflicting costs where the fine was ss. only, or something less than that sum. It seems that the additional levy has been the means of many people—taking the country through— being sent to gaol who would have been equal to paying fines without costs. This means that in all these cases a hardship has been inflicted upon offenders, and upon the community who have had to maintain them while in prison; and all because magistrates have been badly advised, or shown themselves indifferent to the law. Then again, irregularity creeps in through the different sen- tences of different magistrates. It is not at all an uncommon thing for people who know police court business to inquire as to who will be sitting on a particular day, with a view to anticipatinga result. There would be none of this with a Stipendiary ; he would not vary as different classes of magis- trates vary. The question is to a large extent one of coat ; but this might be easily got over by grouping two or three places. For instance, st. Helens, Widnes, and Newton might form a centre; while Warring- ton, Runcorn, and Lymm would constitute another group. There would be no difficulty about the Stipendiary going from place to place, having . different days for different towns. In this way, the work of administering justice would be well done, and it would be economically done. There would be no need for magistrates' clerks at £5OO or £6OO a year. Capable clerks to keep a record of proceedings could be obtained for a third of those sums; and in this way, and by adopting the system of grouping, it is not too much to ex- pect that something would be saved. The present justices would not be abolished, but they would be in their proper places as subordinates. They would not be left to go astray so frequently; and there would be less of unseemly squabbling between bench and bar, and between members of the bar; for a Stipendiary, knowing the law, and having some regard for the dignity of his office, would soon put down anything of the kind. Another thing worth mentioning is that there would be an end of the delay in commencing business which character- ises courts presided over by" the great unpaid." It is simply scandalous that a number of busy men whose duties call them to a police court should so frequently have their time wasted because some very busy or very idle magistrate is not in attend- ance when he should be to take his seat upon Vie

bench. As it happens, unfortunately for the com- munity, magistrates are for the most part appointed not because of fitness for their duties, but because they have rendered some service to the party 'which happens to be in office, and been more or ,less persistent in presenting what they call their "claims." This is neither satisfactory nor healthy; on the contrary it is demoralising. Politics ought to have nothing whatever to do with appointments of this kind ; but they seem to have been consi- dered at St. Helens when, out of the 24 gentle- r/lon who constitute the borough bench, 22 are either Tories or Liberal Unionists! In the ap- Pointment of a Stipendiary, nobody would think of asking whether he was a Liberal or a Tory; it Would be a question of getting the best man for the post ; and it goes without saying that it would be best for the community.

CO-OPERATION has not succeeded , Co-opera rive • in s Congress. olving labour and social rro- blems as was anticipated, a quar- ter of a century ago, by some of the enthusi- astic advocates of the movement; but it has taken hold of the community, and the figures 'which were given in the speech made by Mr. Act- l'AND, M.P., who presided over the Annual Con- greBB, at Lincoln, on Monday, show that it has made great progress. The " turn-over "at the re- tail stores has increased, in twenty-five years, from £4,000,000 to• £28,000,000, while the number of members has increased from 175,000 to over 1,000,000. Private traders, who are in competi- tion with co-operative societies, contend that the large dividends whi ch are paid by some of these societies are obtained by charging higher prices; and it is just possible that this may be so in some eases, for it is well known that the margin of pr - fit in the provision trade is a narrow one. Still, there is some profit, and, unless the management be absolutely bad, that profit is divided amongst the members. It has always seemed to us that the best thing to be said of the co-operative move- Ment was that it encouraged habits of saving and thrift—habits in which the English have hitherto Shown themselves wanting as compared with some of our continental neighbours. Mr. ACIAND, on Monday, referred to another advantage, namely, tllat there was less likelihood of strikes where co- oPerators were numerous, because men were more likely to count the cost when it affected accumu- lated savings, while masters hesitated in grappling With men who could hold out for some time. There •la Something in this, and here is a case in point. lloring a memorable strike in the cotton trade, an Operative leader, who was 'a co-operator, remarked et. a stiike meeting that if they were all like him With " a bit of brass saved," they could go to Black- Pool until the masters sent for them ; but he knew 41. any of them had nothing by tl4em ; and he 1141- .118*x' them to take what was offered rather than Starve and be hdaten in the end. If the nation ae one great co-operative firm, as certain of the ocalists contend it should be, there would un- til oubtedly be less room for strikes; but we seem a Ong, long way from anything of the kind ; for operation cannot be said to have met with any great measure of success in the manufaaturing de- Parttnent. There are hundreds of working-men who have lost their savings in co-operative manu- facturing companies, and, although something has been learned, the way out in this respect has not )'et been found. But success is born of failure where effort is directed with intelligence, and perse- /erence ; and more will be accomplished than has Yet been accomplished in the wide field of co - ePerative enterprise.

Rollicking IT is difficult if not impossible to in get a full knowledge of the cir- Japan. cumstances attending the attack upon the Czarewitch whilst in Japan. He seems to have got into a scrape along with certain mem- bers of his suite, and been wounded by a native soldier or policeman. A Vienna journal says "With regard to Japan, the Imperial travellers lid not by any means wish to benefit by their interesting experiences, but were merely filled With the desire to get as much pleasure out of their journey as possible, and it was for this rea- !en they visited certain parts of the town of Otsu In which they should not have set foot." The Ituference to be drawn is that the royal rollicking blades have been fooling around in the "chain- Pile Charley" style ; and it may be that, in being Punished for misbehaving themselves, they got no 111 ere than they deserve. It would seem from a .neacript issued by the Emperor of Japan that the altlithorities of Otsu where unaware that the Illiejan Princes were amongst them, and the probability isthat they were going about incognito in order that, "in the heyday of the blood," they. "TIM do what they wished without official watch Z. ward. The Emperor of Japan speaks of met- ;g out " just punishment" on the" dastardly cul- Lrlt and if the punishment be " just " there nothing more to be said. If, however, lt should transpire that the future Czar has been at fault than his assailant it will be as well IT let the matter end where it is. When the Crown t.rinee was in India not long ago, special prepare- u3ns had been made at one place to receive him ncially, but he—like a young Russian bear— all that had been done for him, and -"bade off in a style the very reverse of royal. like property, has its duties as well as its kivileges, and if the duties are neglected and the trivileges abused, it is a matter of course to say soon or late, evil consequences will follow. 418 is a lesson which the Czarewiteh had to learn; if he has fully learned it in Japan by having 4.6eliftltl to 1110 endangered in foolish escapade, it will be hint in the future when he comes to be the Ruler of Russia.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Dr. Maclagan, the new Archbishop of Talk, is a Scotchman. Thelate Archbishop (Dr. Magee) was an Irishman. The turn of the Englishman will perhaps come next, especially if wo get Home Rule for England.

There is still talk of raising a big Emigration Fund for transporting the Jews to Palestine. But the scheme will be a failure, if it be carried out. The modern Jew does not want to plant or to delve; and,as he cannot well live upon his brother Jew, he prefers to live upon the Gentile.

A man's Liberalism must be very robust to resist the Torifying influence of the House of Lords. Lord Robartes, who went into the Upper House in 1882, and has been looked upon as a Home Ruler, has just gone over on that question to the other side. But it doesn't much matter. The loss of one lord doesn't count when, as the by-elections show, the labourers are joining the Home Rule ranks by the score.

The _swifts and some other members of the swallow tribe have returned. They cannot be said to be weather-wise, or they would have remained South a little longer. What a Whitsuntide it has been! "Hail smiling morn 1" sounds very pretty; but when the hills are tipp'd—not with gold but with snow, and the "hail" comes in lively showers, it is obvious that there is such a thing as another view of the matter.

The present writer can at any rate speak feel- ingly, for he was in the snow storms of the Lake District on Saturday, and the hail storms on Sun- day. And yet as Mark Tapley would have said— "lt might have been worse"; for neither snow nor hail is as wetting as rain, and it is rain which is the kill-joy in the lake country. But even as to that one can say that it is splendid for the waterfalls.

Snow, blinding snow, with the trees in full foliage was certainly a novel sight—when the blinding effect was over. The hedgerows seemed to have burst suddenly into blossom; the dark firs were converted as if by magic into" Christmas trees "; while the mountains were sublime in their newly acquired grandeur. There was one thing however which was comical, and that was to ob- serve the bewildered look of the cattle as they ruminated on the advisability of eating white grass.

A labourer our party met on the heights above Coniston, said so far as he could recollect it was about 30 years since there was such a heavy snow- fall at Whitsuntide; but on that occasion it was two inches thick oa the ground. It did not remain long in the valleys on Saturday and Sunday, although the thermometer on Sunday night fell 14 degrees below freezing point. Grange is sheltered and relatively warm; but on Monday morning there was ice to be found a quarter of an inch thick.

There are people who wonder why Mr. Ruskin has buried himself on a lonely hillside near Coniston ; but, if they will take the trouble to see what they can see from Brantwood, they will cease to wonder. With the lake for a foreground, the village in the middle distance, an the Old Man and Wetherlam as giant guardians in the background, the picture is superb—it is per- fect. Yes, Ruskin has shown rare judgment in this as in other matters of grandeur and beauty. May he live long to enjoy and to describe the sheen and shade of the glorious scene.

Last week, " Truth " took the " World " to task for an unfounded statement as to a pro- bable application to Parliament to relieve the Prince of Wales in what was spoken of as his finan- cial embarrassment. In doing so, "Truth" affirmed that the Queen had several times come to the aid of the Prince, and was about to do so again. This week "Truth" follows the example of the " World " in contradicting its own state- ment. Would it not be as well to leave H.R.H. alone ? It would seem that it is the editors who are embarrassed rather than the Prince.

So far as information has leaked out, the Indian Government appear to be to blame, along with the late Mr. Quinton, for the blundering which ended in the massacre at Manipur. The Commissioner may have exceeded his instructions,but the instruc- tions themselves were unsatisfactory. Parliament ought certainly to inquire into the matter with a view to getting at the truth and the whole truth. A telegram from Calcutta says :—" The man who speared Mr. Grimwood has confessed his guilt and has been sentenced to death." This may be all right, but it will be as well to delay the execution of prisoners who may be able to give evidence.

The death of Lord Edward Cavendish as a vic- tim of influenza has naturally excited a large amount of interest and sympathy. But greater than the loss in the political world is that sustained m the world of art by the death, from the same cause, of Mr. Edwin Long, R.A. Who that has seen his "Pool of Bethesda," or "Diana or Christ," can ever forget these paintings? His work was in every respect worthy; it appealed,as all great work does, to all classes—exciting the interest and touching the sympathy of the masses, whilst satis- fying the highest canons of art. As he was 52 only, Mr. Long may be said to have been cut down in the plenitude of his power.

Mr. Coningsby Disraeli has been figuring again in the character of the Juvenile Plunger. °He has been writing to the " Times" to explain the defeat of the Tories at the recent elections. It is all due to what he describes as their "eternal and infernal apathy." But if their apathy is "eternal," it must be accepted as inevitable. Why therefore write to the " Times " about it? But oh, to say that it is " infernal !" We have said hard things at times about the ill deeds of the Tories; but we have never felt called upon to describe their attitude as "infernal." We leave such language to Mr. Disraeli ; he is constantly amongst them, and he knows them doubtless more thoroughly than we do.

Tories are requested to note, and bear it in mind during the next election campaign, that Lord Salisbury at Glasgow, on Wednesday, was con- strained to acknowledge the patriotic conduct of Mr. Gladstone, and the Opposition in refraining from discussing pending foreign affairs. But what a contrast it affords to their own action when Mr. Gladstone was Prime Minister! Who does not remember how every opportunity was taken to embarrass the Government with reference to the Penjdeh difficulty with Russia, the Geneva arbitra- tion, and the Gordon expedition? The Jingoes were on the war-path then; but they are asleep now, for they are Tories, and there is a Tory Government in power.

Mr. Herbert Gladstone has given Sir Albert Rol- lit a Roland for his Oliver touching the Primrose League. Sir Albert says Mr. H. Gladstone's colour should be sulphur not primrose; and the "chip of the old block" retorts by quoting Shakes- peare's reference to those who "go the primrose way to the everlasting bonfire." The quotation is apt, but it is not new ; it was made in this column some time ago. Then as to Sir A. Rollit's sul- phurous reference it may be mentioned that a Blackburn evening journal was recently in the habit of publishing what it called a "Primrose Edition " ; but having regard to the colour of the paper the title given by the public was "The Brimstone Edition."

"The Hospital" is wasting time by labouring to prove that a field labourer may work twelve hours a day without injury to his health. But what of that? Would it settle the question if he could work twenty-four hours without injury? Is it the end and aim of being that all possible labour shall be got out of the labourer? Has he no title to leisure, and the cultivation of his taste —if only for growing pansies? Enough of this. It is time to direct attention to the other fellow— the lord of the labourer—the man who never did a day's work and who never means to do. Let him be put in the scale, and, as he is found wanting, let him be reminded of the saying by one of old ,4 if any will not work neither let him ethata.t,

INFLUENZA AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
Hundreds of people are suffering from the influenza, and several fatal cases are recorded. fhe attendance of children at school is considerably affected by the dis- ease.

div.head: WHITSUNTIDR RAILWAY TRAFFIC AT RUNCORN.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDR RAILWAY TRAFFIC AT RUNCORN.

During the holidays on Monday and Tuesday the rail- way traffic was very heavy. There were booked to Liverpool 1,600, to Frodsham 1,100, Chester 330, and Belle Vuo 400. On Tuesday, about 1,100 persons availed themselves of the Liberal Club trip to visit Llan- dudno and Bettwys Coed.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. The Secretary reported that there was a balance in hand of £53 14s. The issue for the month of April in the lending department was as follows :—Theology, 44 ; philosophy, 8 ; science, 69; history, &c., 175; pcetry, 22: fiction, 1,4.55; miscellaneous, 134; total, 1,907 ; being a decrease on the corresponding month of last year of 316. Thirty- nine books had been consulted in the reference depart- ment.

div.head: RUNCORN MERSBY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.
div.p: RUNCORN MERSBY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.

The annual excursion to Liverpool and New Brighton took place on Whit Tuesday when 900 persons were conveyed down the river by steamers. Mr. W. Shaw, the Missionary of the Fife and Drum Band accompanied the excursionists. 'The excursionists had the privilege of inspecting the Indefatigable Trainink Ship. A plea- sant day was spent, and home was reached at nine o'clock. Owing to the low tide the passengers were landed at Weston Point. The profits will be devoted to the fundsof the new Institute.
- SUMMER FASHIONS Ow Showing at J. it W. BUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. RI7NCOIN LIBERAL CLUB Ex CURSION. • -

The annual excursion in connection with Runcorn Liberal Club teok place on Tuesday last, and was an unqualified success. Arrangements had been made with the Railway Company for two trains to Llandudno and Bettwys Coed, and both were well filled, about 1,100 tickets being sold. Capital time was observed on both the outward and homeward journey, and the pleasure seekers had a most enjoyable time amongst the Welsh hills, the weather being bright and genial. Mr. H. Wright hail charge of the arrangements.

FIRM AT RUNCORN. About seven o'clock on Sunday evening the stable at- tached to the premises of Mr. Thomas Clough, butcher, Church-at.. were discovered to be on fire, and in conse- quence of the inflammable material of which the place was built, the flames spread rapidly. The fire brigade under Captain Wright, and the police although unable to preserve the shed from destruction prevented the adjoin- ing buildings from being damaged. The loss is stated at from £BO to £lOO. The origin of the fire is unknown,but it is surmised that some person had been lighting a pipe, and allowed a spark to fall.

IMPUDENT STREET ROBBERY AT WI D was. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday. Mary Ellen Worthingto n. 17 years of age, of 13, Kent-st., was charged with stealing 16s. 3d. from the person of Catherine Quinn, aged 10 years. On Saturday night she was walking along Widnes road, near Simms Cross, on her way to redeem some clothing at the pawnshop, when she met the prisoner who knocked her down, draggel her into an entry, emptied the money from her purse, and then ran away. The prisoner was arrested the same night, and was now fined 405., or a month's impnsonnient.
THE SEWERAGE OF RUNCORN

The various sewers that emptied into the river between Old Quay and No Man's Land, have now been connected with the intercepting sewer constructed by the Ship Canal Company, and the drainage is now discharged on the river side of No Man's Land by means of a syphon. The arrangement appears to be working very well, and the nuisance that arose from the deposit of sewerage on Church Bank will be totally obviated. There was a suspicion that the epidemic of typhoid fever of last sum- mer was caused by this deposit, and it is to be hoped that the new sewerage arrangements will prevent a recurreßce of this dread disease. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DITTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. ALLEGED UN JUST SCALES AT WIDNES.

Thomas Edwardson, coal dealer, wassummoned before the Widnes Bench of magistrates, on Thursday, to answer a charge of being in possession of unjust scales. On the Ith inst. Mr. ltilputrizk, the inspector of weights and measures saw the scales on the defendant's lurry which was returning with empty sacks. He examined the scales and found them 21bs. loz. out of balance against the purchaser. Mr. J. Knowles who defended said the carter had left behind a bar which was usually fixed in the scale and which made each side equal. There was no intention to defraud, it was simply negligence. The bags of coal were weighed before leaving the yard, and the scales were carried merely to be used should the purchaser desire. The magistrates considered there was no fraudulent intent and dismissed the case on payment of costs.

Mr. J. Ravenscroft was an able accompanist. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. R. ABEL, JUNE., RUNCORN.

Amid many signs of regret the mortal remains of Mr. R. Abel, junr., of Tower House, Greenway-road were interred at the Cemetery on Wednesday. About three weeks ago Mr. Abel was attacked by the influenza, which is almost epidemic in the locality, but more serious symptoms followed, and although everything that modern medical skill could suggest was carried out, he died on Friday night last. He was 22 years of age, and was engaged to be married shortly, a circumstance ' which adds much sadness to the mournful event. The loss to his parents is very great, as he was a young man of genial disposition and was of the utmost assist- ance to his father in his extensive business. He was followed to the grave by all the flatmen in his father's employ the men from the boatbuilding yard, and numerous friends. Mr. Phillip Speakman C.C., was also present. BAssuckrrEs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. RUNCORN ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY. The second annual meeting of this society was held in Bank Chambers, on Friday night, last week. Mr. J. J. Speakman presided. The annual report, read by Mr. F. 1, A. Smith, the secretary, stated that although the profit and loss account showed an adverse balanc% the sale of apropriations made since making up the accounts, a net profit of £BO woulil be realised, thus entirely clearing off the debt, 'and leaving a balance towards the next year's expenses. The society now consisted of 192 members, holding 388/ shares. This being scarcely half of the re- quired number, the directors would again urge the pre- sent members to do all in their power to fiil up the society to its full complement as quickly as possible,and thus enable all concerned to reap the full dvantages of the society.—The report was adopted—The Chairman said there was one feature about the working of the society which was not satisfactory, and that was the de- sire of members successful in securing appropriations, to sell to the society instead of undertaking building opera- tions on their own account. In order that the incentive to sell shares should not be so great, it was decided to re- duce the premium per £lOO from £lO to £B. The retir- ing directors—Messrs. Burrows, Digges, Quinn, and Speakman—were re-elected.__. . .

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 23, 1891.
LORD GERARD.
Major W. C. Lord Gerard, who has hitherto been supernumerary major of the Lancashire Hussars, has now been commissioned as Major, the date of the commission being the 7th inst.
WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Tcwn Hall, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Mr. T. S. Timmins J.P. (chairman), the Rev. J. Clarke,Mr. H. W. Deacon, J.P.,Major Wareing, Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. S. Quinn, and Mr. G. H. Danby (clerk.)

div.head: OCCASIONAL COURT.
div.p: OCCASIONAL COURT.

At this court, on Tuesday morning, before Messrs. John Rylands and James Tinsley, Thomas Sumner and William Swell were charged with being dis- orderly on licensed premises at Newton, on the 18th inst. They were fined 10a. each. REDUCTION OF HOURS OF LABOUR.

We understand that Messrs. Maskery and Co., coachbuilders, of Warrington. have reduced their working hours from 50 to 54 per week. As this has been done without solicitation on the part of the workmen it is a matter of course to say that they are grateful for the concession which has been made to them. SERIOUS ILLNESS OF SIR PHILIP EGERTON.

News reached Oulton Park, Cheshire, on Monday, of a serious development in the illness of Sir Philip Egerton, who has been abroad nearly a year in search.of health. Ms son, Mr. Brian Egerton, on receipt of the intelligence, at once left Cheshire for France, where his father is now lying. Lady Eger- ton is confined to her room at Oultou with influenza. ODDFEI4LOWS7 CONFERENCE. In the course of the proceedings of the Annual Moveable Committee of Oddfellows, at Salisbury, on Thursday, the Relief Committee dissented from the recommendation of the directors in the case of St. Helens district for relief in three specisl cases. A lively debate ensued, with the result that the paragraph in the committee's report was omitted. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt. div.head: CON TI N VAN CB OF CHESTER _RACES.
div.p: THE CON TI N VAN CB OF CHESTER _RACES.

The Town Council of Chester,on Wednesday, con- sidered the question of continuance of horse races on the Roodee. A letter was read from the Bishop of Chester and a number of memorials were pre- sented urging the Council not to sanction a new lease of the Roodee for the purposes of racing until an opportunity had been afforded to the public to fully consider the matter. A resolution remitting the question back to the Racecourse Committee was adopted.

div.head: NEWTON FAIR.
div.p: NEWTON FAIR.

The annnal May fair for the sale of horses, cows, &c., took place on Monday at Newton. The attend- ance of dealers was unusually large, and the show of horseflesh exceptionally good. Prices ranged nigh, draught horses bringing as much as £4O, while others of an inferior class could be bought for £2O. COW 6 were selling at about the average, good milkers going at £2O. Buyers, however, were rather scarce, and the business done was hardly up to the average of previous years. LAWN MOVVERS.—Garland, 51, Bridge-at., Warrington. and at Earlostown.— Advt. RUNCORN MODEL YATOII CLUBS.

The first handicap race of the season in connec- tion with the club took place in the iVestoa Canal on Saturday afternoon. There was a very good entry and some capital sailing was witnessed. In the first heat, Hoxworth's Willie beat Hindley's Ethel; 2nd heat. Cooper's Annie beat Bibby's Olive; 3rd heat, Pritchard's Blanche, beat Hill's fox; 4th heat, Hoxworth's Joey beat Shaw's Bessie; sth heat. Bibby's Muriel beat Hoxworth's Volunteer. In the second heat Annie beat Willie; Joey beat Blanche; Muriel beat Sam (bye in first round.) In the final Hoxwerth's Joey won first prize, Bibby's Muriel second prize, and Cooper's Annie third prize. SUDDEN DEATH AT EARLESTOWN. On Tuesday morning, about two o'clock, a man named Richard Fearns, proprietor of a travelling shooting gallery, from Manchester, died suddenly in his van, on the Market Place. The deceased, who was about 48 years of age, had been on the Market ground for several days, having come there from Golborne, where he had been attended by Dr. Dobbs: He was apparently in good health on Mon- day, but towards evening he did not feel well, and retired to rest about 8 o'clock. lie gradually grew worse, and a messenger was sent to Dr. Mouncey, whose assistant promised to send some medicine, but before it arrived the man died, death being due to heart di,ease and asthma.
