div.head: NATIONAL PROVINCIAL BANK Or ENGLAND.
div.p: NATIONAL PROVINCIAL BANK Or ENGLAND.

This great banking institution, which has recently opened a branch in Warrington, in its annual report, just issued, sets forth a very prosperous state of things. The balance sheet shows a net profit for the year 1890 of over half-a-million. The directors recommend that a bonus of 6 per cent. be paid, free of income tax, to the proprietors in July next (making, with the dividends and bonus already paid. 20 percent. for the year), and that the balance of £74,892 9.5. be carried to the profits of 1891. The share capital issued last year has been fully sub- scribed, and the amount received for premiums on the sale of the 2,500 unappropriated shares credited to the bank premises account, in accordance with the last annual report. During the year branches have been opened not only at Warrington but also at Finchley-road, Hampstead, both of which will, it is expected, prove advantageous to the bank and useful to its customers. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at 3. A. W. Durrote Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. THE LATE CANON HOPWOOD OF WINWICK. On Whit-Sunday, at the Parish Church,Winwick, a handsome stained glass window was unveiled as a memorial of the late Canon Hopwood. The total cost of the window, including the stone work, has been about £3OO, which has been defrayed by a number of the late Rector's friends and some of the parishioners and members of the congregation. The window is the work of Messrs. Shrigley and Hunt, Lancaster, who may congratulate themselves on the production of a piece of exquisite workmanship, of which it would be difficult, save in a cathedral, to find the equal. It is what is known as a "Jesse," window, and is similar to one which may be seen in Wigan Parish Church. The inscription,which appears at the base of the window; runs thus :—" To the glory of God and in memory of Frank George Hopwood, M.A.. Oxon., Rector of Winwick MDCCCLV. to MDCCCXC." There was no formal un- veiling of the window, but it was dedicated by the use of a special prayer, in the service. Canon Penr- hyn also made a brief reference in his sermon. Preaching on the Christian temple and the rever- ence due to places of Divine worship, he remarked that the window had been erected in memory of him who had for so many years ministered in that Church. It was hoped that the memorial would contribute to the greater reverence and edification of the congregation. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at J. Sc. W. DUTTON'S Sankey-it., Warrington.—Advt.
MR. E. IMISON, OF RUNCORN, ON RELIGIOUS EDUCATION.

The annual distribution of prizes to.the children of the Parish Church Sunday Scbools, Runcorn, for regularity of attendance and proficiency in lessons, took place on Sunday afternoon. Mr. E. unison, before handing the gifts to the scholars' made a speech,, in which he said the only claim he had to the position that day was having passed through the school as a scholar some 30 years ago. He could not help contrast- ing the dry monotonous Bible reading, which was the way of teaching in those days, with the carefully pre- pared lessons and systematic teaching of the present time, when the children had the benefit of well studied lessons which would help them to become better Church- men and Churchwomen. Let them not undervalue the teaching in Sunday schcols, nor think it did not matter how the lessons were learnt, for they would find, as time went on, how much value there was in the teaching of their young days. In saying a word to the teachers, he would remind them how needful their work was, and how the value of Sunday school work in the Church was increasing year by year, for they all knew that according; to the legislation el the day we are to have free educa- tion—but in what form shall we receive it? There could be no doubt that if the voluntary schools were.made free, there would be some alteration in the control of those schools, and although the present system of manage- ment might remain fora time, ultimately we should hear the cry for "public control of public schools." What kind of religious training then, he asked, would be given in the day schools, when the management of those schools comprised men of various religious thoughts and opinions? Would they allow the Apostles' Creed, which had just bean repeated, to be taught as fully and as fear- lessly as they. as Churchpeople, would have it taught? If they believed that the teachings ef the Church was of any value, they must recognise the growing responsibil- ity of oar Sunday schools, and it was most imperative that the work should be done as efficiently as possible. The prizes were then distributed.

div.head: TRUANT SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION,
div.p: TRUANT SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION,

The District Education Committee's report contained a recommendation that the Board join other School Boards and School Attendance Committees, in urging the County Council of Lancashire to consider the question of pro- viding Truant School accommodation in Lancashire.— Mr. Deacon urged that there vv as great need for such ac- commodation, that which existed being inadequate, and it being exceedingly difficult to get a boy in from that district, because there was not room, and when they got him and he came out and attended school badly again, the Board could not get him back till some months after. This fact had a bad effect on the attendance; and the great thing must be to be able to deal with a boy imme- diately he began to attend badly. The Committee there- fore were unanimously of opinion that the County Council should be requested to provide Truant School accommodation. There was a great feeling against sending a boy to an industrial school merely because he played truant.—The minutes of the Committee, with the recommendation in question, were adopted.

div.head: SCHOOL M-ANAGEMSNT COMMITTER
div.p: SCHOOL M-ANAGEMSNT COMMITTER

This Con-TM—it-tee reported that they had arranged that the holidays at the schools this year should be Whit week and three weeks at midsummer, commencing at Joon on June 26th and ending on the morning of July 20th.— The Chairman asked if the like rule was being adory.ad at the denominational schools.—The Rev. J. Clarke said he did he did not think so. As far as those with •which he was connected was concerned it had been arranged

give the two holidays together instead of at different times, as it was thought unadvisable to give a week first and then three weeks in June and July. He thought it better to give four weeks in June. The attendance at St. Mary's school was very much influenced by the influenza, and four weeks' holiday at once would allow more time for this to pass away. He did not know of any district where the holidays were the same as those of the Widnes School Board.—The Chairman thought the matter would be one for the consideration of the com- mittee another year; and that it was desirable that the Board schools and the denominational schools should have their holidays at the same period —Major Wareing and Mr. Quinn thought the teachers would prefer the four weeks' continuous holiday. The minutes were confirmed. SITES AND BUILDING COMLIITTEE,

This Committee recommended that the following ten- ders be accepted, viz. :-1, Messrs. Lea and Sons. for cleaning and repairs required at the Simm's Cross and , Warrington-road Scho)ls. 2, Mr. C. J. Sutcliffe for painting, cleaning and repairs,at the West Bank Schools. 3, Messis. Lea and Sons, for new floor at the F..imin's Cross Infant School. 4, Messrs. Dunbar,Kelly, and Co., for the granolithic pavement required at the various Board School play grounds (the payment to be deferred to the next school year). 5, Messrs. Johnson and Co., for slating required at the West Bank Board School.— The Chairman remarked that the Board's Schools did wear out in a most extracrdinary way, but the Board were not answerable for the weather or the climate, or the children's rough ways. £5OO had been asked for the annual cleaning,repairing,painting, and whitewashing of the schools, and the amount spent and to be spent would exceed that by £22.—Dr. ()glee& thought that each member of the Board should be furnished with a copy of the specification of such expenditure. This, he said, in reply to the Chairman would be in accordance with the I practice of the Local Board. He intimated that he I would send in a resolution on the subject for next meet- ing.—ln reply to Mr. Deacon as to whether the expenses for repairs were, as in some towns, the result of bad work, the Chairman said there was no re-construction.— The tenders recommended for cleaning, painting, and repairs were accepted.—On the item as to Messrs. Lea and Son's tender for flooring being considered. Major Wareing objected to painters and decorators being employed to do joiners' work, and said it was the first time he had heard of such a thing. The Board through confining themselves to local tenders were reduced to the necessity of employing anybody they could get.—The Chairman explained that one reason for the Committee's recommendation was that the committee had found that when two different contractors were employed in the same school they got in each other's way ; and damaged each other's work. It was resolved that the item as to flooring be referrei back that separate tenders might be obtaheed for repairing it and for new flooring. As to the recommendation for the acceptance of Messrs. , Dunbar, Kelly, and Co.'s tender for paving the play- grounds, Dr. O'Keeffe took exception to the proposal to defer payment till the next school year, on the principle that the Board ought not " to hand down an incubus to future generations." He proposed that that minute be not passed.—The Chairman said the Board had not the money to spend this year. After some , conversation the item was withdrawn.—The recommendation for the acceptance of Messrs. Johnson and Co.'s tender was then agreed to.—There was no other business of importance.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF OUIRDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF OUIRDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, ott Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present, Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., Edwards, J. Baguley, Baxter, E. Aaron, Lewis, J. W. Bagitley, Pickering, J. Weir, J. Parr, J. Ashton, (clerk).

div.head: OUTDOOR RELIEF.
div.p: OUTDOOR RELIEF.

Mr. Speakman gave notice of a motion for next meet- ing as to the resolution adopting the regulations for the distribution of outdoor relief, approved at the con- ference of the Poor Law Authorities at Northwich. Mr. Aaron gave notice of his intention to move the adoption of new rules drawn up by the Committee appointed for that purpose. SALARIES, FRES, &C.-THE COUNTY RATE.

The Clerk presented a return of salaries and fees of officials and indoor and outdoor relief for the year ended 31st March, 1891, and of amounts of county rate for the years 1884- to 1890 inclusive. The Clerk kElenry binaker) received salary and fees £475 12s. 2d. ; Medical Officers: Dr. McDougall, £ll9 175.; W. H. Carruthers, £5O Ils.; Adam Argo, £9O ; T. P. Weaver, £lO3. total £363 81. Relieving Officers: George Ward, £122 10s. ; Thomas Riley, £154. ss. 7i.; W. R. DePrez, £136 10s. 9d., total, £435 6s. sd. Workhouse appointments: John Robin- son, medical -officer, £95 17s. id.; Joseph Cunnah, master, £9O ; Ellen Emma Cunnah, matron, £5O; M. A. Humphreys, nurse, £25; Robert Naylor, schoolmaster, £4O 12s. 6d. •, Miss Nuttall, schoolmistress, £4l 55., total, £342 14s. 7d. Other officers, John Dun, treasurer, £25; John Frodsham, collector, £4O ss. 10d •, Henry Coleburn, vaccination officer and registrar, £lll 4s. id. ; T. Bowyer, inquiry officer, £5; E. Howard, inquiry officer, £5; S. 'Tomlinson, attendance officer, £10: Rev. L. D. 1,. Bennett, chaplain, £4O, total, £236 9s. 11d. Rural Sanitary Authority Officers :Jos. Adams, medical officer, £120; James Farrington, inspector, £150; assistant overseers, £B9l 123. ; superannuation allowances, £B2; total £3,097 3s. id. The indoor relief for 1890-91 amounted to £1,104 10s. sd. ; out door relief, same period, Runcorn district, £2,182; Frodsham dis- trict, £BB2 103. 7d.; Budsworth district, £6Bl 14s. 9d.; total, £3,726 us. 7d. The cost of the non-resident poor was £55 is. sd. and of lunatics £743 9s. 4d.-The Clerk also submitted again the particulars as to county calls produced at the last meeting and published.-Mr. Speak- man said there was no comparative statement there to show how the rate had been increased by lid.-Mr. Bax- ter said the call from the County Council was £7,000 as against about £4,000 for several years past.-Mr. Parr stated thit it was certain the rates were increasing to the extent stated and unfortunately he had as vet seen no benefit from it.-Mr. J. Baguley said when -the esti- mates were presented, they were told the increase in the rate was lid. in the £ and at Halton the increase in the rate was nearly 4d. They had a rate of Is. Bd. in the £. -The Chairman remarked that that increase might be caused by the highway rate, or probably their balance had got very low.-Mr. Baguley said the benefit for this half year was £94 more than that of the corresponding half year in 1890. They had no balance.-A Member asked how it was that Mr. Stokes who had asked for this information was not present ; and it was stated he was very ill with influenza.-Mr. Speakman said he held in his band a third budget of the County Council,and if the members of the Board had a copy it would be very useful to them and allay. a good deal of the feeling that seemed ! naturally to have arisen at the increased expendi- ture of the Council. He might give the members of the I Board a little idea of how the increase of lid. in the £ had arisen. At one there was a penny or thereabout taken from the rates by the Weaver Trust not being able to subsidise the county, as they had done in the past. It was not the fault of the Weaver Trust, but simply through loss of traffic on the river and that was to be I mourned, because the trustees were in the unfortunate position of having a debt of about £251,000. It appeared to him that the trustees had not had a sinking fund to meet future contingencies but had continued retying the county £lO,OOO or £15,000 a year, when they had the money. Trade had left the Weaver to the extent that they were without that sum to spare. Taking that into consideration,the only increase in the county that needed explanation was id. in the £. The main roads of the county were absorbing,and would absorb for a consider- able length of time, a very great amount of money. It was stated that the roads in different parts of the country had been starved, but they were now being put into a good condition, and for two or three years the rate was bound to go up, to meet this increased expenditure on the roads.-Mr. Edwards said Mr. Speakman only ac- counted for ltd. but 'Mr. Baguley said at Halton the in- crease was 4d.; how did that arise ?-Mr. Speaknian said while he was speaking of the Counts, of Cheshire Mr. Bartley was speaking of the parish -of Halton, which was a very different thing. No doubt the clerk would be able to explain to Mr. Baguley how the rate at Halton had increased to that extent.-It was decided after some , discussiTa, that the subject be deferred until next meet- I ing, and that in the meantime the Clerk should obtain further information, and make his return with a com- parative statement. It was also resolved that the re- turns should be printed, together with the County Coun- cil Budget referred to by Mr. Speakman, and circulated

amongst the members.—The Chairman read a letter he had received from Mr. T. Lea, who said he was un- able to attend the meeting, and asked that consideration of the case of Mrs. O'Malley should bo deferred to next meeting.—Mr. Ward, the relieving officer accused, said he had received a letter from Mr. Edwin Imison, who stated that he saw from the Examiner that lie was said to have recommended a person named O'Malley to see Mr. Lea, regarding Mr. Ward's alleged rough treatment. Somebody's imagination had been running riot, as no complaint had been made to him. He knew nothing whatever about the case.
GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT RUNCORN.

Colonel Ducat, ILE., an Inspector to the Local Government Board, held an inquiry, at Runcorn Town Hall, on Wednesday, into an application of the Board of Commissioners for permission to borrow £245, for a period of five years, for the purchase of scavenging plant. Mr. E. Marshall (secretary), and Mr. M. Barker (surveyor) were the only persons present. The appliances included three horses, three sets (.1 har- ness, one canal boat, a quantity of rope, Ex.—ln answer to the Inspector, Mr. Marshal/ said,the loans at present obtained by the Board amounted to £12,570, of which £1,606 had been repaid, leaving the indebtedness ef the town at £10,964.—The Inspector said from the figures supplied to him the Board appeared te be £2,650 in arrears with their repayinents.—Mr. Marshall said that was not so. The Board liquidated the loans by mean; of a sinking fund, and since 1879 the Board had paid off loans amounting to nearly £3,000, but he was unable to tell without a search, which would take a considerable time, the particulars of the loans.—The Inspector said there was no objection to the sinking fund described so I-mg as the loans were paid off within the specified time. —Mr. Marshall said last year they paid £295 into the sinking. fund. He estimated that dila rear they would pay £36s.—Colonel Ducat asked to be supplied with the particulars of the loans paid off, and closed the inquiry.
NEW MAGISTRA.TES FOR WARRINGTON.

A number of names of local gentlemen having been aubnaitted to the Duke of Rutland, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, for appointment as justices of the peace for the borough of Warringt three of these gentlemen have been communicated with and have notified their willingness to accept the position ; and they have, we understand, all been accepted. These gentlemen are Alderman J. E. Wright, architect and surveyor, Sankey- street, and residing at 37, Wilson-Patten-strelt.; Councillor E. Greenall, junior, wine and spirit merchant, Bridge-street, and residing at Hill Top, Latchford ; and Councillor James Fairclough, corn merchant, 5, Wilson Ptitten-st. All these gentle- men are Conservatives in politics. As a public man Alderman Wright is best known in connection with the work of the Town Council, he having been a member of that body since 1882. Councillor Greenall has been a member of the Corporation for about six years, and, it is understood, he is now the nominee of the Conservative party for the aldertuanic post rendered vacant by the resignation of Alderman Davies. Mr. Faircloug,,ll was a member of the Town Council for a short time, but was a defeated candi- date.at the elections last November. Within the last few weeks, however, he has been elected unopposed to the Council for the Latchford Ward, filling the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Joseph Taylor. THREE LIBERALS NAMED, BUT DECLINED. We learn that the list of names submitted to the Chancellor of the Duchy included three Liberals, namely, Mr. F. A. Roberts, a member of the Lanca- shire County Council, and Warrington Town Coun- cil ; Mr. George Dakin, wholesale grocer; and Mr. John Geddes, wholesale . tea and coffee merchant, but none of the three have consented to accept the position. Mr. Roberts declined as far back as 1831 to allow his name to be placed on the Commission of the Peace, and Mr. Geddes has also, we believe, previously declined.
ILLNESS OF SIR GILBERT GREENALL.

j We regret to learn that the member for the I borough is indisposed—suffering, we are informed from the prevailing malady. Until lately, Sir Gil- bert has enjoyed good health for a person of his advanced years, but he has not been able to journey to London and attend to his Parliamentary duties. It is understood that he will not come before the constituency at the next general election. The Conservatives have been considering who shall be their next candidate ; and rumour has it that the choice is likely to fall upon Mr. J. Charlton Parr, J.P., of Grappenhall Heyes.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon, when there were preseut : Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. C. B. Johnson, J. Goldsworth, Marsh, Griffith, James Burchall, Jos. Birchall, J. Ranson, J. Whalley, Edward Birchall, J. Ellison, R. A. Graves, W. I Lowe, W. Twist, J. Peover, W. Middlehurst, Daine, Davies, J. W. Wareing, E. Syder, J. Mercer, Hulme, Kenwright, Langton, Buckley, W. Borrows and A. F. Mann (acting clerk). A NEW CLERK Wawrao.—Before the ordinary meeting of the Board a private meeting of the members was held to consider the appointment of a new clerk. After a long discussion it was decided to advertise for a successor to the late Mr. Hartley who should devote the whole of his time to the duties of his office at a salary of £3OO per annum, out of which the necessary office staff should he provided. There were other emoluments estimated at , about £3OO, and security to the amount of £5OO would be required. Nsw CHAIRMAN.-Mr. James Rurchall, senior vice- chairman, was unanimously elected chairman of the Board, in succession to Mr. W. Tyrer, whose resignation was announced by the Local Government Board. -Messrs. W. Daiue and P. Longton were elected senior and junior vice-chairmen respectively.

THE SUDDEN DEATH OF THE CLARK.— MT. W. Paine referred to the great loss which the board had sustained by the sudden death of their late clerk, Mr. Hartley. He eulogised the high character and abilities of the late Mr. Hartley, and said, they had lost an estimable servant. He •moved that a letter of condolence be forwarded to the widow and family.— Mr. Wareing, in seconding. said Mr. Hartley had been cut ' off in the very flower and youth of his manhood, and it was difficult to realise that they should no more see his familiar form or*hear his well-known voice. It was a terrible thing that at such a short interval they should be called upon to mourn the loss of such a man as Mr.Hart- ley.—The Chairman said that Mr. Hartley's death was an irreparable loss to the Union.—Mr. H. H. d'A. Willis, J.P., as an ex-officio Guardian,testified to the respect and regard which had always peen entertained for him.—The resolution was carried unanimously. ANOTHNR RESIONATION.—A letter was read from Mr. J. Leatherbarrow, resigning his guardianship for Whiston township. THE VACANCY AT 80r.0.-4 he Local Government Beard wrote that by the death of Mr. Hartley, who was the returning officer for the election at Bold to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Chadwick, the election proceedings would fail and a new order would be required.—The Guardians decided to apply for orders for elections at Bold and lirhiston, and the question as affecting Prescot was left over. Ilsmr.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 554 inmates this week, 563 last week, 486 in the corresponding week last year; 85 vagrants had bees relieved against 69 last year. This was the principal business.

div.head: FR,ODSIIAM.
div.p: FR,ODSIIAM.

WIIIT-MONDAY FESTIVITIES.—By 9 a.m.on Monday. the bright summer's sun had enticed a large number of visi- tors to Frodsham, in order to see amcngst other things, the gathering together of the members of the several benefit societies, which on this, their annual festival day, march in procession, headed by bands of musicians, to the Parish Church. Frodsham, for a special service. The societies represented on the present occasion were as fol- lows :—Court Independence,No 410 of Ancient Foresters, headed by the Parish Church Bible Class Band; the Modern Druids, Marden Queen Lodge, headed by the Widnes Band ; Grand United Order of Oddrellows, Em- Mem of Hope Lodge, No. 516, headed by the Frodsham Military Band; and the Independent Order of Rechabites, Delight of Frodsham,Tent No. 230, headed by the Helsby Brass Band. The first three tents were fairly represented in comparison with previous years. but the Rechabites had a small number in attendance, although there has been an increase since the last festival. On arrival at the church the members were ushered to their respective seats, and the service of the day gone through, after which the Vicar (the Rev. H. M. Blogg, M.&.) preached from St. John iii. 16—" For God so loved the world that He gave His only Son, that whosoever believeth on Him shall have everlasting life." In conclusion, he referred to the fact of the several clubs being founded upon the principle of love, and expressed a hope that God would bless the members in their homes, bless their wives and bless their children, and all who were near and dear to them, and help every one to realise how much God had done foi them, not only temporarily,but in that fle gave His only begotten Son in order that every one might have everlasting life. On the re-assembling Of the members, the respective patrons of the clubs were waited upon, as is usual, and thence to the Lodge-rooms, where dinner. &c., had been provided. During the day large numbers of people from Mallches- ter,Warrington. Chester, Runcorn,Liverpool, and Nortn- wich came to the town and to the hills.

div.head: NORTH WALES MYSTERY.
div.p: THE NORTH WALES MYSTERY.

Mrs. Duncan was visited on Wednesday night by her cousin. Mrs. Smith, of Birmingham, whom she recog- nised, and thanked for corning to see her. The husband has again been visited in gaol by his solicitor. Mrs. Duncan raterday morning was reported still better. Mr. r. B. Farrington, C.E., Conway, accom- panied by Superintendent Williams, has made a survey of the scene of the outrage for the purposes of the prose- cution. A MUTUAL DELUSION. A Helsin,gfors correspondent. telegraphs : The Bettws-y-Coecttragedy has created a considerable sensa- tion here. It appears that Duncarj was employed hy M. Jaederholm. The father of the woman considered Dun- can wealthy, and favoured his daughter's marriare,while Duncan erroneously thought M. Jaederholm to be rich. Both Mr. and Mrs. Duncan seemed to be very happy, and the news of the outrage was received with great sur- prise. It is presumed that the man is insane.

div.head: WHIT-MONDAY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: WHIT-MONDAY AT WARRINGTON.

Whit-Monday in point of weather proved a mush more congenial day than its immediate predecessors had been,and accordingly was made the most of by ' the Warringtonians, although indeed it was hardly I either as to temperature or brightness as inspirit- ing as could have been desired. Prom the Central and Bank Quay Stations about 1,600 persons be- took themselves to Liverpool and about 1,000 to Manchester. There were about 500 excursionist 8 from the town to Southport,as many more to Prod- sham, hundreds to Chester and Blackpool,and about 100 to Birmingham. Many preferred to go further afield, and availed themselves of a cheap trip for some days to the metropolis. There was the usual advent of cyclists to the town and district, while the more old-fashioned methods of locomotion by horse power were also extensively used by holiday- seekers. Business, of course, was generally con- signed to oblivion for the day. Ihe Whitecross Wire Ropery had their first an- nual picnic on Monday. Leaving Warrington at '7-30 a.m., they journeyed by road through 1100 Green to Knutsford, at which place refreshments were partook of. After viewing the procession and the different places of interest, a run was made through Chelmford to Alderley. After a substantial dinner,the Edge copperraines,the Wizard,and other places of interest were visited. The return journey was through Bowden and Lymm, arriving in War- rington at 8-30 p.m., after a most enjoyable day.

Business in Edinburgh wa—s suspended on Thursday, the Queen's birthday being celebrated. div.head: YON LONGFORD WORKS.
div.p: YON LONGFORD WORKS.

Dear Mester Editur,—it's welly time Somebody had a go i' savage rhyme, Abeawt yen Longford Works, or, one fine day, There'll be some rukshuns, an' th' Owd Lad to play! Just look at me, aw'm now't but skin an' bone; An' not lung sin' aw poo'd deawn sixteen stone ; So when aw turn eawt nea.w, aw th' nayburs sneawt, "Go in, owd moo, theawr't noan fit to ba eawt ! " Eawr Doctor sed aw're goin' to my doom, By shiftin' eawt o' teawn, an' nearer Hulme ; An' th' strungest mon i' Sodom couldn't stop Moor then a month abeawt yon Pizon Shop! Why, th' London and North West, I hoar um say, Is goin' to tak' their trains another way. Becoze they caun't stop ev'ry hole an' chink, Fro' th' carriages, and so keep eawt o' th' stink. Pastjocksy Lane, if yo should chance to ride, Yo're shure't ha' trouble i' yore poor inside, An', like a woman i' a wobbly ship, Yo'll gether "second seet" while on yore trip ! If this he true —an' theer'sno reawm for deawbt-- Wotever are eawr Cea.wncillors abeawt ? Are we to coss um aw fro "pow to post," For lettin' one owd stager rule ther roast ? An' while this same owd joker works his whims, Are we to twiddle thumbs an' warble hymns? Then, while he's makin' up a thumpin' bill, Are we to stump up. tho' it mak's us ill, An', like a l'arson's Skoo o' frickent lads, Sit mum, while Owd John fiddles wi' his fads? It's quite high time eawr Ceawncillors should know, No siagle Audermon mun "boss eawr show " ; We know John's strung,—but, hang it aw they're strunger, An' marmot stond his bossin' anny lunger ; Or, if they dun, there'll be a recknin' day, When some on urn 'ufi hey to clear the way For better men : wo winnot be put deawn, Brth biggest on as ever coom it'h' teawn ! So, let uni tak' a warnin' fro a chum, An' sit no Wager i' the Ceawacil, dumb; Eawr dander's gradely up, an' yo'll soon find, Ther's no mistake, we'n quite made up eawr taind, That, come what will, thoose wo shall sarve us reet, We'll help um in the Ceawncil to a seat ; But thoose we shurk ther work, beyond a deaubt, We'll gie urn ther deserts, an'—purr um eawt! WM 0' PEGS. Warriton, 15, 5, 91.
THE FINANCES OF CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

From the third annual badget of the ,'County Coancil, referred to by Mr. P. Speakman at Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday, we extract the following figures. The estimated income for the current year ending Mandl, 1892—including the balances in hand—is .£140,316 Ss. 7d. A 4 the esti- mated expenditure for the same period amounts to £222,016 14s. 31, there,will be required to be raised by the rates the following sums :—From county rate, £61,025 12s. id.; from bridge rates, £283 13s. 101.; from the police rates combined, £20,205 19s. 91. ; and the above will require a county rate ot 51. in the Land police rates equal to liol. in the against a county rate• last year equal to &id. in the and police rates about 2ici. in the L. Practically there is an estimated increase in the county rate of 10. in the over last year and this increase is caused by there being a smaller balance by £12,586 to commence the present year than there was twelve months a4O; also by an increased expenditure in main roads; also in pro- viding for the contingencies in relation to tho annual elections to the County Council and also there being no credit payment estimated as likely to be received frona the he river Weaver during the year. With respect to the item Illa in roads, which appeared to be the largest item estimated for, there is an estimated increase in the expenditure, but as the County now had to bear the full charge of the costs of the rural main roads and the work being performed by the County work- men; the highway boards are entirely relieved from any expenditure in this respect, and also the local boards and other highway authorities being re-imbursed to almost their total cost of main roads from the county rate there should be a very considerable decrease in the highway rates of the county which are levied locally by the highway boards and local boards and boroughs. The County Council had now to provide for items which are new to the county expenditure, amongst which are the following :—Adjustment of financial relations, County Council Association, County Council elections, railway rates and charges, river pollution, sea fisheries, technical education expenses, entire cost of main roads, also the management of the exchequer contribution account, in- cluding new grants on account of school fees of pauper children, and the costs of Union officers, and also the technical education grant, and the matter in relation thereto.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A DANGEROUS DOG AT LARGE.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, Samuel Green, labourer, of 18, Hind-street, was charged that he being the owner of & dangerous dog did not keep it under proper control on the 9th inst. P.C. Critchley said about five minutes past ten on Saturday night, the 9th inst., two girls named Mary and Elizabeth Rawlinson corn- plained that one of them had been bitten by the dog on the defendant's doorstep. She had been bitten by it *ace before in his yard. Agnes Rawlinson, a child about five years of age, then deposed the dog having bitten her en the arm.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay 15s. 6d. costs, and that the dog be destroyed.

div.head: SUSPICIOUS CYLLItACTSES
div.p: SUSPICIOUS CYLLItACTSES

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, John Dunn and Win. Raymand were brought up on suspicion of having stolen from the Ship Canal Works a quantity of copper washers found in the possession of one of them. Police-Sergeant Monaghan deposed to seeing the pri- toners in Church-st., the previous evening, one of them carrying a bag with a bass inside. Seeing it was very heavy he asked him what he had got inside and he re- plied" Only a bit of copper." He (the Sergeant) found that he was carrying a large quantity of copper washers. The prisoner said "I picked them up at Hollins Green. To tell you the truth a saddler gave them to us." Such articles being strange things to come from a saddler,wit- ness took the prisoners into custody. They were re- manded to the custody of the Cheshire county police.
FURIOUS DRIVING

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Sa.turday, Albert Halliwell, was charged with furiously driving a pony and trap to the danger of passengers in Sankey-st., on Sunday the 10th inst. P.C. Corcoran said the defen- dant was driving at such a rate that he shouted at him, but he took no notice. There was another young man with him, and witness told him to take the reins, as he was incapable of driving. Witness stopped the trap and the defendant's name and address. He went away, and then came back and asked him how he dared stop him in the middle of the street. P.S. Jones, P.C. Woods and Mr. Burrows, county court bailiff, corrobmated. Sergt. Jones said if the defendant had not been stopped the trap would have been driven against the Union Bank Thera were two or three hundred people at Market Gate at the time, waiting for the procession of the Labourers' Union.—Peter Ratcliffe, ostler at the Ram's Head, said the pony was going at the rate of only four or five miles an hour.—The defendant was fined 20s. and costs.

div.head: CONVIVIAL COMEDIAN,
div.p: A CONVIVIAL COMEDIAN,

At the Borough Police Court. on Tuesday, Edward Yasey, a married man, and a comedian, who said he had been performing last week at the Empire Theatre, was tharged with being drunk and disorderly in Erwood-st. that morning. The confused and imperfect state of his dress, and the battered condition of his face gave him a very sorry and dissipated appearance, under which he preserved a certaiit air of gentility which contrasted strangely therewith.—P.S. Jones said a gentleman came to him and told him that the defendant was ill-using his wife in Friars Gate, and on going there he found him drunk and "completely covered with blood." He would not come away, as though he wanted to be locked up, consequently he took him into custody.—The prisoner, fa reply to the Chairman, said he had a couple of drinks and did not remember what occured afterwards. He bad to appear in Manchester on Tuesday.—The Chair- man: Before the magistrates or before the public? (Laughter.)—The prisoner admitted that he had been twice before the magistrates.—The Chairman: You won't be fit to appear in public for some time. (Laugh- ter.)—He was fined ss. including costs. A STARTLING APPARITION IN TEE STREET._

John Green, a tramp, who appeared in court clothed only in shirt and trousers, an.i who said he came from Stockport, was charged that he was found wandering in a state of nudity in Winwick-at., on Saturday afternoon. The constable who proved the case said the prisoner was in the street with absolutely no clothing on; and witness on accosting himcould not get a word out of him. It was stated that the prisoner was out of his mind ; but he was better now than when he was apprehended. In re- ply to the Mayor. the constable said the prisoner had ripped up all his clothes.—The Mayor (to the prisoner) : Have you been drinking ?—The prisoner: I had got a little drink, and I wasstopping out at night.—The Chief Constable: Inspector Cox says he had the appearance of having been drinking.—ln reply to the Mayor, as to why the man was allowed to appear in court, ill-clad as he was, said when men were like this, it was best to let them have their bout out. If they were supplied with fresh clothing, they would only go somewhere else and do the same thing ; and there was such a thing as having too much sympathy with a man like him.—The Mayor (to the prisoner) : If we let you off, where will you go ,to ?—The prisoner: I will go to Manchester.—The man was discharged, the Chief Constable promising to see him well out of the tr.wn ; and he was soon after fitted .out with a suit of decent clothes, and despatched in the -direction in which he wanted to go. THEFT or Two &mamma.

Yesterday, before Mr. John White and Alderman garrison, John Warburton, aged 17, lately employed at 3lessrs. Rylands Brothers' wire works' residing at 33, School Brow, was charged with stealing 2s. the property of Sarah Hallows, coal dealer, 49, Greenell-st., the previous morning. Chief Constable Hunt stated that the prisoner met a lad named llrmston employed by the prosecutrix, when he was out retailing coal, with a horse and waggon, and offered to carry some of the coal, and the offer was accepted. l'resently Urinston wanted change, and gave the pri- soner a 2s. piece to get some, but he never came back ,with it. The prisoner, on being subsequently asked about the mcney, produced sixpence, and said that was all he had out of it. Police-Sergeant Taylor appre- hended him, and he told him he had a shilling, and had that a boy named Dagnall a shilling. It was discovered that there was no such boy, and that the prisoner had had a good dinner, and bought pipes and ether articles with the money. A woman with whom the prisoner lodged, his mother tieing in the Workhouse, and he hav- ing no father, gave him a good character, and the Bench contented themselves with recording a conviction •against him. STEALING 9s. FROM A PUDDLER.

At the Borough Police 6t-i-r-t, on Monday, Michael Preston, living with his father, Wm. Preston, lodgipg- housekeeper, 23, Bank-street, was charged with stealing on Saturday night, from the person of Michael Welsh, puddler at Bewsey Forge, lodging at 23, Bank-street, the sum of 9s. Chief Constablo Hunt said the complainant was returning fromwork on Saturday afternoon, with his wages 30s. in his pocket, when he was met or way- laid by the prisoner who lived on such men as he, and they went into the Bay Horse in Winwick-street, and had two pints of alo, the complainant paying for them. Welsh subsequently paid for drink for Preston at the Royal Arms, and afterwards went tea shop and paid a bill there and to his lodgings and paid his landlord's bill. The prisoner stuck to him and asked him to pay for another quart which he did, and after drinking his pint fell asleep. Soon after the prisoner was seen to put his hand in the complainant's pocket, draw something out and put it into his own. Information was given to the police at the request of the prisoner's father. Police Con- stable Monaghan deposed to apprehending the prisoner at his fathers house. He was drunk and lying on the seat in the kitchen, the complainant being in his com- pany. The nriconer was so violent on being arrested that he had to be carried all tbe way to the pohce station by SeNeant, Alonaglian and other officers.—Evidence was gin by Michael Welsh who deposed that after paying

vrt-at he owed, he had 7s. 10d. and seine loose money,but after finally leaving the prisoner he had not a halfpenny piece. John Bums having also given testimony the pri- soner was sent to jail for a month with hard labour. A RUFFIANLY ASSAULT ON A WIFE. At the Borough Police Court yesterday,Thomas Jack- son, aged 19, wire weaver, was charged by his wife Elizabeth Jackson, fustian cutter, with assaulting her on the 16th inst. Mr. Browne appeared for the complain- ant and Mr. Forshaw for the defendant. Mr. Browne said the parties, who lived in Beer-st., were married last Walking Day, and it seemed to have been a most miser- able life. The complainant for protection from her hus- band had been obliged to have her little sister living with her. On Saturday morning he got up and said he would go and fetch a knife and stick her through. She and the I little girl, who was screaming.attempted to get into the street but he prevented them. The same day the husband and wife agreed at the mother's house to separate. She and her little sister were taking some things from the defendant's house, as desired by him, when he came and thumped her with his fist and kicked her on the knee, and asked the little girl to pick up an ornament, and as she was doing so kicked her fingers. The defendant could earn good wages, but lay in bed and would not go to work.—Mr.Forshaw said he had a good defence, but pleaded guilty on his client's behalf on condition of the Bench making a separation order. The complainant gave evidence corroborating her solicitor's statement, and said he had previously assaulted her several times, having given her a black eye once, and thrashed her the night before her confinement; and the i baby was n a weak state and subject to fits.—Defendant laid the blame on his mother-in-law's blackguarding him. She was present in court and ex- claimed that he had slept with his mother for five weeks. —The defendant complained of his wife not providing breakfast, and that he had had to pay £4 for her debts. —Another woman in court: Yes, that he has. (Laugh- ter.)—Alderman Harri6on : Another mother-in-law. (Re- newed laughter.)—The Bench mulcted the defendant in costs and made a separatioa order. _ _ _ _

THEFT FROM A CLOTHES LINE.—Two WOMEN OF METTLE. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, George Andrews, Ship Canal labourer, of Latchford, and a native of Somersetshire, was charged with stealing, on the previous day, from a clothesline in the back yard of Ellen Burke, 3, Naylor-et., three holland aprons the property of Winifred Burke, a young woman lodging with her.—Chief Constable Hunt stated that about 3 o'clock on Sunday afternoon, the prisoner was seen in the yard, and later on was observed by Elizabeth Lawrenson, a fellow-lodger of the owner, to be taking the aprons off the line. She went in and informed the complainant, and they came out and demanded the aprons from him. They could see he had something bulky in his pocket, but he denied having them, and would not give them up. Ellen Burke and the complain- ant followed and laid hold of him, the former wrestling with him, and pulling him to the ground a time or two. He struck the complainant twice, and if he (the Chief Constable) had known this sooner would have been charged with the assault. The prisoner got away from her twice,but she seized him again,and this timehe could not get away.—The prisoner said he came from Latch- ford with some mates, and had a drop of drink which overcame him. They went into the Gun public-house and there invited the complainant to drink with several more. He and a mate went with her to her home and had drink with her there. They then went out and being overcome with drink he supposed he had taken the aprons for devilment. The complainant gave evidence, and denied speaking to him, in the Gun Inn, and that he or his mate was in the house, and Ellen Burke corro- borated the latter statement, and the Chief Constable said Mrs. Burke kept only women lodgers, and would allow no men in her house.—The prisoner adhered to his statement, a-,d wanted the case adjourned that he might produce the man he named.—The Chief Constable said five aprons had been stolen, and perhaps the " mate " had got two of them.—The prisoner was fined 20s. including costs; in default 14 days.

div.head: MINOR. CASES.
div.p: MINOR. CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.—Before Alderm;n-Bui:g-e;;Whairman) and Councillor Voisey. A DISORDERLY YOUTH.—William Fudge, a boy, was charged under a warrant with being disorderly in Church- st., on the Bth of Feb. He pleaded not guilty.—F.C. Smith preyed the case, and said the defendant on the day in question, a Sunday, Was running about that street with three other boys, shouting and yelling as people were coming out of church. All of them except the de- fendant, who did not appear, were fined 2s. ed. and costs on the 16th of Feb. The defendant had since been working on the Ship Canal at Ellesmere Port. He was now also fined 2s. ed. and costs.
DnuNK.—John Cheadle, was charged with being drunk in Peter-st., on the 13th inst. He had been lying helpless on the footpath, and had to be taken home in a cab. He was fined ss.
HAVING A CRIMNBY ON FlRE.—Joseph Massey, grocer, corner of Priestley-st.' was fined is. for having his chimney on fire on the 13th inst. _ _
MONDAY- . —Before the Mayor (Alderman W. Francomb) - - -
in the chair ; and Alderm- en. Holrae4 and Sutton.
ARMY DRSERTION.—Renry Rogers, having deserted, on the 15th inst., H.M.2nd Cheshire regiment, stationed at Sheffield, was sent to Strangeways gaol to await an escort.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLT.—MichaeI Callaghan, 32ad appearance, who called himself a Ship Canal labourer, but who the Chief Constable stated, was one of those who would not work, was fined 103. and costs, in de- fault 7 days, for being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st., on Saturday night.—John Noon was charged with being drunk and disorderly and with assaulting Bridget Higgins, his mother-in-law, on Saturday night, in Orford-st. The evidence of Inspector Cox and P.C. Clough showed that the defendant was drunk and abus- ing his wife, using very bad language to her, near their house in Delan's-yard. His mother-in-law came out and spoke to him, and he struck her on till breast and neck, and knocked her to the ground. The officers had, it was stated, " a fine scuffle" to get him to the Police Station, his coat being torn to pieces in the struggle with them. The prisoner said he only shoved Mrs. Hig- gins away because she was tearing his clothes, but In- spector Cox said she never" handled" him.—The pri- soner was fined ss. • in default 7 days.—John Corcoran, drunk and disorderly in Church-st., on Sunday morn- ing, was fined ss. ; in default 7days. Dnumx.—Benjamin Houghton, drunk in Orford-st., on Sunday morning, was fined ss. ; in default 7 days. TUESDAY.—.Before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman) and E.

M. Crosfield. DISORDERLY CHARACTERS.—John Perkins and Edward Duffy, labourers, for being drunk and disorderly and fighting in Friars Green, the previous night, were fined ss. and costs each.--Margaret Stokes, wife of Alfred Stokes, of Howarth-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Antrobus-st., and with wilfully break- ing the window of her sister-in-law in that street, early that morning, doing damage to the extent of es. P.C. Woods said he heard a disturbance in the street, and the prisoner came running towards him in her stocking feet with her clogs in her hand. A man followed her and said she had just broken three windows. The prisoner's sister-in-law deposed that Stokes broke her window with her clogs, about one o'clock that morning, charging wit- ness with having her (Stc!kes's) husband there,which was not true. She broke witness's mother's and brother's windows the same night.---:The prisoner's husband was called, and said by the advice of the magistrates he had left his wife because she was always messing with other men and had pawned his clothes.—The Chief Constable said she had been brought up before for smashing win- dows. She was committed to prison for a month's hard labour.

OBJECTIONABLE OTITBITILDI NOB . —John Carr, Ellen Broderick, Wm. Yates, Sarah Cook, Peter Hines and John Rooney, whose addresses were respectively 10, 11, 12 and 13, Rose-yard,and 72, Cockhedge-lane respectively were prosecuted by Mr. Norman, chief Inspector of nuisances, for having outbuildings in a filthy condition, and fined is. each.—Mr. Norman mentioned that pro- secutions of this description were producing a good effect.

Scnoor. CASES.—At the instance of Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officor, the following convictions were recorded against persons for not sending their children regularly to school :—Peter Clough, labourer, Fennel-It.; Thomas Jones, Ship Canal labourer, Scott-st.. James Moseley, wire drawer, Lovely-lane; Wm. Peel, forge- man, Bewsey-road ; and Moses Williams, forgeman, Pierpoint-st., fined Ss. each. Benjamin Matthewman, wire weaver, Scott-st ; Charles Roberts, forgeman, Buckley-a., and John Stokes, forgeman, Bank Quay, 2s. 6d. each, Martin Varley, forgeman, Pierpoint-st., 2s.

TKURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman), Dr. Gornall, and Captain Ridgway. ASSAII/M ON A WIFE. George Povey, employed by Messrs. Forshaw and Co., was charged with assaulting his wife, Martha Povey, on the 19th inst. Mr. Forshaw, solicitor, appeared for the defence, and said the defen- dant promised to sign the pledge, and asked the magis- trates to content themselves with binding him over, his wife being ready to forgive him. The Bench ordered him to pay costs, and bound him over in his own recogniz- ances for £5 to keep the peace for six months. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. SIIIIIOI7B ACCUSATIONS AGAINST CONSTABLES. John Evans, a soldier, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st.' the previous night, also with asaulting Eliza- beth Ellen Fleming and P.C.'s Amson and Barlow.—P.C. Amseh deposed to the woman Fleming coming up to him and complaining that the prisoner and another soldier were shoving her and another woman about. Witness complained to him of his conduct, and went away; and just as he had done so the prisoner ran up to Fleming and struck her knocking her against the wall. The as- sault was not very serious,and witness gave him another chance to go but subsequently found him drunk and us- ing very bad language and he and P.C. Barlow took him to the Station. He was very violent and struck witness and Barlow.—P.C. Barlow said the prisoner struck and kicked him. A military sergeant gave prisoner a good character, and he was fined ss. and costs, or 7 dars. The Chief Constable said had the man not assaulted the police he would have been left to be dealt wlth by the military authorities.—George Baguley, was chargel with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-st., on Wed Heeday night. The defendant said he had not had a drop of

drink since a week last Monday. P.C. Lewis said about twenty minutes past eleven on the night in question V was on duty in Horsemarket-st., and saw the prisoner there drunk near tbe British Workman public-house singing and shouting. • He requested him to go away, but he refused, though he afterwards did so. They followed him and he said "If you come any further I will show you what I will do for you." They got his name and address. He then went into Mrs. Locker's house,and about twenty minutes after came ;nit and said with an oath that witness was the man that had been knocking him about. Witness, with the assistance. of P.C. Hollinworth, took him into custody.—P.C. linworth gave corroborative evidence.—Mrs. Locker said the defendant came to her house bleeding like a pig, and said he had been fearfully ill-used by a police officer. They came together te Market Gate to see another officer, and P.C.Lewis was there. He said he would give the prisoner more than he had had, as he had it in for him. rhey went into Buttermarket-st and there P.C. Hollinworth came up and laid hold of Baguley and held his head down and shoved him up the street. P.C. Lewis came up and took off his cape and belt and struck the defendant,catch- ing witness also ever the shoulder. She remonstrated with both officers, and Lewis threatened to give her as much if she interfered with him. Then Hollinworth said, "I leave it in for him, and I will give it him," and gave the defendant a kick which knocked him to the ground, and he lay there. She exclaimed that their con- duct was barbarous. The defendant was as sober as she was, and she was a teetotaller.—Mrs. Chadwick deposed to hearing screams in the yard adjoining her mother's house and finding the defendant and P.C. Lewis there, and that the former complained of the latter's ill-usage. She confirmed Mrs. Locker's evidence as to what took place at Market Gate and in Buttermarket-at. She said the defendant was sober, and that he was bleeding "furiously" at the mouth and nose. She said to the police the man had been up before and had not a very good character, but they ought not to uselhim like that. A gentleman advised her to take the number of the con- stables and bring them before the Watch Committee.— Both the constables denied the woman's statement.— George Makin said about a quarter to twelve he was coming past Market Gate and saw the prisoner on the ground and P.C. Lewis was trying te pick him up. He saw nothing before that. Another constable cams, and they took the prisoner along Buttermarket-at. He did net see them strike or kick the prisoner. Witness picked a cape up. He thought that fell in the struggle. He did not think the officers handled the prisoner mere roughly than necessary. He saw the women there, and they said one if the policemen had kicked the man.— P.C. Lewis said his lamp and his cape fell to the ground and the witness picked them up and handed them to him. The Bench considered there was a doubt in the case and discharged the defendant. VAGRANCY. - Thomas Walsham was charged with being found sleeping in a shed in Ashton's Yard, Bridge- st., that morning. The prisoner charged the constable who appeared against him with giving him three or four punches. The constable said he and Sergeant Rowbotham gave him a good shaking to rouse him; that was all.—P.C. Arnson said he was in the station when the prisoner was brought in, and he made no complaint about being struck.—The prisoner: He was going to strike me again in the police office if an officer had not stopped hina.—The chairman asked him if that officer was in court, and the prisoner said he was not. —A fine of ss. includixag costs—in default seven day's imprisenment--was imposed.

div.head: FRlDAT.—Before Mr, ...John White and Alderman
div.p: FRlDAT.—Before Mr, ...John White and Alderman

Harrison. CLAIMS FOR MAINTINANCE.—Sophia Brandwood, shop- keeper, claimed a sum of .£2 193. arrears due for main- tenance from her husband, Samuel Brandwood, file cutter.—Mr. Forshaw appeared for the complainant and Mr. Browne for the defence. An order was made for payment of 6s. a week, and the case adjourned to see whether the defendant paid.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNBSDAY.—Before Mr. John Rylands (chairman), and
James Tinsley. DRUNK.— John Riordan, drunk on, the 2nd inst. Fined 2s. 6d. and costs. .

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY —Frederick Yardsley and John Mannion drunk and disorderly on the 12th inst., at Houghton Green ; Mannion was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, and a warrant was issued for the apprehension of Yardsley who did net appear. REMOVING PIGS WITHOUT • LICENSH.—Joseph Owen, drover, was charged with removing two pigs from War- rington to Rixton without a license,contrary to the Con- tagious Diseases Animals Act. Evidence was given that he was driving four, and had licenses only for two. He was fined ss. and costs.

Tgerr OF A CAMP:— John McCarthy and Thomas Larkin, were charged with stealing at Croft, on the 29th of May, 1890, a cage value 55., the property of William Holley, of Padgate. The prosecutor said on the 28th of May, 1890, he was thrashing with a machine at Mr. Bate's farm, at Croft. The prisoners were employed on the farm assisting at the machine. Witness lent Thomas Mulligan a cage to carry some rats in request- ing him to return the cage on the following morning. He did not do so.—Mulligan brought the cage of rats to his lodgings, intending to take the cage to Holly's next day. McCarthy and Larkin lodged with him. They went next day to Warrington and sold the rats promis- ing witness to take the cage to Holley. Mary Clare, wife of Henry Clare,of Golborne-st.,Warrington,deposed to purchasing from McCarthy the rats and the cage, the latter for 25., Larkin being in his company. McCarthy said he sold the cage because Holley owed him Is. 6d. and mould not pay it; and Larkin said he only showed him the bill. McCarthy was fined 10s. and costs, and Larkin was dismissed. TEM CHARON OF BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A DAUGHTER.— John Dutton, of 8, Short-st., Golborne, was brought up on remand from the Occasional Court, charged with committing a brutal assault upon his daughter Maria Dutton, aged about 14, on the evening of the 9th inst. The circumstances have already been reported. In the absence of his wife the prisonor while drunk, told his daughter he would give her sixpence to go upstairs with him. She refused, and went across to a neighbour's and told her mother who was there. The prisoner followed her, and on being asked by her mother for an explanation denied the girl's statement and struck her on the head and arm with a poker, then the mother.—Mary Ann Tatham, the neighbour, said on the prisoner coming in Mrs. Dutton " chastised " him with making the pro- posal to his daughter, and he denied the statement, and got up to strike his wife. Witness knocked him down on a chair, but he got up again and committed the assault.—P..C. Dochrev deposed to apprehending the prisoner, and his replying to the charge " It is rather funny; I don't know what made me do it. I knew nothing about it till the sergeant told me next morning." —Frisoner pleaded hard to be dealt leniently with,stating that the matter was a family affair and drinking two or three glasses of beer, to which he was unaccustemed,had overcome him. He was sent to prison for a month, the chairman informing him that it was out of regard to his family net to him that the Bench did not send him for a fencer time.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TICURSDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brock aid Mr. E. Stapleton
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TICURSDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brock aid Mr. E. Stapleton
Bretherton.

MISCELLANEOIIS.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon the following for drunkenness :—Joseph Holden, Thomas Shone, Mary Daley, George Jones, John Moires, Mary Moires, Frederick Makin. and Frederick Rigby.— For allowing a chimney of his house to be on fire Richard Glassey was fined Is. and costs.—On the application of Superintendent Neblett, John Murty of Moss Bank was ordered to pay 2s. a week towards the maintenance of his son in a reformatory school.—A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed upon William Hill, bf Farnworth, for permitting his dog to be at large unmuzzled. TREF-T.—Rebecca Lacey, a married woman of Hale- wood, pleaded guilty to stealing a quantity of beef and bread valued at 2s. 6d. from the house of William Mercer, Limekiln-lane, Halewood. The woman said she would net have done it had she not been drunk. She was fined 20s. and costs.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas. DIZUNKENNESS.—Patrick Vaughan, Wm. Baker, Patk. Mlgariff, Joseph Redfern, James Finnegan, Geo. Holmes, Jelin Allerton, and Christopher Hough, were each fined in sums varying from 2s. 6d. to ss. for drunkenness. Patrick Lytham pleaded guilty to being drunk and in- capable. Superintendent Large said the man's incapabi- lity arose in some measure from the fact that his arm was dislocated. He was discharged. ROBBING HIS EMPLOYER.—Richard Rose (14), an er- rand boy in the employ of Mr. James Byrne, grocer, Church-st., was charged with stealing two sovereigns belonging to his master. On Saturday night Mr. Byrne placed four sovereigns on a shelf, and shortly after- wards found that two had been removed. He accused the boy of the theft; and after protesting his innocence, he at length went into the cellar, and produced the money, which he had hidden there. Mr. Byrne did not press the charge, and the boy was dismissed with a cau- tion, on his stepfather entering into sureties for his good behaviour. The prisoner said he had been tempted by some Widnes boys.

ASSAULT.—JaI7nes Miller was charged with assaulting John William Blakemore, a Canal constable. On Satur- day night, Blakemore was taking a drunken waterman to his boat, when the prisoner commanded him to let the man go, and on being told to mind his own business, struck the constable several times, and attempted to throw him down. In self-defence the constable drsw his staff, and a stiff struggle took place. The prisoner al- leged that the constable was drunk, but inspector Bow- yer said he was sober when at the Police Office. The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs.

MANCHESTER V. WAREINGTON.—This important fix- ture was played on Saturday in very wintry weather. Warrington, winning the toss, began batting shortly after o:te o'clock, Sydney and J. J. Crosfield facing the deliveries of Irving and Holland. With only 16 scored, J. .1. ran himself out, and with an additional run Lee was caught first ball. Three runs later snow began to fall, and the players adjourned for luncheon. On resum- itg, R. Smith was lbw at 30. At 47 Irving broke through S. M. Crosfield's defence; included in his 25were the three 4's and two 3's. Captain Manson treated the spectators to a bit of hard hitting, three 4's being hit in 'succession, and then retired for 21. C. G. Lawton was 'soon despatched, the result of a very good catch. T. Jolley and the Rev. F. C. Thnins could render no assist- anee to G. Clarke, and eight wickets had fallen for 85 Iwhen L. A. Voisoy came in. Both men scored freely, land at 3.30 the 100 was greeted with cheers, 80 runs hay- ing been out on in 70 minutes. W. H. Houldsworth relieved Holland at 114, and the innings quickly termin- ated. Clarke's 38 was an invaluable innings, including four 4's and three 3's. Voisey's 28 (not out) was the result of good cricket. Manchester sent in the brothers A. C. and J. A. M'Laren, A. C. being the first to retire, it being a very tame stroke which dismissed him. C. H. Haigh soon skied a ball which Voisey held safely-2 for 16. A. Knowles was next in, and also next out at 47, being caught be- hind the wicket. Two runs later J. A. M'Laren was bowled by R. Smith for 27, which included five 4's. With the score at 67,E. Radcliffe was caught by Le 6 for five. T. P. Bellhouse and W. H. Houldsworth put on 20 runs before the latter was finely caught by S. M. Crosfield for 28, in which he had hit three 4's, four 2's, and singles. Irving seemed to be ill at ease when facing Smith, but the seventh wicket was intact when the cen- tury was hoisted, as the result of an hour and 35 minutes' play. Four runs later an accident happened the home wicket-keeper, who had to retire, the captain taking the gloves. At 105 Irving was bowled by R. Smith. • The others were quickly despatched for 112. the last man being caught behind the wicket by Mr. Cros- field. Both teams fielded well, and had the weather been more favourable, a very large crowd would have wit- nessed the match. Score :

div.head: QUEEN AT DERBY.
div.p: THE QUEEN AT DERBY.

The Queen visited Derby on Thursday to lay the foundation stone of a new county Infirmary, breaking her journey to Balmoral for that purpose. Her Majesty, was accompanied by Prince and Princess Henry of Bat- tenburg. The town was very effectively decorated, and many thousands of people were in the streets. The wel- come given to the Queen was very enthusiastic. Reply- ing to an address from the Corporation, the Queen expressed her sorrow at the death of Lord Edward Cavendish and her sympathy with his father, with Lord Hartington, and the other members of his family. In laying the foundation stone of the new Infirmary the Queen said she took a warm personal interest in the institution, which she hoped would be of great value to the county.
