THE NEW MAGISTRATES.

Sir,—l was asked yesterday the following question— 'What de you th; nk of the new magistrates P"—meaning I suppose, what was my opinion of the discretion exer- cised in the selection made. I replied, "Th. least said the soonest mended." This opinion I still hold.
A DISGUSTED TORY.
A DISCLAIMER.

Sir,—Your report of Police Court cases last week in- cluded one in which a Joseph Caldwell was fined for causing a horse to be worked whilst in an unfit condition. I desire to point out that lam not the individual; and if you wilt kindly insert this: in your next issue I shall be much obliged.—Yours &c., JOSEPH CALDWELL, Baker. Warrington, May 21, 1891.

THE NATIONAL VIGILANCE ASSOCIATION AND CAPTAIN VERNEY. `Sir,—As numerous reports have appeared in the Press t. the effect that Captain Verney was a member of the National Vigilance Association, I trust you will permit me, through the medium of your journal, to give a direct denial to that statement, and to say that Captain Verney has never, in the remotest degree, been directly or indirectly connected with this association, nor any of its branch Committees. He has never subscribed to our funds, nor communicated with us, on any subject what- ever.—Yours, Szc.,
. , WM. ALEX. COOTE, Secratary, National Vigilance Association, 267, Strand, W.C., May 14th, 1891.
THE RECENT APPOINTMENT OF JUSTICES OF THE PEACE.

The Tory Duke of Rutland, at the request of Sir Gil- bert Greenell, prompted probably bf.his faithful hench- man, Mr. John White, 'has just appointed three new •J.P.'s, all of whom, of course, are true blues. Since the present Tory Government came into office, no fewer than 13 new magistrates have been appointed for Warrington all of whom have been members of the Tory party. Dur- ing the time the Liberal Government was in office, from 1880 to 1885, there were 12 justices appointed, of whom eight were Liberals and four were Conservatives. The contrast between the action of the two political parties is strikingly significent. Toryism, and Warrington Toryism especially, would conserve and preserve every bit of patronage of every kind for the members o f its own order, and, while only too glad to avail itself of the help freely rendered by so many Liberals of ability in the management of the public business of the borough. it has, so far,on every possible occasion, refused to allow the slightest participation in the honours which usually follow public service. The Toryism of the clique which dominates the policy of the party as enunciated in the Sankey-at. Emporium of Virtue is of the most contemp- tible character. It seeks to retain the mayoralty, the al- dermanic seats, and every other position of importance for the most subservient amongst its clientale,but the end is not far off. The last appointments show that the list of eligible (?) candidates for the office of Borough Magis- srate, must be nearly exhausted—some people say it was exhausted long since—and we shall soon, I hope, see a better state of things.—Yours,

RATEPAYER. (Our correspondent will see, from the news we give in another column, tint in this case—an exception to the rule—three Liberals were also asked, but they have declined, to allow their names to be placed on the list of the Commission of the Peace.—En. Ex.]

SPORTSMAN-LIKE CONDUCT AT E kRLESTO WN! Sir,—l wish to draw your readers' attentien to the -high-handed astion exercised by the gentlemen (?) com- prising the committee of the Earlestown (Viaduct) Cricket Club on Saturday last. It is one which, I feel sure, all lovers of fairplay and sport will condemn as unjust.

The e facts of the case are as follows : It appears that several young gentlemen, who are well behaved and highly-connected, have been in the habit of visiting the Institute grounds to witness the matches. They appear to have supported the visiting teams, which has given great offence to the home supporters. This so annoyed several of the latter that they made them a "mark." It took a critical form prior to the Leigh match ,when a certain club official sent a message that he would take 60 to 40 that they would defeat Leigh. This challenge ended in smoke, the official flying "The flag of distress." Another member of the elub showed a bolder front, by laying ss. to 2s. 6d. that Leigh would not score 40, before the latter batted. The member lost his bet, and what was the result? They are all expelled the grounds for one winning the paltry sum of ss.,this occurrence taking place on Saturday last. Now, I agree with the committee in putting down betting. but at the same time when they intended to adopt this course. why did they not deal out the same punishment to all the culprits? If they had done this, they would have had the hearty support of the public. It was in their hands to do so; but no, the great crime these yuung fellows had committed was lending their support to the visitors. What narrow-minded bigotry! Would it not have been better if they had notified these obnoxious individuals that they wished to dispense with their presence on the ground? This would have saved
all unpleasantness, and the condemned culprits humilia- tion.—Yours, Ex.,
Earlestown,
FAIRPLAY.
P.S.--For private reasons I refrain from publishing my name, but at the same time the Committee can rest assured the writer is in no way interested in the indivi- duals "black-balled."
METAPHYSICAL WOOL-GATHERING.

Sir,—Your indefatigable correspondent " Veritas "ap- pears to have had an attack of metaphysics. Now the briefest and wittiest metaphysical definition I over met with was that in Punch—" What is matter ? never mind; what is mind ?no matter t" Will " Veritas "allow me to co:ntnenci the above to his notice as a remedy likely to assuage the ill effects of this disease and to divert what he is pleased to call his mind into healthier and brighter channels. But how true his dictum that—" in order to know there must be on the one hand one who is capable of knowing, that is, a subject; and on the other, there must be something to be known, that is an object." The research that resulted in the unearthing of this deep aphorism must itself have been both deep and wide. I shall accept it as a maxim, and forthwith apply it. " Veritas " is the" subject"—i.e. the one to know, and the most melancholy conclusion from these metaphysical unsubstantialities—the 6' denial of God in nature"— the object, i.e. the thing to be known. But here I ask who ever in the course of this discussion denied the existence of God in nature? It must have been a very serious mis- reading that led to such an inference from what I have said, and I am not aware that anyone else is responsible for so unwarrantable an assertion.

From the plaintive tenor of his opening sentence, I infer that he is aggrieved that his question as to the an- thropomorphism of the Old Testament should have been treated so curtly. To my mind the attempt to prove the anthropomorphic character of the God of the Old Testa- ment is on a par with the need of proving that two and two are four. One demonstration should be enough for a lifetime, and every grown up person should be beyond the need of it.

But Ido not know that " Vetitas " is an adult, and judging from some of his remarks I am led to infer his non-arrival at years ot discretion. So I will give a few instances which bear out my assertion that " man has created this God out of his own imagination." Thus— " And saw that it was good." Now such an expression occurring in its connection is what we might expect frosn a human experimenter as expressive of satisfaction at the result of a successful experiment. True Omni- science would have known as a foregone conclusion,that it would succeed, and for such a Being tho expresaion ' would be merely a vain and needless reiteration. We have this naan-conceived God again in the character of experimenter in the Eden episode. Here again we have a case where the experiment would be quite logical and justifiable were the experimenter human and finite, as a means of gaining knowledge. But in an assumed All- wise and All-seeing Deity it would be merely a piece of purposeless cruelty, the result being to him foreknown and by him foredoomed. But the book is full of such evidencies of man-made-godism, the offspring of imagin- ations uncorrected and uncontrolled by what was then unattainable knowledge. For the history of the human race is typified by the history of the growth of the in- dividual. In youth the imaginative faculties are first to develope, and are in active play ere the judgment is ripe to act as moderator and director there- to. So most early writings are full of wild imaginary tales and fables, and notably is this the case with the 01'. Testament. Hence there is so much in it which we cannot accept along with our fuller knowledge of adverse and contradicting facts. But this anthorpo- morphism—this conception of the Deity as but a greater man with man-like faculties—kas filtered down to our own time.—l am, Sir, 3-ours, &c., JOHN PEERS. Penketh, 18tk May, 1891.

MR. DIONUM AND INACCURATE QUOTATIONS. Sir,—l thought tkis correspondence had now closed, but my combative and irrepressible friend having found a mare's nest, he must needs again rush into print. He finds that I have not given certain passages from Mosheim in extenso,and so he hastens to accuse use of naisquoting. But surely Mr. Dignum cannot have forgotten the diffi- culty both he and I have laboured under. We have endea- voured to compress into the compass of newspaper letters matter which has filled large books, and been the sub- ject of an extensive literature. The necessity of being brief has been a severe restriction upon both of us. A large portion of our letters nas consisted of quotations, and in the case of my quotations from Mositeini,l only gave pas- sages that I thought were essentib.l. Had I given the quo- tations mere fully my case would not have been weakened, nor Mr. Dignum's strengthened. Has Mr.Dignum made his case any better by giving the quotations more fully? I submit not. Mr. Dignum quoted the ancient fathers in support of his view that the Gospels are authentic, and he gave the idea that these fathers are reliable witnesses. I, on the other hand, dissented from this, and endea- voured to show that they are not reliable. In this, I think, I fully succeeded. Indeed, any- one who reads the first volume of Mosheim's Ecclesiasti- cal History will see that 1 have understated rather than overstated my case. The work abounds with passages affecting the character of the early Christian, and impu- ting fraud to early Christian writers. It was not neces- sary to give passa.gcs in full to prove my case. And in one instance, when I gave a quotation from the Rev. Charles Kingsley, touching the morals of the earliest Christian communities,l went to your office the following day.and expunged the passage for the sole reason that I knew it would greatly surprise and shock many of your readers. and I wished to avoid giving any of the unnecessary pain. You, sir, can bear witness to this. The author of " Ecce Homo "in one of his works says," An author has always to decide whether he will write short or long; and it is a choice of evils. If he writes long, the public will decline te read him; if he writes short, they will misun- derstand him."

Coming to the quotation from Dr. Westcott's "Intro- duction to the Gospels "—my only offence has been an involuntary one. I took the quotation from the Ency- clopedia Brittannica. Ido not possess a copy of this work, which is a very expensive one, and so I made notes from the copy in our Reference Library. In mak- ing these notes,l put down gospels for gospel—surely not a very heinious offence—but one that anyone might make. Until Mr. Dignum pointed it out, I was not aware of having made it. But Mr. Dignum says I did not give this quotation in full—that I ought to have added the words, "as given in the fragment of Mura- tori." But since Mr. Dignum has added these words, why has he not completed the passage? To have done so would only have made his case worse and worse. The passage has reference to the origin of the Fourth Gospel, and here it is in full. The origin of the Gospel is already legendary,' as given in the fragment if Muratori (A.D. 170). It is there said that being requested by his fellow disciples and bishops to writs, Jehn desired them to fast for three days, and then to relate to one another what revelation each had received either for er against the project. The same night it was revealed to Andrew, one of the apostles,that while all called (the past) to mind (or while all revised— cunetis recognoscentibus--)John should write everything in his own name." I think if I had given this quotation in full, it would not have improved Mr. Dignuin's posi- tion,but I thought it so childish that I disdained copying it, and only made a note of the quotation from Dr. Westcott, and unwittingly madq the mistake of saying gospels instead of gospel. A certain King Louis of France used to tell his knights never to argue with an infidel, but to run their swords through his belly. Mr. Dignum has certainly improved upon this, for he has argued with me first, and it is only when he finds himself hard hit and badly pressed that he trice to do me personal damage by impugning my veracity. However, I hop. we shall forget any little acerbities that have escaped during our little combat, and that we shall remain the same good friends we wen before.—Yours truly, JOIIN GANDY. --- STATE PRIESTISM : SOME STRANGE CONTRASTS.

Sir,—ln the Examiner of last Saturday, Mr. Robert Foulkes dares to impugn the priestly dogma of Apostolic Succession, and I heartily endorse his rejection of that ecclesiastical figment. In this and another letter I will, with your kind permission, take a wider range than your correspondent, and compare the reverend fathers of the State Church in their official capacity with the Master whose example they profess to follow, leaving your intelligent readers to draw their own conclusions.

1. The Founder of Christianity was Jesus of Naz- areth, a Jewish artizan of lowly birth, who followed the laborious occupation of a village carpenter to main- tain himself and assist the humble family with which he was connected. The arch priests of the Establishment are taken from a class who never work at all, but live I in idleness and luxury upon the produce of other men's toil. The bare idea of a working-man-Bishop would be simply intolerable to the aristocratic and very genteel people who could have us believe that they have got a monopoly of the Christian religion. 2. In the solitude of his mountain home, shut out from the noise and turmoil of the busy world,and associ- ating only with persons in the same lowly circumstances as himself, Jesus had ample time and opportunity for meditation and communion with his Heavenly Father, and thus acquired the physical, mental, and spiritual powers that were needed for his great work on earth. I need hardly tell your readers that the reverend fathers undergo no such training as this. It is not alone with nature and with nature's God that they are prepared for their offices. In our great seats of learning where rank and fashion do congregate, and where poor men have no place, the embryo rulers of the State Church are to be found conning musty tomes of Greek and Roman

div.head: TUI E EXAMINER, S A Itini)4, Y , MAY 23, 1.891
div.p: TUI E EXAMINER, S A Itini)4, Y , MAY 23, 1.891

mythology, and other literature in order that they may be thoroughly furnished unto all good works! And lest they should be wearied with such well doing, their course of study is agreeably enlivened with comic part- ies, boat racing, tcwn and gown rows, and other amuse- ments peculiar to university life. 3. Notwithstanding the poverty of his surrounaings, Jesus was the messenger sent trom Ged te redeem men from the power of the grave, and bring life and immor- tality to light. There was no doubt, no uncertainty about his mission, for it was attested by a series of miracles which constrained even his enemies te admit that God was with him. And when delivering his mess- age he spake as man never spako before,and the common people thronged around him wherever he went and heard him gladly. The reverend fathers hold no commission from God, and, therefore, have no signs of apostleship. They have no gift that is not common to all Christian men, and their utterances in the pulpit and elsewhere are entirely lacking in the power and demonstration of the Spirit 'which distinguishes the man of God from the mere hireling. In short their commission comes from earth and not from heaven. Mere creatures of the State, raised up to perform State functions, tl'ey owe their ap- pointments and emoluments to the Prime Minister of the nation, whose choice is almost invariably determined by political rather than by religious considerations. If the Premier be of the Gladstonian pattern, he will appoint prelates of his own politics to vote for his measures in the House of Lords ; if he be a Salisburyite only Bishops having the true Tory proclivities will receive his patron- age....

-I think the truthfulness of what I have advanced will not be controverted even by the most rabid supporter of State priestism. But it may be urged that, men and circumstances having wonderfully improved since the time of Jesus, a learned and aristocratic priesthood is required that Christianity may be introduced to the upper classes, and, through them, percolate to the poor people known to our modern religionists as "the lapsed masses." Well, we shall be willing to assent to this when it has been proved, not taken for granted, that the natural depravity of men of all sorts and conditions has been eradicated; and that the simple order of things set forth by the personal example of the Prophet of Nazareth has been revoked by divine authority. Until this is done, I must continue to regard the right reverend and most reverend fathers of the State Ct :eh as unnatural excre- scences that disfigure and injure the beautiful simplicity of the Christian ministry as exemplified in the life and teaching of Jesus.—Yours faithfully, lONA.
TOM MANN.

Torn Mann, the celebrated co-champiorz with John Burns and Ben Tillett, of the cause of Zile dock labourem and of the principles of trades-unionism, was born At Faleshill, in the War-gick- shire coal district, on April 15th, 1856. Ile commenced le battle of life, like many ,her celebritita, by working .s a pit boy. in 1870 he re- ioved with his family to .irmingliam, and in 1877 he

. In 1881 he became a member of the Amalgamated Engineers, and was subse- quently appointed representative of the Battersea branch of that organisation on the London Trades Council. Later on he was selected for the presid- ency of the Dock. Wharf, and Riverside, and Gen- eral Labourers' Union. It was during the year 1889 that his name was first brought into the prominence that has made it so famous, it being in this year that the great dock strike took place in London, the most determined and gigantic industrial struggle of which there is any record; and which was brought to a triumphant issue through the exertions of John Burns, Tom Mann, and Ben Tillett. On July 18th, 1890, at the instance of the Union of which Mann was president, some 500 men working at Hay's wharf, Bermondsey,. struck for extension of the time allowed for dinner, and for payment for the time, and Mr. Mann became a central figure in the support of this agitation. In consequence of men being employed at Hay's wharf in place of the strikers, the wharf was picketed by the latter ; and as the result Mann obtained, to some ex- tent what is so necessary to bring the celebrity of public agitators or reformers to a climax, the des- tinction of martyrdom, for he was arrested, and charged at the Southwark rolice Court with disor- derly conduct, and with causing a crowd to as- semble near the wharf, but was discharged. Mr. Mann has deservedly earned for himself a high place among industrial heroes, by his eloquence, his ability, and his indomitable energy;' and he has also shown himself a man of considerable lite- rary ability, and able to championise the cause of labour with pen as well as tongue, as evidenced by his contributions to the "Nineteenth Century," and other compositions. The fact that he has been selected as the representative of London labour on the recently formed Royal Commissionris of itself an abundant proof of his high qualifications as a leader of the working-classes. Mr. Mann is a con- ditional advocate of the adoption of the eight hours' system, and has just published a. pamphlet in which he recommends that a bill should be passed, leaving it to be decided by the local autho- rity according to the wish of the workers in, any trade in a district whether the eight hours. day shall be accepted by them or not. Mr: Mann con- cludes his pamphlet with a characteristic sen- tence :—" We are striving to realise the ideal that Thomas Carlyle yearned for, that John Ruskin has preached and worked for, and which the poet Burns bids us pray for."
MR. T. IV. LEGH, M P., AT ST. HELENS.

Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for the Newton Division, on Saturday lectured on "Travels Abroad," in the Cyril-st. Mission Room, St. Helens. The gathering was held un- der the auspices of the Eccleston Christ Church Working- men's Recreation Club. Mr. Legh, who was well received, described a personal journey through Egypt, and spoke of the manners and customs of the Egyptians. In conclusion, he said there was an uneasy section of English people who,since the British occupation of Egypt in 188 E, had advocated the withdrawal ol British troops. But he was perfectly certain that a visit to Egypt would prove to anyone the necessity for the reten- tion of the troops in that country. The Egyptians were now governed better,and were not subjected to the same tyrannical rule as they were formerly. To his wind the fact of the matter was that if Egypt was net occupied by England it would be occupied by some other power, and it was absolutely necessary for English interests that the English troops should remain in Egypt. (Applause.) During the evening a miscellaneous concert was held.

div.head: ST. HELENS WATER SUPPLY:
div.p: ST. HELENS WATER SUPPLY:
STARTING OF NEW WORKS.

On Thursday the Mayor of St. Ile-len—a (Councillor E. Johnson) formally started the engine of the new St. Helens Corporation Water Works, at Kirkby, and in doing so practically completed a great water scheme which had been in course of developement since 1882. Up to the year named the water supply of St. Helens was of a very inadequate character and the necessity of obtaining a more serviceable source of supply, and one of vastly increased yield- ing capacity was forced upon the authorities. At first a site near Cronton was favoured but strenuous opposi- tion was experienced in that quarter, and the Knowsley and Kirkby districts were finally selected for recom- mendation as the best sites for the boring of water wells. Alderman J. Mcßryde, chairman of the Water Committee, and Mr. D. M. F. Gaskin, C.E., the borough water engineer, made a preliminary examination of the district and their conclusions as to its adaptability with its red sandstone formation for water supply purposes were subsequently confirmed. after exhaustive investigations by Professor HuII,F.G.S., and Mr. C. E. de Rance, F.G.S., Parliamentary sanction to tho purchase of the sites and the water undertaking 'of the Corporation was subsequently obtained, and the bill,which contained clauses for the protection of the in- terests of Lords Derby and Sefton, the adjoining land I owners, received the Royal assent on July 24th, 1882. It was decided to carry out the works at Knowsley, in the I first instance, and the then Mayor (Councillor Richard Pilkington) cut the first sod of the new scheme on the 28th October, 1882. The works were completed four years later, and Alderman Mcßryde started the engines which were formally named "James Mcßryde," on the 11th of June, 1886. On that day Alderman Mcßryde also cut the first sod of the Kirkby works, and the foundation stone of the building was laid by Alderman D. McKechnie, Mayor, on July 31st, 1888. The starting of the engines at Kirkby was the occasion of Thursday's proceedings, and that cere- mony signalised the completion of the water scheme. The new works consists of two 11 feet wells, each 150 feet in depth, connected by a heading of 9 feet by 6 fret, , and a bore hole, 24 inches in diameter diminishing to 18 'inches. sunk from the bottom of one of the wells to a total depth of 510 feet from the surface of the ground. This work was completed in September, 1887 by Mr. J. Villiers and Messrs. R. Daglish and Co., St. Helens. sup- plied the pumping engines, boilers, Sec. Messrs. J. and T. Yearsley St. Helens), had the contract for the erec- tion of the superstructure and 'Mr. William Harrison (St. Helens), supplied the engine foundations and boiler seatings. The parliamentary estimate of the cost of the entire scheme was £95,000, and what has proved a happy circumstance to the Council and ratepayers of St. Helens the work has beer carried out at a much less cost. The Knowsley station cost £20,249 and the Kirkby station £18,621. To these charge 3 are added the cost of the pumping mains from Kirkby to Ecxleston Hill and Brown Edge reservoirs, £18,244 ; parliamentary expenses £3,591, compensation mains, up to the present time, £2,593 and mortgage stamps £358, making the total expenditure £63,655. This is £31,345 below the esti- mate, which however included £17,000 for duplicate engines and houses. These have not yet been erected and may not be required for many years to come. The whole of the works have been carried out under the personal supervision and control of Mr. Gaskin, the borough water engineer, and to that gentleman with Alderman J. Mcßryde the Corporation and town of St. Helens are indebted for the successful termination of the vast undertaking. From its first conception nearly ten years ago to the end of yesterdays proceedings, there has been but one trifling accident and there has been neither loss of life nor injury to the limbs of any of the workmen. The water obtained at Knowsley averages one million gallons per twenty-four hours and it is estimated that the Kirby wells will yield about the same quantity with an additional two and a half million gallons from the bore hole. It is an interesting fact that during the dry season of 1888 the St. Helens Corporation supplied some 393 million gallons of water from the Kirkby wells to the Liverpool Corpor- ation reservoir at Prescot. Temporary engines and mains were laid down and after the payment of all costs the St. Helsns Corporation had a credit balance of £5,488 on the undertaking. The consumption of water in St. Helens and the quantity required for manufacturing purposes has enormously increased during re- cent years and is a striking testimony to the progress of the town. In 1876 when the present water engineer was appointed to the office, the average daily consumption for all purpases was one and a half million gallons and the total supply 547 millions, 1890 the daily average had increased to over three million gallons and the total supply to one thousand and fifty-one million gallons. The increased consumption has been of an annual rapid growth, and whilst in 1889, the supply for manufacturing purposes amounted to 424,848,000 gallons,the quantity last year reached the unprecedented I total of 519,739,000 gallons or an increase of 94.890.000 gallons in twelve months. So rapid, indeed, is the con- sumption of water on the increase, that a scheme for a new and still more extensive water supply is becoming a necessity, and we understand the authorities are al- ready moving in the matter. On Thursday forenoon the Mayor and members of the Council assembled at the Town Hall, and were driven in landaus to Kirby, including a ride through Knowsley Park, the fine residence of Lord Derby. The new works attracted general admiration, and the Mayor started the engines amid loud cheers. Alderman Mcßryde per- formed the "baptismal" ceremony, the engines being named "Edward Johnson." The company then drove to the Knowsley Pumping Station, where the Mayor en- tertained the following private guests to luncheon : Alderman Harrison, Mcßryde, McKechnie, Wilcock, and Cook. Councillors Leach, W. H. Foster, Morgan, Hunter, Beecham, Massey, Gaskell, John Forster, Brown, Walsh, Thomson, Nuttall, Johnson, (West Sutton) ; Mearns, Jones, Foote, Martin, Green and McLachlan ; Messrs. Jeeves tTown clerk), G. T. Lee (chief clerk), D. M. F. Gaskin (water engineer), Broom (borough survey- or), A. Lancaster (librarian), S. Glover (gas manager), Dr. Robertson (assistant medical officer), Colonel Windus, Rev. J, T. Preece, Messrs. E. Baxter, J. Yearsley, R. B. Daglish, H. L, Riley, C. Culshaw, F. Dromgeele,J. Dux- bury, and G. Marsh. The toasts of " The Queen," "The Chairman of the Water Committee," "The Mayor," "The Borough Water Engineer," and " The Contractors" were honoured.

div.head: EARLBSTOWN RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: EARLBSTOWN RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB.

The annual general meeting of the members of the above club was held at the Prince of Wales Hotel, Earlestown, on Friday evening. Mr. T.Egan presided, and there was a large number of members present. Mr. G. Shinn submitted a statement of accounts, which showed a satisfactory state of , things, the season closing with a balance of ..C1 10s. Bd. in hand. The balance sheet was adopted. The election of officers for next season was then proceeded with,and resulted as follows :—President, Mr. H. F. Gooch; vice-presidents, Dr. Patterson, Messrs. S. Williams, R. Lythgoe, and W. Melling; committee, Messrs. T. Pearson, R. Wright, J. Crank, J. Lowe, A. Lane, T. Egan, J. Williams, W.Charnley, ' and J. Catterall : treasurer, G. Edwards; hon. sec., Mr. J. Slinn ; assistant sec., Mr. W. Croft ; captain Ist team, Mr. A. Williams; vice-captain, Mr. G. Baker; captain 2nd team, Mr. G. Conway. Votes of thanks were accorded the retiring secretary, Mr. C. H. Lea, the captains, and the chairman. Fixtures for next season have already been arranged with, Runcorn, Wigan Temperance, Trantnere Wanderers, West Leigh, Widnes "A," Frodsham, St. Helens "A," St. Helens Recs. "A." Several matches have also been arranged for the second team.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN' AT RUNCORN, Szc. BY AN OCCASI^NAL CORRESPONDENT:
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN' AT RUNCORN, Szc. BY AN OCCASI^NAL CORRESPONDENT:

Mr. B. G. Jenkins F.R.A.S. is the author of an astronomical almanack and chart, which forseasts ths state of the weather for the present year,. based on scientific observations maae. A confiding public has enabled a second edition of 10,040.t0 be issued, and doubtless these thousands,believing their oracie, have been anticipating a "dry and warm month." There certainly has not been much wet, but warmth! Ugh, it makes one shiver, even when beside a warm fire to think of the biting east wind that is blowing outside, laden with its crop of " germs " or " microbes "of influeaza, to say nothing of the snow that paid us a visit last week end. Lowell knew something about it when he wrote May is a pious fraud of the almanack ; A ghastly parody of real spring, Shaped out of snow and breathed with eastern winds. I commend these lines to Mr. Jenkins as a guide in. his future predictions of May weather. Whit-Monday retains its hold upon the affection of the Runcorn people as a holiday,and they turned out in thousands to see the " Clubs " walk in the morning and the Sunday scholars in the afternoon. The display of the Schools was as usual. a very fine one, and was to some extent an index of the work they are carrying on amongst the 3 oung peo- ple. The clubs, however,only demonstrate in a half hearted fashion. Out of nearly 20 Friendly Societies. in Runcorn, only four were represented, and there was not more than 80 members in the ranks of any one of these. If the thing is worth doing at all it is worth doing well, and in future years a conference of officials might arrange a show which would be worth corning miles to witness, and in future, too. pipes might with advantage be refused admission to the ranks. It did not accord with the eternal fitness of things to see a man dressed in his Sunday best,with a bright coloured sash across his breast, assidously sucking a short clay pipe. It didn't seem part of the demonstration.

The Runcorn Board of Guardians were, on Tues- day, again engaged in endeavouring to ascertain the cause of the increase in the amount of the poor rate for the current half year. The Clerk produced the figures asked for by Mr. Stokes, but they were of no avail in cutting the Gordian knot, and he was asked to make a comparative statement &bow- ing the expenditure of the Union for the past- three or five years. All this, however, is by the way. The Guardians blame the County Council for this increased call upon the pockets of th 4 ratepayers, and us "poor, poor farmers" are filled with wrath at that youthful institution;and the members repre- senting agricultural districts will find a difficulty in retaining their seats at the next election.

Fortunately, Mr. Speakman, one of the Runcorn representatives on the County Council, was present at the meeting on Tuesday, and his presence had restraining influence upon the denunciations of the members; but Mr. Parr who never wraps up his meaning, said he saw no benefit that the county had yet received from the formation of the Council. The explanation given by Mr. Speakman of the cause of the increase of the county rate was one which will be received with great regret. The trade of the river Weaver is falling off, and in consequence the Weaver Trustees are unable to make their usual contribution of £lO,OOO to £15.000 a year to ease the rates; hence the heavier call upon, the ordinary ratepayers. This reduction in the revenue of the Weaver is placed at the door of the Salt Unian;, who, it is alleged, are making less salt at Northwich, and more at other places than was formerly the case, and Mr. Speakman held out no hopes that the Weaver Trust would be able to resume their eon- tribut.on to the County Funds. However this does not account for the whole of the increase in the rates, and the Guardians were referred for informa- tion to the financial budget presented by the county treasurer a fortnight ago. The Guardians will re- sume the discussion at the next meeting.

div.head: CORONATION OF THE MAY QUEEN AT HAYDOCK.
div.p: CORONATION OF THE MAY QUEEN AT HAYDOCK.

On Saturday afternoon the village of Ilaydock was oa fete on the occasion of the coronation of the May Queen. The arrangements werenarried out by a Committee formed by the Rev. Mr. Bartram, and consisting of Messrs. E. Bradshaw tsecretary), J. Matthews, T. Marsh, T.. Derbyshire, J. Heaton, T. ' Heaton, J. Ralphe, J. Pulfer, T. Hazeldine, Mrs. Bar- tram, Mrs. T. Heaton, Mrs. J. Heaton, and Miss Davies. The young lady chosen for royal honours was Miss Griffith. The maids of honour were Misses M. A. Heaton, May Heaton,Ellen Heaton, Ada Reaton,and E.Derbyshire. The crown bearer was T. Beatty, and the sceptre bearer James Dearden. The procession started from the field at 3 o'clock and proceeded to the "Huntsman" and from thence to the "Ram's Head," returning to the field where the Queen was crowned at a quarter to five. The pro- cession was headed by a boy dressed as Buffalo Bill, then came the Havdoek Brass Band, after which followed the Queen and her maids in an open carriage, the remainder being made up of flower girls, colliers, butchers, bakers, milk-maids, hospital nurses, servant girls, soldiers, and niggers After the coronation there was the May pole dance, which was executed in a marvellous manner, con- sidering that the children had only had eight days' prac- tice. Following the dance were numerous games, while the band played for dancing. The children who formed the procession, which was of an undenominational char- acter, were regaled with tea, one portion of which was provided by Mr. Griffith, and the other by Mr. Forshaw. Hams were given by Mr. Andrews, and Mr. T. Harrison, of the "Ram's Head," provided beer, lemonade &c., for the band.

The building committee, who have had under con- sideration the plans for the erection of the new church for the parish of Sutton, met on Friday night and de- cided to accept the tender of Mr. S. Webstor,centractort of Bootie, for the erection of the church.

div.p: LTMM.

FRIENDLY SOCIETY DEMONSTRATION.—The annual pro- cession of the AnciEnt Order of Druids took place on Monday. Starting from the Nag's Head the procession went round Statham, Broom Edge, and Oughtrington, headed by the band in connection with the Church of England Temperance Society.

Trn PorimkrioN OF LYlol.—The recent census re- turns for Lvmm show that the population of the town- ship to be 4,995. It had been hoped that the number would have been 5,000. The census of 1851 was 3,156 ; in 1861, 3,769 ;in 1871, 4,541 ;in /881, 4,665. It will thus be seen that the increase each decade was 613, 772, 114., and 330. ACCIDENT IN THE STREHT.--On Monday, a conveyance from Warrington was passing through Lvmns, when the driver pulled up. A woman who was skiing in the front struck the horse, to make it go on. The animal sprang forward, throwing one of the'vromen in the back seat out of the vehicle. Fortunately, she was not much in- jured, but being frightened, she went home by train. DRUNIC.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Thursday morning, before Dr. Brabazon, Bernard Brady, of War- rington, was charged with being drunk and disorderly In Lymm on the previous day.—Police-sergeant Wynne proved the case. It appeared the prisoner attempted to jump into the canal at the Iron Bridge when being shown the way to Warrington.—He was fined 24. 6d. including costs.

A JOCULAR DRUNKAID.—On Tuesday, before Dr. Bra- bazon Harry Smith was ohargedwith being drank and disorderly at Heatley the previous evening. P.C. Beb- ing,ton said the prisonnr was very drunk, and was quarrelling with people. When taken into custody and asked for his name he replied " Jack Robinson." On tho following morning, however, he gave his name as Harry Smith.—He was fined 55., or in default imprisonment for seven days. Defendant went to. prison. . .

CONGREGATIONAL Cuunca.—The annual services in connection with the Church and Home Missionary Society were held on Sunday. The Rev. J. Howard Fry, Sand- bach, preached in the morning. A children's service was held in the afternoon. In the evening a public meet- ing,' wa9 held, the chair being taken by Mr. Richard Dut- ton, in place of Mr. Gerard N. Ford, of. Manchest.er, who was unable to attend. The Rev. J: H: Fry delivered a most interesting address en Home Mission work. A col- lection was taken after each service in aid of the funds. of the society.

STELIXG COPPER—The two young men,. James Dunn and William Raymond, who were apprehended at War- rington, by D.S. Monaghan, on a charge of stealing a quantity of copper rivets from the Ship, Canal Company on the 15th or 16th of May, and handed' over to P.C. Buchanan, Lymm, were brought up before Dr. Brabazon on Tuesday, and remanded until' the following day. Prisoners were brought up in custody on remand on Wednesday, and further remanded on bail'in two sureties of £lO each too appear at the Altrincham Petty Sessions on Monday morning. CROWNING TNT? QUERN AT LIVIL—The village of Lynn!: was en fête on Thursday afternoon, the occasion being the coronation of the Band of Hope QUeen, for the townships of Lymm and Oughtrington. The weather was unfavourable ;but in spite of this, there was a large attendance, estimated at from three to fbur thousand children of various Sunday schools,daintily:attired. The Band of Hope Queen this year was Miss Maggie Gibben, who was attended by her maids of honour and train bearer in their carriage. The crowning, ceremony took place in a field near the Congregational Church. After the ceremony the children dispersed to their severa? schools, where tea was provided at the expense of the committee, and in the evening many attractions were placed before the public in the field where the crowning took place.

LIVERPOOL PROVIsIONS, PRID A.Y.—The beef and pork markets rule quiet, without alteration in values. A quiet tone has prevailed, and prices show some irregularity. hut no decided change can be reported. In hams short outs meet a moderate demand; but long cuts sell slowly. Shoulders are quiet but steady. Cheese meets a moderate sale-at the quo- tations. Batter is without special feature. Lardt is thedurn easier. The crews of the Norwegian barques Condor, from Liverpool for Finland, and;Gang-ev Rolf, from CardiT.for Stockholm, have arrived at Shields, and report a terrible storm in the North Sea, and the abandonment of their vessels after fruitless endeavours to keep them afloat. THE STRIKE OF LONDON TAILORS. Up to one o'clock yesterday afternoon, 6,000 men hadi reported themselves to the Dendon Strike Committee: The number will, it is expected,. be eoesiderably in- creased. About 200 men and women in the employ of o well-known Regent-sb. firm of' tailors, who struck on Thursday, have decided to resume woris,their employers having acceded t 5 their demands% MR. PARNELL IN3BELYAST. There was a slight disturbance at the rati9way termißus on Mr. Parnell's arrival at one o'olock yesterday, in Bel- fast. His supporters turned up in.strong force and gave him a hearty reception,but a too enthusiastic M•Carthy- ite, who assumed a threatening attitude towards the hon. member, was promptly arrested" by a detective ser- geant, who detained him until the crowd dispersed. At Drogheda and Goraghwood addresses- were presented to Mr. Parnell,who brießy responded. DEATH OF SIR R. N. FOWLER, M.P.

Sir Robert Nicholas Fowler, Bart, M‘P., died suddenly yesterday morning from heart disease. He was senior member for the City of London, and was twice Lord Mayor. He was 72 years age, and a member of the firm of Messrs. Dimsdale, Fowler, Barnard;, and Dimsdale, bankers. In 1886, Sir Robert was- returnee to Parlia- ment unopposed, and at the previous election, when there was a contest, he headed the poll by a- I.rge majority. Sir Robert had been unwell for some-time, but dis- charged his duties up to the time of the rising of the House. During Thursday night, however,. he became suddenly worse at his residence in, Harley-st., and expired before his medical attendant could be sum- moned.

div.head: TFIE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.
div.p: TFIE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.

Mr. Gladstone, Mrs. Gladstone, and Mr.. Henry Glad- stone left London yesterday morning I& Hawarden.. The right hon. gentleman appeared weak, and walked from the carriage to the train with the aid of, feaning on the arm of his wife. The saloon was- heated to the temperature of the room in which Mr. Gladstone had passed the last few days. Mt. Gladstone-,. Mr. John Mor- ley, and Mr. Justin McCarthy will none-of them be suffi- ciently recovered from the effects of the influenza to ad- dress the annual meeting of the Women's Liberal Federa- tion in the St. James's Hall, on the 27.k1i inst., a* pre- viously announced.

_ Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs. Gladston& and other members of the family, arrived at 111v:warden about a quarter-past four o'clock for the' afternoon. The train passed through Liverpool-road Staticre shortly before four.
ANOTHER DRA'PH.
Sir Vincent Corbett, Bart., died yesterday to orn g from influenza, at his seat, Acton Reynoid Hall, near Shrewsbury. THE FUNERAL OF LORD EDWARD' CAVENDISH.

. - A large number of gentlemen left St. Pancras yesterday, to attend the funeral of Lord Edward Cavendish at Chatsworth, including General Ellis,- representing the Prince of Wales, and Sir Henry- James.- A correspondent telegraphs :—Rain is falling heaviiy at Chatsworth Park, but large crowds assembled to wit- ness the interment of Lord Edward Cavendish ;.business practically suspended throughout the'/stern Division of Derbyshire. At 10.30 a short service was held in the chapel at Chatsworth House. The funeral procession left the house 'a half-past two, headed by the tenantry, after whom came the hearse,. family household servants, and deputations. At the church gate the coffin was removed frain,the hearse and borne into the church on the shoulders of. six workmen. The coffin was of polished oak, with:, heavy brass furnishings, bearing the inscription—" Edward Caven- dish, born January 28th, 1848; died May 1.8, 11391.." The full length of the tc,p of the coffin was covered with flowers.

The theory is now strengthened that the knife Ind saw were only used in dismembering the body,.and some im- portance is given to the discovery on Sunday of a razor near the scsne of the murder.
A tool dealer has identified Conway:- as the man to whom he sold the knife and saw which, have been, al- ready discovered.
The inquest on the boy Martin svas,opened yesterday,. and adjourned until Thursday,after the father had given, formal evidence of identification.

At the close of ths inquest the prisoner, Conway was taken before the magistrates. Evidence was given that a pair of trousers belonging to the pritsoner, which wero• much stained with blood, were foundat his lodgings. He was then remanded.

GREAT PRIZE FIGHT IN A-AERICA. JACKSON v. CORBETT.

Telegrams, dated San Francisco, yesterday morning,, give brief details of the great prize fight between Peter Jackson, the coloured pugilist who created such a. favourable impression in this country some timeage,and the American heavy-weight, Corbett, who achieved fame by his comparatively recent d•A!iat of Jake Kilrain. In the States the match was looked for- ward to with considerable interest, and it was gene- rally expected that a long andtstubborn battle would' be fought. Anticipations have been fully realised, for after sixty-one desperate and determined round& the. referee had to declare it a draw. Up to, the 41st round,. aec*rding to a Dalziel telegrran,the contest was in favour- of Jackson. A later Central News telegram, states that the battle continued desperately and that,the men being physically unfit to continue, the directars of the club. in, which the match took place decided after the sixty-first round that it must cease, and the referee- declared' it a draw.

TEE LAND Punentasi BlLL—Committee on the Land Purchase Bill was resumed, Mr. Chance resumed the debate upon the second reading of his clause relating to advances in the cams of sales by- mortgagees. Mr. McCartney opposed the clause. He ob4,ected to special provision being made for the mortgagees, who, he argued, were- in tiee same position as landlords. Mr. Maurice Healy and Mr. T. Healy supported the clause. Thee Committee divided, when Mr. Chance's clause was rejocted by la votes to 40. Discussion upon ether amendments followed. A further amendment moved by Mr. Chance making certain mcdifications in tho clause regulating the application of section 20 of the Land Law Ireland Act, 1887. relating to advances was agreed to. Mr. Mathew Kenny moved a new clause providing certain rules for the regulation of 3uh- Tenancies. On a division the clause was negatived by 98 to 45.

SAD DEATH or • Wom•w.—On Tuesday morning a married woman who resides at Golborne, named Vas- worth, died under peculiarly sad circumstances. On Fri- day last the death of her father took place, and on Mon- day she attended the funeral. From all apearanees at this time she was apparently in her usual health. Ilswever, about seven o'clock on Tuesday morning she was taken, suddenly ill, and a messenger was sent to summon medi- cal aid. Although the messenger was not long awayvet before the doctor could arrive a second messenger was despatched, with the intelligence that she had expired.. Ske leaves a young family, and the deepest sympathy is manifested by the inhabitants of ciptizarp% at the, loss which they have sustained.

ST. HELENS VOLUNTEERS IN CIMP.
TWO MEN DISMISSED.

The members cif the 2nd V.. 13., South Lannelire Regiment have spent the present week under can- vas, at Rhyl. The position of the camp w:r_. an excellent one, being about a quarter of an hont's march from the town, and five minutes' walk from' the sea. The corps assembled at the headquarter on Friday evening, and having been formed its marching order, started for the station. They were headed by eleven members of the cyclists' section: under the command of Lieutenant F. White. The men walked by the aide of their machines to which their guns. were attached, and they looked very smart. Then followed the band, under the conductorship of Bandmaster Hail, and as they proceeded through the they played ai selection of lively airs. Oh arrival at the station they were drawn up on the platform, and the special train having been brotro.ht in they took their places. There' was about 250, men in thcr train. Rhyl was reached at ten &retook, and the men at once marched to the camp, • where thery were supplied with. seppex, which was awaiting them. The camp wa* ,ande: the command of Colonel W. W. Pilkington, and the other officers were Lieut..-Coloxel R. Pilkington, Liezt.-COlonel White, Captain Woleenden and Lieut. Robinsor4,Major McTear and Lieat. McTivar, ; Major Cook, Captain Dickenson, and, Lieuts. Thomson , and A. Pilkington,Captain Shaw and Lieut. Flopgoad, Lieut. R. W. H. Thomas, Captain Lewis,- Caprain a•rrd Adjutant Jacobs, Surgeon Knowles,- Sergeant-Majr Tyson, and Quarterauster Balshavr. Gb Saturday. evert- ing 51 men arrived erom•St. Helens. C!-h Friday Saturday and Sunday, the weather was ce a very in.. cricment character, ani'many of the menisuffered fromi cold and were under znedical treatment: On Menday the weather was grand., and during the :norfsing a large number of excursioniats from St. Helens visited the. camp and appeared ta•balnuch interested ie the anera- tieno. When the mon 'mustered for the second parade; the Colonel announced that he had a very painful duty to pc:form, and that wastb dismiss two on frora.the. corps for misconduct. The men in question were escorted from the guard tent and brought before the Colonel, who expressed his :egret at the dutritiev had to. perform, but said they must.have disipline,s-rd he would+ have it. He then dismissedthe two men,. remarking. that it was no disgrace to ale corps or to tie company' of' which they were members, but to the two men them- selves. The drill was then prceeeded with. There were" on parade 320 men of all ranks, including 264 rank and! fire,.22. non-commissioned offiners, 20 band and!bglers„, and'.l4 members of the cyclist corps. In they afternoon, themen had sports, prizes being awarded in a number of.! events, consisting of whAlbarrow races, a 7.20" yards. handicap, etc. On Monday evening about sirty of the • men-returned to St. Helens, having completed three days. in camp,and others returned on Tuesday and Wednesday. • On Thursday the camp broke up.

D UNCORN UNION, FEMALE NURSE WANTED.—The 1.1) Guardians of this Union are desirous of receiving applications for the appointment of a Nurse for their Infirm- avy. Applicants must be between 25 and 40 years of age,and Ise single women or widows without encumbrance and have a knowledge of midwifery. The person appointed will be re- quired to attend to the sick inmates to superintend theclean- ing of the wards under her care and generally to assist and obey all the orders and directions of the Gnardians and the Master and Matron of the Workhouse. The salary will be £25 per annum with rations,lodgings,washing,and uniform and £4 per annum in lieu of beer; and the apnointment will be sub- ject to the approval of the Local Government Board, and determined by either party on one month's notice. Applica- tions in candidates own handwriting, stating age and , experience, accompanied by recent testimonials to be sent to Imeon or before the 28th instant. By order. JOHN ASHTON, Clerk to the Guardians. Runcorn, 21 May, 1891.

Home comforts and every care is taken of young people placed at this college by their parents to be taught. Write for Prospectus to MADAME DRAKE, Norwich. PRESCOT UthON.-APPOINTMENT OF CLERK. The Guardians of the Prescot Union intend at their meeting on the 4th June next to proceed to the election of a properly qualified person, not more than 45 years of age, to act as CLERK too the Guardians. Candidates must be prac- tically acquainted with the laws and proceedings relating to the administration of the Poor Law Union Assessment Com- mittee Acts, Public Health Acts, and the Elementary Educa- tion Act s,and be fully competent to keep the various accounts In strict accordance with the orders of the Local Government Board, to examine, check, and be responsible for the accuracy of all accounts, to prepare all returns required by the Local Government Board and the Guardians. conduct the official correspondence of the Board and to supervise all the office arrangements. The person elected will hold the offices of Clerk to the Union Amessment Committee, Rural Sanitary Authority, and School Attend- ance Committee and will also receive the appointment of Superintendent Registrar. lie will be required to devote the whole of his time to the duties of the several offices and will not be permitted to take any other public position. Salary £3OO per annum out of which sum the necessary office staff must be provided. Other emoluments estimated at £3OO. Security to the amount of £5OO to be given. Applications stating age accompanied with copies of testimonials to be addressed to the Chairman of the Board, Union Offices, Whiston, and sent in by 10 o'clock on Monday, the Ist June next. marked "Clerkship." Cs.nvassing the Guardians will be a disqualification. Selected candidates will have notice to attend on the day of election. By Order, A. F. MANN. Acting Clerk. Union Offices, Whiston, 21st May. 1891.
